APPEND.summary: APPEND adds a string to the end of a key's existing string value, creating the key if it is missing. It returns the resulting string length.
APPEND.explanation: APPEND adds the supplied string to the existing string value at key. When the key is absent, Redis creates it with an empty starting value, then returns the resulting string length.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The string to append to the existing value.

APPEND.returns: Integer reply: the length of the string after the append operation.

example.title: Append fragments to a string
example.code:
redis-cli <<'EOF'
DEL greeting
APPEND greeting "Hello"
APPEND greeting " world"
GET greeting
EOF
example.explanation: Creates the key on the first append, adds the second fragment, and reads the resulting string.

useCases.title: Incremental string construction
useCases.scenario: Build a message or text buffer incrementally by adding fragments to one Redis string.

useCases.title: Compact fixed-size samples
useCases.scenario: Store fixed-width samples consecutively in one compact value for lightweight time-series data.

interview.question: What does APPEND do when the key does not exist?
interview.answer: APPEND takes a key and a string value, adding that value after the key's current string. If the key is missing, Redis creates it, and the command returns the string's length after modification.
interview.followUp: What happens if the key contains a non-string value? The command requires a string value, so it cannot append to another Redis data type.

interview.question: What is the syntax and basic behavior of APPEND?
interview.answer: Its syntax is `APPEND key value`. The value is appended to the existing string, or used as the initial content of a newly created key.
interview.followUp: How can a caller verify the resulting content? Use GET on the same key after APPEND, as in the documentation example.

interview.question: What does APPEND return, and what is its time complexity?
interview.answer: APPEND returns an integer equal to the length of the string after the append. Its amortized complexity is O(1) when the appended value is small, because Redis grows its dynamic string capacity efficiently.
interview.followUp: Why is the complexity amortized rather than unconditionally constant? Reallocations can require additional work, especially as the stored string grows.

keyPoints: APPEND extends an existing Redis string by placing the supplied text at its end.
A missing key is initialized as an empty string before the supplied value is added.
The `key` argument identifies which string value Redis should modify.
The `value` argument supplies the text that Redis adds after the current contents.
The result is the updated string length, expressed as an integer reply.
For small appended fragments, repeated appends have amortized constant-time complexity.
Fixed-size samples can be concatenated into a compact string representation, such as a simple time series.
gotchas: The operation is amortized O(1) only when the appended fragment is small; this does not mean every append has constant cost for arbitrarily large input.

AUTH.summary: AUTH authenticates the current Redis connection. It accepts a password, or a username and password when Redis ACLs are used.
AUTH.explanation: AUTH checks the password for the current Redis connection. With ACLs, you can also provide a username. If you omit the username, Redis uses the default user. A successful check returns OK; a failed check returns an error.

parameters.name: username
parameters.description: Optional ACL username. If omitted, Redis uses the default user.

parameters.name: password
parameters.description: Required authentication password. With requirepass, this is the server password; with ACLs, it is the user's password.

AUTH.returns: Returns the OK status when authentication succeeds. Returns an error when authentication fails.

example.title: Authenticate with a password
example.code: AUTH "temp-pass"
example.explanation: Authenticate the current connection with a server password.

useCases.title: Authenticate with a server password
useCases.scenario: A Redis server uses the requirepass configuration option.

useCases.title: Authenticate an ACL user
useCases.scenario: Redis 6.0 or later uses ACL users with separate credentials.

useCases.title: Unlock a connection
useCases.scenario: A client has connected but Redis requires authentication before normal commands.

interview.question: What does AUTH do?
interview.answer: AUTH authenticates the current connection. Use AUTH password for a server protected by requirepass, or AUTH username password with Redis ACLs. A successful authentication returns OK.
interview.followUp: What username does the one-argument form use with ACLs? It uses the implicit default username, named default.

interview.question: What is the AUTH syntax?
interview.answer: The command syntax is AUTH [username] password. The username was added in Redis 6.0. The password is required in every form.
interview.followUp: What happens if the password is wrong? Redis returns an error, and the client must try another password.

interview.question: What is the time complexity of AUTH?
interview.answer: AUTH has time complexity O(N), where N is the number of passwords defined for the user. This applies when Redis checks the user's configured passwords.
interview.followUp: Why should passwords be long? Redis can try many passwords in parallel, so short passwords are easier to attack.

keyPoints: AUTH authenticates the current Redis connection.
Use the password-only form when the server uses requirepass.
Redis 6.0 and later support username-and-password authentication through ACLs.
The username is optional. If missing, Redis authenticates the default ACL user.
A correct password returns OK and lets the connection run commands.
A wrong password returns an error.
AUTH takes O(N) time, where N is the user's number of defined passwords.
gotchas: Redis can test many passwords quickly. Use a strong, long password.
With ACLs, AUTH password uses the default username when you omit the username.

BITCOUNT.summary: BITCOUNT returns the number of 1 bits in a Redis string. It can inspect the whole value or an inclusive range of bytes or bits.
BITCOUNT.explanation: BITCOUNT reads a Redis string and returns how many bits have value 1. You can count the whole string or an inclusive range, using byte positions by default or bit positions with BIT.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the Redis string key.

parameters.name: start
parameters.description: The first position in the range. It is a byte offset by default, or a bit offset with BIT.

parameters.name: end
parameters.description: The last position in the range, inclusive. It is a byte offset by default, or a bit offset with BIT.

parameters.name: unit
parameters.description: Selects byte offsets with BYTE or bit offsets with BIT. BYTE is the default.

BITCOUNT.returns: An integer equal to the number of bits set to 1.

example.title: Count set bits
example.code:
SET mykey "foobar"
BITCOUNT mykey
BITCOUNT mykey 1 1
BITCOUNT mykey 5 30 BIT
example.explanation: Store a string, count all its set bits, count one byte, then count a bit range.

useCases.title: Count active days
useCases.scenario: Store one bit per day for a user and count the days with value 1.

useCases.title: Count matching users
useCases.scenario: Use bitmap positions for user IDs and count how many users match a condition.

useCases.title: Count a large bitmap incrementally
useCases.scenario: Process a large bitmap in ranges and add the returned counts in the client.

interview.question: What does BITCOUNT do?
interview.answer: BITCOUNT counts the bits set to 1 in a Redis string and returns an integer. Without a range, it examines the complete string.
interview.followUp: How can you count only part of the value? Pass inclusive start and end positions. They are byte positions unless BIT is provided.

interview.question: How are ranges interpreted?
interview.answer: The syntax is BITCOUNT key [start end [BYTE | BIT]]. BYTE is the default unit for start and end; BIT makes them bit offsets.
interview.followUp: What does a negative offset mean? It indexes from the end, where -1 is the final byte or bit for the selected unit.

interview.question: What is the performance cost?
interview.answer: The command has O(N) time complexity, where N is the amount of data examined. For large bitmaps, the documentation suggests counting ranges incrementally or maintaining a separate counter.
interview.followUp: Why might a separate counter help? It avoids scanning the bitmap for every total-count request, and the documentation notes that a small Lua script can update it atomically.

keyPoints: It counts bits whose value is 1 in a Redis string.
With no range, the command checks the entire string.
Range positions use byte indexes unless you choose another unit.
Add BIT to interpret the range as bit offsets.
The BYTE and BIT selector is available starting in Redis 7.0.0.
The result is an integer containing the number of set bits.
gotchas: A missing key returns 0 instead of an error.
The end position is included in the range.
Negative positions count backward from the end when using the matching index unit.

Bitmap.summary: Redis bitmaps use string values as compact sequences of bits. Set or read individual positions, count enabled bits, and combine bitmap keys with BITOP.
Bitmap.explanation: A Redis bitmap is a string used as a sequence of bits. Each bit has a zero-based offset and can be read or changed independently. Bitmap commands also count enabled bits and combine several bitmap strings with logical operations. The newer BITOP operators support set differences and related combinations.
Bitmap.syntax:
SETBIT key offset value
GETBIT key offset
BITCOUNT key [start end [BYTE | BIT]]
BITOP operation destkey key [key ...]

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The Redis key containing the bitmap string.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: A zero-based bit position.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The bit value to store: 0 or 1.

parameters.name: destkey
parameters.description: The destination key for a BITOP result.

parameters.name: operator and source keys
parameters.description: The logical operator and one or more source bitmap keys.

Bitmap.returns: SETBIT returns the previous bit value. GETBIT returns the bit at the requested offset. BITCOUNT returns the number of set bits. BITOP returns the length of the resulting string.

example.title: Basic bitmap operations
example.code:
SETBIT visits 42 1
GETBIT visits 42
BITCOUNT visits
BITOP AND active_and_paid active paid
GET active_and_paid
example.explanation: This stores one boolean value, reads it, counts all enabled values, and creates a bitmap containing positions enabled in both source bitmaps.

useCases.title: Boolean properties
useCases.scenario: Track whether a user, player, or item has a property by assigning it a stable bit position.

useCases.title: Membership counts
useCases.scenario: Count how many positions are enabled in a bitmap.

useCases.title: Set operations
useCases.scenario: Find common, combined, different, or exclusive members across aligned bitmap sets.

useCases.title: Audience targeting
useCases.scenario: Build an audience from several campaign or interest bitmaps.

interview.question: How do SETBIT and GETBIT work?
interview.answer: SETBIT changes the bit at a zero-based offset and returns the previous bit value. GETBIT reads the bit at an offset. A bitmap is stored inside a Redis string.
interview.followUp: How would you count enabled positions? Use BITCOUNT on the bitmap key.

interview.question: How do you count set bits?
interview.answer: BITCOUNT returns the number of bits set to one in a bitmap. It is useful for counting members or enabled flags. The documented command has linear complexity in the amount of bitmap data it examines.
interview.followUp: How can you count only part of a bitmap? Use the range options supported by BITCOUNT, choosing the documented byte range.

interview.question: What does BITOP do?
interview.answer: BITOP combines source bitmap strings and stores the result under a destination key. AND keeps bits present in every source, OR keeps bits present in at least one source, XOR keeps differing bits, and NOT inverts one source.
interview.followUp: What does ANDOR do? It keeps a bit when it is set in the first bitmap and in at least one additional bitmap.

keyPoints: Use SETBIT to store a binary state at an offset. Use GETBIT to read that state.
Use BITCOUNT when you need the total number of enabled positions in a bitmap.
The basic BITOP operators are AND, OR, XOR, and NOT.
DIFF keeps positions enabled in the first bitmap but disabled in all the other supplied bitmaps.
DIFF1 keeps positions enabled in at least one later bitmap but disabled in the first bitmap.
ANDOR keeps positions enabled in the first bitmap and at least one other bitmap.
ONE keeps positions enabled in exactly one of the supplied bitmaps.
gotchas: BITOP writes its result to the destination key, so an existing value there is replaced.
When bitmap positions represent the same people or objects, keep the source bitmaps aligned and use the same length.

Bloom filter.summary: Redis Bloom filters provide compact, fast membership checks. A negative result is certain, but a positive result may be a false positive.
Bloom filter.explanation: Redis Bloom filters store hashed item data instead of full items. They use little fixed-size memory and quickly test membership. A negative result is certain, but a positive result only means the item may be present because hash collisions can cause false positives.
Bloom filter.syntax:
BF.RESERVE key error_rate capacity [EXPANSION expansion] [NONSCALING]
BF.ADD key item
BF.EXISTS key item
BF.MADD key item [item ...]
BF.MEXISTS key item [item ...]

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The Redis key that names the Bloom filter.

parameters.name: errorRate
parameters.description: The desired probability of false positives, from 0 to 1.

parameters.name: capacity
parameters.description: The intended number of entries.

parameters.name: item/items
parameters.description: One item, or multiple items, to add or check.

Bloom filter.returns: BF.RESERVE returns OK on success. BF.ADD returns 1 when the item is newly added. BF.EXISTS returns 1 when the item may exist and 0 when it definitely does not. Multi-item commands return one result per item.

example.title: Create and query a Bloom filter
example.code:
BF.RESERVE bikes:models 0.001 1000000
BF.ADD bikes:models "Smoky Mountain Striker"
BF.EXISTS bikes:models "Smoky Mountain Striker"
BF.MADD bikes:models "Rocky Mountain Racer" "Cloudy City Cruiser"
BF.MEXISTS bikes:models "Rocky Mountain Racer" "Cloudy City Cruiser"
example.explanation: Creates a filter for one million items with a 0.1% target false-positive rate, adds items, and checks one or many items.

useCases.title: Skip expensive lookups
useCases.scenario: Check a filter before reading a large database or disk-backed store.

useCases.title: Detect duplicate names
useCases.scenario: Check whether a username, email, domain, or slug may already be used.

useCases.title: Avoid repeated recommendations
useCases.scenario: Check whether a user has already seen an advertisement or bought a product.

useCases.title: Screen financial activity
useCases.scenario: Check transaction history or blocked payment identifiers before deeper fraud checks.

interview.question: What problem does a Bloom filter solve?
interview.answer: A Bloom filter is a compact probabilistic structure for membership checks. It can prove that an item is absent, but a positive result may be false because different items can set the same bits.
interview.followUp: Why is it useful before a disk lookup? A negative result lets the application skip the more expensive lookup, while a positive result allows the lookup to continue.

interview.question: How does a Bloom filter work?
interview.answer: Adding an item hashes it and sets one or more positions in a bit array. Checking an item hashes it again; if any required bit is clear, the item is definitely absent. If all are set, the item may be present.
interview.followUp: What reduces false positives? Using more bits per item lowers collision risk, although it uses more memory.

interview.question: Which Redis commands are used for common Bloom filter operations?
interview.answer: Use BF.RESERVE to create a filter, BF.ADD or BF.MADD to add items, and BF.EXISTS or BF.MEXISTS to test membership. BF.RESERVE takes a key, an error rate, and an intended capacity.
interview.followUp: What happens when the initial capacity is exceeded? Scalable Bloom filters add another filter, usually with greater capacity than the previous one.

keyPoints: Bloom filters are useful when memory use must stay small and predictable.
The configured error rate controls how often a positive result can be incorrect.
The number of bits used per item is chosen during creation and affects accuracy.
BF.RESERVE creates a filter before you add data when you want to set its capacity and error rate.
Use BF.MADD to add several items in one command.
Use BF.MEXISTS to test several items and receive one result for each item.
gotchas: Treat a positive result as a hint. Confirm it in the source database when correctness matters.
Choose the expected capacity and error rate when creating the filter.
A scalable filter can add sub-filters as it grows, but capacity planning still affects its accuracy and memory use.

BLPOP.summary: Removes and returns the first value from the first non-empty Redis list. It waits when no listed list has a value, unless the timeout expires.
BLPOP.explanation: BLPOP removes one value from the left side of the first non-empty list among the keys you provide. If all lists are empty, the connection waits until a push adds data or the timeout ends. The reply contains the key and removed value, or null after a finite timeout.

parameters.name: key [key ...]
parameters.description: One or more keys naming Redis lists. Redis checks them from left to right.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Maximum wait in seconds. Zero waits indefinitely; decimal values are allowed.

BLPOP.returns: An array containing the key and popped value when successful. With a finite timeout and no value, it returns a null reply.

example.title: Pop a job
example.code:
RPUSH jobs "send-email" "build-report"
BLPOP jobs 5
example.explanation: Adds two values, then waits up to five seconds for the first value.

useCases.title: Simple work queue
useCases.scenario: A worker waits for jobs in one or more Redis lists and handles each returned value.

useCases.title: Ordered queue selection
useCases.scenario: A consumer waits for data from several queues and gives priority to the first key listed.

useCases.title: Event waiting
useCases.scenario: A program waits for a list item instead of repeatedly checking Redis.

interview.question: How does BLPOP choose a key?
interview.answer: It checks the keys from left to right. It removes and returns the first value from the first key whose list is not empty.
interview.followUp: What happens if two keys become non-empty in one transaction? Redis uses the key order in BLPOP, not the order of writes inside the transaction.

interview.question: What does the timeout mean?
interview.answer: A zero timeout means wait forever. A positive timeout is the maximum wait in seconds and may be fractional. If it expires without data, the command returns a null reply.
interview.followUp: What does an empty list inside MULTI/EXEC do? It returns null instead of blocking.

interview.question: What does BLPOP return?
interview.answer: The command returns two items: the key that supplied the value and the value itself. If the timeout expires, it returns null instead.
interview.followUp: Why might BLPOP be unsafe for reliable work queues? The value is removed before processing, so a client crash can lose it.

keyPoints: BLPOP removes the leftmost value from the first non-empty list.
Provide one or more list keys.
The timeout sets the maximum wait in seconds and can be a decimal.
Use timeout 0 to wait without a time limit.
The order of keys controls which list wins when several contain values.
When no listed key has data, the connection waits for a push.
A successful reply includes the source key and the removed value.
gotchas: Behavior can differ in clustered Redis. Check the rules for multi-key operations before using keys from different cluster slots.
An empty list does not make BLPOP wait inside MULTI/EXEC. It returns a null reply instead.
BLPOP removes the value before the client processes it. A client crash can therefore lose the value.

BRPOP.summary: BRPOP removes and returns the last value in a Redis list. If the supplied lists are empty, it waits until a value is available or the timeout expires.
BRPOP.explanation: BRPOP waits for a value when all given lists are empty. It checks the keys from left to right, then removes a value from the tail of the first non-empty list. If the last value is removed, Redis deletes that list.

parameters.name: key [key ...]
parameters.description: One or more list keys. Redis checks them from left to right.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Maximum wait time in seconds. Zero waits forever.

BRPOP.returns: On success, an array containing the key and the popped value. If the timeout expires first, RESP2 returns nil and RESP3 returns null.

example.title: Pop from a list
example.code:
RPUSH jobs "build" "test"
BRPOP jobs 5
example.explanation: Adds two values, then waits up to five seconds and removes the last value from the list.

useCases.title: Blocking job queue
useCases.scenario: A worker needs to take the newest job from a queue and wait when no job exists.

useCases.title: Priority queues
useCases.scenario: A consumer watches several list queues and wants a predictable priority order.

useCases.title: Efficient waiting
useCases.scenario: A client needs to avoid polling Redis repeatedly while waiting for work.

interview.question: What does BRPOP do?
interview.answer: BRPOP removes and returns the last item in a list. If every supplied list is empty, the connection waits until an item arrives or the timeout ends.
interview.followUp: How does it choose among several keys? It checks keys in the order supplied and uses the first non-empty list.

interview.question: How does the timeout work?
interview.answer: The timeout is measured in seconds. A value of zero means the command waits without a time limit.
interview.followUp: What changed in Redis 6.0? The timeout began accepting a double value instead of only an integer.

interview.question: What can BRPOP return?
interview.answer: With RESP2, an expired wait returns a nil reply. With RESP3, it returns a null reply; a successful call returns the source key and popped value.
interview.followUp: What happens when the popped item was the last one? Redis removes the now-empty list.

keyPoints: It is the blocking form of RPOP.
The command removes the rightmost value.
Key order controls which list wins when several lists contain values.
The result identifies both the list key and the removed value.
An empty list is removed after its final value is taken.
The work grows with the number of keys supplied.
gotchas: A zero timeout does not stop waiting. Use it only when an indefinite wait is intended.
When using several keys in a cluster, check the documented multi-key operation rules.

CLIENT.summary: CLIENT is a container for Redis client-connection commands. Use its subcommands to inspect, name, control, or close client connections.
CLIENT.explanation: CLIENT groups commands that manage Redis client connections. Use its subcommands to inspect connected clients, close a connection, control client behavior, or set connection metadata.

example.title: Inspect and name a connection
example.code:
redis-cli CLIENT HELP
redis-cli CLIENT LIST
redis-cli CLIENT SETNAME app-worker
redis-cli CLIENT GETNAME
example.explanation: Run these commands in redis-cli to inspect clients and set or read the current connection name.

useCases.title: Inspect connected clients
useCases.scenario: Find idle or unusual connections during debugging.

useCases.title: Name connections
useCases.scenario: Label application connections so operational tools can identify them.

useCases.title: Close a client
useCases.scenario: Remove a stuck or unwanted client connection.

useCases.title: Exclude a control connection
useCases.scenario: Protect a monitoring connection from aggregate client-memory eviction.

interview.question: What is the purpose of CLIENT?
interview.answer: CLIENT is a container for commands that manage client connections. Its subcommands can inspect client state, close connections, and name connections.
interview.followUp: Which command shows connected clients? CLIENT LIST returns each connected client and state fields such as address, idle time, flags, and the last command.

interview.question: How does Redis limit concurrent clients?
interview.answer: Set maxclients to control the configured client limit. Redis also checks the operating system file-descriptor limit, so the usable limit can be lower than the configured value.
interview.followUp: Why are extra file descriptors needed? Redis reserves 32 descriptors for internal use, so it compares the client target plus 32 with the process limit.

interview.question: Why does Redis use client output-buffer limits?
interview.answer: Client output buffers can grow when a client receives data faster than it reads it. Hard limits close a client when a size is reached; soft limits close it when a size remains exceeded for a period.
interview.followUp: Which client types have special defaults? Pub/Sub and replica clients have output-buffer limits, while normal clients have no default output-buffer limit.

keyPoints: CLIENT is a group of commands for managing client connections.
Use CLIENT HELP to list the available CLIENT subcommands.
CLIENT LIST reports connected clients and their current state.
CLIENT SETNAME assigns a name to the current connection, and CLIENT GETNAME reads it.
A connection name can help identify a client in SLOWLOG output on Redis 4.0 and later.
Recent Redis versions keep idle client connections open unless a timeout is configured.
gotchas: The configured idle timeout does not close Pub/Sub connections.
Do not depend on a fixed order when Redis serves requests from different clients.
Client eviction does not remove replica or master connections.

COMMAND.summary: COMMAND returns detailed metadata for every command the Redis server can process. Clients can use it to inspect runtime capabilities, argument rules, flags, and key locations.
COMMAND.explanation: COMMAND asks the server for metadata about its commands. Redis returns one item for each command, including its name, argument count, flags, key positions, ACL categories, key specifications, and subcommands when available. Clients can use this information to learn the server's runtime capabilities.
COMMAND.returns: A nested array of command details. The command order is random in RESP2 and RESP3.

example.title: Inspect one command
example.code: redis-cli COMMAND INFO GET
example.explanation: This asks Redis for the metadata of the GET command.

useCases.title: Discover server capabilities
useCases.scenario: A client connects to different Redis versions and needs to discover supported commands or server capabilities.

useCases.title: Find command key rules
useCases.scenario: A Redis Cluster client needs metadata about command keys before routing a request.

useCases.title: Inspect command metadata
useCases.scenario: A debugging tool needs to display command flags, arity, or ACL categories.

interview.question: What does COMMAND return?
interview.answer: COMMAND returns an array containing metadata for every command the server can process. The metadata can include the command name, arity, flags, key positions, ACL categories, tips, key specifications, and subcommands.
interview.followUp: Why can a client use this during connection setup? It can inspect the server's runtime capabilities and adjust its behavior to match them.

interview.question: How should arity values be read?
interview.answer: A positive arity is a fixed number of arguments. A negative arity is the minimum number of arguments, and the count includes the command name itself.
interview.followUp: What are the arities of GET and MGET? GET is 2, while MGET is -2 because it accepts at least one key and can accept more.

interview.question: How does COMMAND describe command keys?
interview.answer: The first key, last key, and step fields describe where key arguments occur. For example, MSET uses a step of 2 because keys and values alternate.
interview.followUp: What should a cluster client do for a movable-key command? It should use COMMAND GETKEYS or the command's key specifications to find the key positions.

keyPoints: COMMAND returns metadata for every command supported by the server.
Each command is represented by its own nested array. The number of fields can vary with the server version.
Command names are returned in lowercase, even though Redis accepts command names without regard to case.
The reply includes the ACL categories assigned to each command.
Commands with subcommands include their subcommand metadata in the reply.
gotchas: Do not depend on the order of items in the returned array.
Arity counts the command name. A positive value means a fixed argument count; a negative value means a minimum count.
For commands marked movablekeys, use COMMAND GETKEYS or key specifications to locate keys.

CONFIG.summary: CONFIG is a container for Redis server configuration commands. Its subcommands can inspect, change, or persist configuration while Redis is running.
CONFIG.explanation: CONFIG groups Redis commands that inspect and change server settings while the server is running. Use a subcommand such as GET, SET, HELP, RESETSTAT, or REWRITE; the exact arguments and behavior depend on that subcommand.

parameters.name: subcommand
parameters.description: The CONFIG subcommand, such as GET, SET, HELP, RESETSTAT, or REWRITE.

parameters.name: args
parameters.description: Arguments required by the selected subcommand.

example.title: Read a setting
example.code: redis-cli CONFIG GET maxmemory
example.explanation: This reads the current value of the maxmemory setting.

useCases.title: Inspect configuration
useCases.scenario: Read a server setting before diagnosing or changing behavior.

useCases.title: Update runtime settings
useCases.scenario: Change a supported setting without restarting Redis.

useCases.title: Persist changes
useCases.scenario: Save runtime configuration changes to the Redis configuration file.

useCases.title: List subcommands
useCases.scenario: Find the CONFIG operations supported by the running Redis version.

interview.question: What is CONFIG used for?
interview.answer: CONFIG is a container for runtime server configuration commands. Its complexity depends on the selected subcommand.
interview.followUp: Which command lists the available CONFIG subcommands? CONFIG HELP.

interview.question: How do you read and change a setting?
interview.answer: CONFIG GET reads the current value of one or more settings. CONFIG SET changes one or more settings at runtime.
interview.followUp: How can you persist runtime changes? Use CONFIG REWRITE to update the Redis configuration file.

interview.question: What version introduced CONFIG?
interview.answer: The command has existed since Redis Open Source 2.0.0. It belongs to the server command group and uses the @slow ACL category.
interview.followUp: What should you check before relying on a subcommand? Check its own syntax, permissions, complexity, and version support.

keyPoints: CONFIG is a group of commands for server configuration.
Its subcommands work with configuration while Redis is running.
CONFIG SET changes one or more configuration parameters.
CONFIG GET reads one or more configuration parameters.
CONFIG REWRITE writes runtime configuration changes into the Redis configuration file.
CONFIG is available starting with Redis Open Source 2.0.0.
gotchas: Performance depends on the CONFIG subcommand you use.
Use CONFIG HELP to see the CONFIG subcommands available in your Redis version.

COPY.summary: Copies the value of one Redis key to another key. It can target a different logical database and optionally replace an existing destination.
COPY.explanation: COPY duplicates the value held by one key under another key. It normally creates the destination in the connection's current logical database, but DB selects another database and REPLACE permits overwriting an existing destination.

parameters.name: source
parameters.description: Key whose value is copied.

parameters.name: destination
parameters.description: Key to create with the copied value.

parameters.name: destination-db
parameters.description: Optional logical database index for the destination.

parameters.name: REPLACE
parameters.description: Optional flag that removes an existing destination before copying.

COPY.returns: Integer reply: 1 if source was copied; 0 if source was not copied.

example.title: Copy a string value
example.code:
SET dolly "sheep"
COPY dolly clone
GET clone
example.explanation: Creates a source string key, copies its value to a new key, then reads the copied value.

useCases.title: Duplicate cached data
useCases.scenario: Create a second key containing the same cached value without changing the original.

useCases.title: Cross-database placement
useCases.scenario: Populate a destination key in a selected logical database.

useCases.title: Overwrite an existing key
useCases.scenario: Refresh a destination key by replacing its prior value.

interview.question: What does COPY do, and what does its return value mean?
interview.answer: COPY duplicates the value associated with source under destination. It returns 1 when the copy succeeds and 0 when the source was not copied, including when the destination already exists without REPLACE.
interview.followUp: How can an existing destination be overwritten? Use the REPLACE option, which removes the destination key before copying the value.

interview.question: How does the DB option affect COPY?
interview.answer: By default, the destination is created in the logical database selected by the connection. The DB destination-db option directs the destination to a specified logical database index.
interview.followUp: What deployment constraint applies to DB selection in clustered environments? The source and destination keys must be in the same hash slot for clustered or Active-Active databases.

interview.question: What is COPY's complexity?
interview.answer: COPY preserves the source value while creating a separate destination key. Its worst-case complexity is O(N) for collections, where N is the number of nested items, and O(1) for strings.
interview.followUp: Why does data type matter for performance? Collection values require traversal proportional to their nested contents, while strings have constant-time copying.

keyPoints: COPY creates the destination key with the value held by the source key.
Without DB, COPY uses the connection's current logical database for the destination.
DB destination-db lets the destination use a different logical database index.
REPLACE enables overwriting an existing destination by deleting it first.
A successful copy returns integer 1.
A failed copy returns integer 0.
Copying collections can scale with the number of nested items.
gotchas: Without REPLACE, an existing destination is not overwritten and the command returns 0.
Clustered and Active-Active deployments require both keys to share a hash slot.

createClient.summary: `createClient` creates a node-redis client configured for Redis, defaulting to localhost on port 6379. Supply options such as a connection URL for another server, then connect explicitly before using commands.
createClient.explanation: `createClient` constructs a node-redis client from optional connection settings. The returned client is not connected automatically: call `connect()` before issuing commands, monitor its error event, and call `quit()` when finished.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional configuration object controlling the Redis connection, including a connection `url`, authentication, socket settings, RESP version, and client-side caching options.

createClient.returns: A node-redis client object. The client exposes connection lifecycle methods, status properties, events, and Redis commands.

example.title: Create and use a node-redis client
example.explanation: Creates a local Redis client, connects explicitly, performs a basic write and read, then closes the connection.

useCases.title: Application caching
useCases.scenario: A Node.js service needs to read and write cached values in Redis.

useCases.title: Remote or secured Redis access
useCases.scenario: A program must connect to a hosted or authenticated Redis deployment.

useCases.title: General Redis data operations
useCases.scenario: An application needs Redis commands through an async JavaScript API.

interview.question: What does `createClient()` return and where does it connect by default?
interview.answer: It creates a node-redis client for Node.js. With no options, the documented example connects to Redis on localhost at port 6379 after `connect()` is called.
interview.followUp: How would you target a secured remote instance? Pass a `url` such as `redis://username:password@host:port`, or configure connection options including TLS.

interview.question: Does creating the client connect immediately?
interview.answer: The client must be connected explicitly with `await client.connect()`. Commands should be issued after that connection is established.
interview.followUp: How can readiness be checked? Use `client.isReady` for whether it is ready to send commands; `client.isOpen` reports whether the underlying socket is open.

interview.question: How do you configure a non-default Redis connection?
interview.answer: Pass an options object, commonly `{ url: 'redis://...' }`, to select a host, port, credentials, or database through the connection URL. The documentation also shows socket settings such as TLS configuration.
interview.followUp: How would you handle failures in production? Register an `error` listener and configure options such as `socket.connectTimeout` or `disableOfflineQueue` when appropriate.

keyPoints: Use `createClient` from the `redis` package when a Node.js or JavaScript application needs a Redis client.
Calling `createClient()` without connection options prepares a client for the local Redis server on port 6379.
A connection URL can specify the remote host, port, username, password, and database selection.
Attach an error listener so client connection or command errors are surfaced instead of becoming unhandled events.
Use `isReady` to test whether the client can currently send commands.
Use `isOpen` when the relevant state is whether the underlying client socket is open.
gotchas: Close the client with `quit()` after use so the Redis connection is shut down cleanly.
The default client targets localhost on port 6379; configure another endpoint with the `url` option.

DBSIZE.summary: DBSIZE returns the number of keys in the currently selected Redis database. It has O(1) time complexity.
DBSIZE.explanation: DBSIZE returns an integer showing how many keys exist in the currently selected Redis database. It runs in constant time, so its work does not grow with the number of keys.
DBSIZE.returns: An integer: the number of keys in the currently selected database.

example.title: Count keys
example.code: DBSIZE
example.explanation: Counts the keys in the database that is currently selected.

useCases.title: Inspect database size
useCases.scenario: Check how many keys are in the selected database.

useCases.title: Monitor key count
useCases.scenario: Use a quick read-only count during diagnostics.

useCases.title: Validate changes
useCases.scenario: Verify the effect of writes or deletes in a selected database.

interview.question: What does DBSIZE return?
interview.answer: DBSIZE returns the number of keys in the currently selected database. It returns an integer in both RESP2 and RESP3.
interview.followUp: How costly is the command? It has O(1) time complexity.

interview.question: What is the syntax and scope of DBSIZE?
interview.answer: The command has no arguments. Its complete syntax is simply DBSIZE.
interview.followUp: Which database does it count? It counts the database selected for the current connection.

interview.question: What are DBSIZE's performance and access properties?
interview.answer: DBSIZE has O(1) time complexity and is marked read-only and fast. It belongs to the @keyspace, @read, and @fast ACL categories.
interview.followUp: What should you check in a cluster? Check the documented multi-key operations behavior because clustered environments can change the command's behavior.

keyPoints: It counts keys only in the database selected by the connection.
The result is an integer reply.
The command has constant time complexity.
Its ACL categories identify it as a keyspace and read operation, and as fast.
Redis Open Source has supported this command since version 1.0.0
gotchas: In a Redis cluster, the result can behave differently. Check the multi-key operations rules before relying on the count.

DECR.summary: Decrements the integer value stored at a key by one and returns the updated value. If the key is missing, Redis starts from zero.
DECR.explanation: DECR subtracts one from the integer represented by a key's string value and returns the resulting integer. A missing key starts at zero, while a wrong type, non-integer string, or value outside the signed 64-bit range causes an error.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Name of the key whose integer value is decremented.

DECR.returns: Integer reply: the value of the key after decrementing it.

example.title: Decrement an integer value
example.explanation: Connects to Redis, initializes a string integer, decrements it once, and prints the resulting value.

useCases.title: Inventory counters
useCases.scenario: Maintain a remaining quantity, such as available inventory, where each operation consumes one unit.

useCases.title: Capacity tracking
useCases.scenario: Track a number of available permits or slots and atomically reserve one.

useCases.title: Work and quota counters
useCases.scenario: Reduce a retry, quota, or pending-work counter by one per processed item.

interview.question: What does DECR do when the key does not exist?
interview.answer: DECR decrements the integer value stored at a key by one and returns the new value. If the key is absent, Redis treats its initial value as zero.
interview.followUp: What happens with a non-numeric string? Redis returns an error because the stored string cannot be represented as an integer.

interview.question: What is the time complexity of DECR?
interview.answer: The command runs in O(1) time. It performs a single integer update and returns the resulting value.
interview.followUp: How would you decrement by an arbitrary amount? Use DECRBY with the key and the desired decrement.

interview.question: What constraints apply to the value stored at the key?
interview.answer: DECR accepts one required argument, the key name. The key's value must represent a signed 64-bit integer, otherwise Redis returns an error.
interview.followUp: What reply should a client expect? An integer reply containing the value after decrementing.

keyPoints: DECR subtracts exactly one from the integer value associated with the supplied key.
A missing key is initialized to zero, so the first DECR produces negative one.
The required argument identifies which Redis key will be modified.
The response is the updated integer, allowing the caller to use the new value immediately.
DECR has been available since Redis Open Source 1.0.0.
The operation has constant time complexity.
gotchas: The command fails when the key stores a non-string value or another incompatible Redis type.
Only signed 64-bit integer values are supported; larger numeric strings are rejected.

DECRBY.summary: DECRBY subtracts an integer amount from a key's stored integer value and returns the updated value. Missing keys start at zero, while non-integer values and out-of-range results cause errors.
DECRBY.explanation: DECRBY subtracts the specified integer from the value stored at a key and returns the updated value. A missing key starts at zero; the command fails when the stored value is non-integer or the result cannot fit in a signed 64-bit integer.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key.

parameters.name: decrement
parameters.description: The integer amount to subtract from the value.

DECRBY.returns: An integer reply containing the value of the key after decrementing it.

example.title: Decrement an integer value
example.code:
SET inventory 10
DECRBY inventory 3
GET inventory
example.explanation: Stores an integer string, subtracts three atomically, then reads the resulting value.

useCases.title: Decrement a resource counter
useCases.scenario: Track remaining inventory, credits, or quotas by subtracting consumed units from an integer counter.

useCases.title: Record consumption
useCases.scenario: Maintain a retry or allowance counter that decreases whenever an operation is consumed.

useCases.title: Apply atomic counter changes
useCases.scenario: Update a shared numeric counter with a single Redis command.

interview.question: What does DECRBY do when the key does not exist?
interview.answer: DECRBY subtracts the supplied decrement from the integer value at a key and returns the value after subtraction. If the key is absent, Redis first treats it as zero.
interview.followUp: What happens with a non-integer value? Redis returns an error rather than coercing the value.

interview.question: What are DECRBY's arguments and return value?
interview.answer: The command accepts a key and an integer decrement amount. Its integer reply is the key's value after decrementing.
interview.followUp: What numeric boundary applies? The operation is limited to signed 64-bit integers.

interview.question: When does DECRBY return an error?
interview.answer: DECRBY requires the stored value to be an integer-compatible value. Redis returns an error if the value has the wrong type or cannot be represented as an integer.
interview.followUp: How would you initialize a counter safely? Store an integer string, or rely on the absent-key zero behavior before applying the decrement.

keyPoints: It subtracts the requested integer amount from the value associated with the key.
The decrement argument is an integer subtraction amount.
The result is the updated integer value, not the amount subtracted.
For example, decrementing a value of 10 by 3 produces 7.
Use it for counters whose values fit within signed 64-bit integer limits.
gotchas: A missing key is treated as zero before the decrement.
The value must be an integer-compatible string; otherwise the command errors.
Values and results are constrained to signed 64-bit integer range.

DEL.summary: DEL removes one or more specified keys and ignores names that do not exist. It returns the count of keys successfully deleted.
DEL.explanation: DEL removes every named key that currently exists. Missing keys are ignored, and the command reports how many keys it actually removed. Supplying multiple keys lets one command delete several cache entries.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The first key to remove; required.

parameters.name: key ...
parameters.description: Zero or more additional keys to remove.

DEL.returns: Integer reply: the number of keys that were removed.

example.title: Delete cache keys
example.code:
SET session:123 "active"
DEL session:123 session:missing
EXISTS session:123
example.explanation: Creates a key, removes it along with a nonexistent key, then verifies that the existing key is gone.

useCases.title: Cache invalidation
useCases.scenario: Remove a cached response after its source data changes.

useCases.title: Session revocation
useCases.scenario: Invalidate a session or token immediately during logout.

useCases.title: Batch cleanup
useCases.scenario: Clean up several related temporary keys in one request.

interview.question: What does DEL return?
interview.answer: DEL accepts one or more keys and removes the ones that exist. Its integer result is the number of keys removed, so missing keys contribute zero.
interview.followUp: How would you avoid blocking the server while removing a very large value? Use UNLINK when asynchronous reclamation is preferable.

interview.question: What is the syntax of DEL?
interview.answer: The command syntax is `DEL key [key ...]`. The first key is required, and the bracketed repetition permits additional keys in the same command.
interview.followUp: What constraint matters when deleting several keys in a cluster? Keys may need to satisfy the cluster's multi-key operation requirements.

interview.question: What operational concern does DEL have?
interview.answer: DEL has O(N) time complexity, where N is the number of keys being removed. It is categorized by Redis as a keyspace write command with slow-command classification.
interview.followUp: What alternative has the same deletion purpose but moves memory reclamation away from the main execution path? UNLINK.

keyPoints: DEL deletes one or more named keys from the Redis keyspace.
The command requires one key and optionally accepts additional keys.
The integer reply counts only keys that were actually present and deleted.
Redis classifies DEL as a keyspace and write command, and marks it as slow.
Its running time grows with the number of keys removed.
gotchas: Deleting a nonexistent key does not produce an error or increase the returned deletion count.
In cluster deployments, multi-key deletion can have different behavior; consider Redis cluster multi-key operation rules.

DISCARD.summary: DISCARD cancels a Redis transaction. It removes all commands queued for execution and returns the connection to its normal state.
DISCARD.explanation: After MULTI, Redis queues commands instead of running them immediately. DISCARD removes every queued command, ends the transaction mode, and, if WATCH was active, stops watching those keys.
DISCARD.returns: Simple string reply: OK in RESP2 and RESP3.

example.title: Cancel a transaction
example.code:
MULTI
SET user:1 Alice
DISCARD
GET user:1
example.explanation: Starts a transaction, queues a write, cancels the transaction, then reads the key. The SET is not applied.

useCases.title: Cancel invalid work
useCases.scenario: A validation check fails after commands have been queued.

useCases.title: Abort optional changes
useCases.scenario: An application decides not to apply a planned group of changes.

useCases.title: Stop a watched transaction
useCases.scenario: A watched key changes before the transaction should run.

interview.question: What does DISCARD do?
interview.answer: DISCARD cancels the current transaction. It clears all commands queued after MULTI and returns the connection to its normal state.
interview.followUp: What happens to watched keys? DISCARD removes every watch created by WATCH for that connection.

interview.question: What is the time complexity of DISCARD?
interview.answer: The command takes O(N) time, where N is the number of commands waiting in the transaction queue. It has no command arguments.
interview.followUp: How could queue size affect cancellation cost? A larger queue means more queued commands must be cleared, so cancellation takes longer.

interview.question: What does DISCARD return, and when was it added?
interview.answer: DISCARD returns the simple string OK in both RESP2 and RESP3. The command was introduced in Redis Open Source 2.0.0.
interview.followUp: Which related commands are commonly used with it? MULTI starts queueing, EXEC runs the queue, and WATCH or UNWATCH controls key watching.

keyPoints: It clears every command queued in the current transaction and leaves transaction mode.
Use DISCARD when the transaction should not be executed.
The command has been available since Redis Open Source 2.0.0.
Its running time depends on how many commands are queued.
gotchas: DISCARD also removes all key watches created by WATCH on the same connection.

DUMP.summary: Returns a Redis-specific serialized representation of the value stored at a key. The result can be used with RESTORE, but does not include expiration information.
DUMP.explanation: DUMP serializes the value held by a key into Redis’s opaque internal format. The resulting bytes can later be supplied to RESTORE, but expiration metadata is not included, so retrieve the remaining lifetime separately with PTTL when needed.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key to serialize.

DUMP.returns: Bulk string reply containing the serialized value, or a nil reply when the key does not exist.

example.title: Serialize a value
example.code:
SET mykey 10
DUMP mykey
example.explanation: Stores a value, then returns its Redis-specific serialized representation.

useCases.title: Serialize for RESTORE
useCases.scenario: Move or recreate a value

useCases.title: Portable value handling
useCases.scenario: Inspect or transfer a Redis value in its native representation

useCases.title: Pair with PTTL
useCases.scenario: Preserve a key’s expiration during migration

interview.question: What does DUMP do, and how is its result used?
interview.answer: DUMP returns a Redis-specific serialized representation of the value at a key. RESTORE can use that representation to create a Redis key again.
interview.followUp: What metadata is not preserved by DUMP? Expiration is excluded, so capture the remaining TTL with PTTL and restore it separately.

interview.question: What does DUMP return for existing and missing keys?
interview.answer: The command returns a bulk string containing serialized data when the key exists. If the key is absent, it returns a nil reply.
interview.followUp: How should a client distinguish an absent key from an empty serialized payload? Check the protocol-level nil/null response rather than only testing byte-string length.

interview.question: What properties does the serialized format have?
interview.answer: The payload includes a checksum for error detection, uses RDB-style value encoding, and embeds an RDB version. RESTORE validates the checksum before reconstructing the key.
interview.followUp: Why can interoperability fail between Redis versions? A version with an incompatible RDB format may refuse the payload.

keyPoints: DUMP converts the value associated with a key into Redis’s own serialized representation.
The serialized result is intended to be consumed by RESTORE to recreate a key.
A 64-bit checksum helps detect corruption in the serialized payload.
The value encoding follows the format Redis uses for RDB persistence data.
Each payload records an RDB version, allowing compatibility checks during restoration.
Access is constant-time, while serialization cost grows with the objects and their average size.
gotchas: Expiration is omitted from the serialized bytes; use PTTL separately if the key’s remaining lifetime must be preserved.
Serialized data may not be portable across Redis versions that use incompatible RDB formats.
A missing key produces a nil reply rather than serialized data.

EVAL.summary: EVAL executes a server-side Lua 5.1 script. It separates explicit key names from regular arguments and makes them available through KEYS and ARGV.
EVAL.explanation: Redis runs the supplied Lua 5.1 source on the server. The number after the script says how many following inputs are key names. Redis puts those names in KEYS and puts the remaining inputs in ARGV. The script can call Redis commands and returns its result to the client.

parameters.name: script
parameters.description: Lua source code to execute.

parameters.name: numkeys
parameters.description: Number of key names that follow.

parameters.name: key [key ...]
parameters.description: Key names used by the script. Provide exactly numkeys keys; Lua receives them in KEYS.

parameters.name: arg [arg ...]
parameters.description: Extra values passed to Lua in ARGV. These should not be key names.

EVAL.returns: The result returned by the executed script.

example.title: Return an argument
example.code: EVAL "return ARGV[1]" 0 hello
example.explanation: This runs a Lua script with no key names and returns the first regular argument.

useCases.title: Atomic multi-key updates
useCases.scenario: Update several keys as one operation.

useCases.title: Server-side application logic
useCases.scenario: Run conditional logic close to the data.

useCases.title: Compose Redis operations
useCases.scenario: Combine Redis commands that are not available as one built-in command.

interview.question: What does EVAL do, and how are its inputs divided?
interview.answer: EVAL sends Lua source to Redis and runs it with the embedded Lua 5.1 interpreter. The script receives key names through KEYS and other inputs through ARGV.
interview.followUp: How should a script receive two keys and one value? Use numkeys 2, place both key names next, then place the value after them; the script reads KEYS[1], KEYS[2], and ARGV[1].

interview.question: What are the execution guarantees and costs of a Lua script?
interview.answer: The script runs atomically, so its reads and writes are not interleaved with other server activity. However, the server is blocked for the script's whole runtime.
interview.followUp: What is the practical design rule? Avoid long-running scripts because they delay every other server operation.

interview.question: What is the EVAL command syntax?
interview.answer: The script source is the first argument. numkeys is the second, followed by exactly that many key names and then optional regular arguments.
interview.followUp: Why must all accessed keys be listed? Redis needs explicit key inputs for correct execution, especially in clustered deployments.

keyPoints: EVAL executes Lua 5.1 code inside the Redis server.
The script argument contains the Lua source that Redis evaluates.
Redis exposes the listed key names to Lua through KEYS.
Non-key inputs are available to the script through ARGV.
EVAL returns whatever value the Lua script returns, converted for the client.
The command's cost depends on the work performed by the script.
gotchas: List every key the script uses after numkeys. Do not build key names in the script or discover them from stored data.
Only the first numkeys inputs are keys. Pass values after those keys as regular arguments.
A script runs atomically, but it blocks other server work while it runs. Keep scripts short.
From Redis 7.4, scripts loaded by EVAL can leave the cache when it reaches its limit. Do not assume every cached script stays forever.

EVALSHA.summary: EVALSHA runs a cached Lua script by its SHA1 digest. Load the script with SCRIPT LOAD first, then pass the key count, keys, and other arguments.
EVALSHA.explanation: EVALSHA runs a Lua script already stored in Redis's script cache. First load the script with SCRIPT LOAD, then pass its returned SHA1 digest, the number of key names, those key names, and any other values. Redis gives the script those values through KEYS and ARGV.

parameters.name: sha1
parameters.description: SHA1 digest of the cached Lua script.

parameters.name: numkeys
parameters.description: Number of key names that follow this value.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Key names passed to the script through KEYS. There must be exactly numkeys of them.

parameters.name: arg
parameters.description: Extra values passed to the script through ARGV.

EVALSHA.returns: The value returned by the executed Lua script.

example.title: Load and run a cached script
example.code: SCRIPT LOAD "return ARGV[1]"
example.explanation: Load the Lua script and note the returned SHA1 digest. Then use that digest with EVALSHA.

useCases.title: Reuse a loaded script
useCases.scenario: A script is called repeatedly and its source should not be sent each time.

useCases.title: Run atomic server-side logic
useCases.scenario: An application needs server-side Lua logic that reads and writes Redis data as one operation.

useCases.title: Prepare a script before batched commands
useCases.scenario: A client uses a pipeline or transaction and must ensure the script is already cached.

interview.question: What does EVALSHA do?
interview.answer: EVALSHA executes a Lua script by its SHA1 digest instead of receiving the script source. The script must already be in Redis's script cache, usually because SCRIPT LOAD was called first.
interview.followUp: What should an application do after NOSCRIPT? Load the script with SCRIPT LOAD, then retry EVALSHA with the returned digest.

interview.question: How are keys and arguments passed?
interview.answer: numkeys tells Redis how many following values are key names. Redis exposes those names to Lua through KEYS; the later values are exposed through ARGV.
interview.followUp: Why must keys be separated from arguments? Redis needs to identify the keys used by the script, especially in clustered deployments.

interview.question: What does EVALSHA return and how complex is it?
interview.answer: The result is whatever the executed Lua script returns. Command cost also depends on the script being run.
interview.followUp: What happens if the script cache is lost? EVALSHA fails with NOSCRIPT until the script is loaded again.

keyPoints: It runs a Lua script using the script's SHA1 digest.
Use SCRIPT LOAD to place the script in Redis's cache before calling EVALSHA.
Values after the key list are passed to Lua through ARGV.
The key names are available inside the script through Lua's KEYS table.
EVALSHA does not define one fixed result type; the script determines the returned value.
Execution complexity depends on the Lua script's work.
gotchas: The script cache is temporary. A restart, failover, or SCRIPT FLUSH can remove the script, so EVALSHA may return NOSCRIPT.
Do not depend on recovering from NOSCRIPT inside a pipeline. Load the script first, or use EVAL as the client documentation recommends.
The first numkeys values after the count are keys. All remaining values are script arguments.

EXEC.summary: EXEC runs all commands queued in a Redis transaction. With WATCH, it runs only if the watched keys were not changed.
EXEC.explanation: EXEC runs every command queued after MULTI, in the order received, then leaves transaction mode. With WATCH, it runs only when watched keys were unchanged; otherwise it aborts and returns a null reply.
EXEC.returns: RESP2 or RESP3: an array of the replies from the transaction. If WATCH detects a changed key, RESP2 returns a nil reply and RESP3 returns a null reply.

example.title: Run queued commands
example.code:
MULTI
SET user:1 Alice
INCR visits
EXEC
example.explanation: Queues two commands, then runs them together.

useCases.title: Group commands
useCases.scenario: Apply several related updates as one isolated operation.

useCases.title: Protect a conditional update
useCases.scenario: Implement a check-and-set update with WATCH.

useCases.title: Create a compound operation
useCases.scenario: Build an atomic read-and-remove pattern with WATCH, such as removing the lowest sorted-set member.

interview.question: What does EXEC do?
interview.answer: EXEC runs the commands queued by MULTI in sequence and returns one reply for each command. Redis prevents another client's request from running between commands in that transaction.
interview.followUp: What happens if a watched key changes? EXEC aborts the transaction and returns a null reply instead of running the queued commands.

interview.question: How are transaction errors handled?
interview.answer: A syntax or argument error can prevent a command from being queued. An execution-time error affects that command's reply, but does not roll back or stop the other commands.
interview.followUp: Why does Redis avoid rollback? The documentation says rollback support would reduce transaction simplicity and performance.

interview.question: How does WATCH change EXEC?
interview.answer: WATCH makes EXEC conditional. If a watched key changes before EXEC, Redis aborts the whole transaction; after EXEC, the watched keys are cleared.
interview.followUp: Can queued commands trigger WATCH? No. They are only queued until EXEC, so their changes do not trigger the condition during that transaction.

keyPoints: EXEC runs all commands queued in the current transaction and ends transaction mode.
Commands run in their queue order as one isolated operation.
If the connection closes before EXEC, the queued operations are not performed.
Watched keys are cleared after EXEC, whether it succeeds or aborts.
A successful EXEC returns an array containing one result for each executed command.
gotchas: A command can fail during execution, but Redis still runs the other queued commands. Transactions do not roll back partial results.
Behavior can differ in a Redis cluster, especially for operations involving multiple keys.
Commands are not executed when they are queued. Their effects begin only when EXEC runs.

EXISTS.summary: EXISTS determines whether one or more Redis keys exist and returns the number found. It can check multiple keys in one command.
EXISTS.explanation: EXISTS examines each supplied key and returns how many of those keys are present. Supplying the same existing key more than once counts that key once for every occurrence, and checking N keys has O(N) complexity.

parameters.name: key [key ...]
parameters.description: One or more keys to check for existence. A repeated key is counted once per occurrence.

EXISTS.returns: Integer reply: the number of keys that exist among the specified arguments.

example.title: Check key existence
example.code:
SET key1 "Hello"
EXISTS key1
EXISTS nosuchkey
SET key2 "World"
EXISTS key1 key2 nosuchkey
example.explanation: Creates two keys, then checks one or several keys and returns the count that currently exist.

useCases.title: Cache-presence checks
useCases.scenario: Before reading or updating cached data, determine whether a requested key is present.

useCases.title: Batch existence tests
useCases.scenario: Check several candidate keys and use the returned count for conditional logic.

useCases.title: Post-operation verification
useCases.scenario: Verify that deletion or another lifecycle operation removed the expected keys.

interview.question: What does EXISTS return?
interview.answer: EXISTS takes one or more key names and returns an integer equal to the number that exist. For a single key, that result is effectively 1 or 0.
interview.followUp: What is the complexity for checking several keys? It is O(N), where N is the number of keys supplied.

interview.question: How does EXISTS handle multiple keys?
interview.answer: The command accepts `key [key ...]`, so a call can test multiple keys at once. Its result is the count of existing keys among the arguments.
interview.followUp: What happens if one existing key is repeated? Each occurrence is counted, so repeating it can increase the result.

interview.question: What operational caveat applies in Redis Cluster?
interview.answer: EXISTS is a read-only keyspace command that determines whether one or more keys exist. In clustered deployments, multi-key behavior varies, so cluster-specific multi-key rules must be considered.
interview.followUp: Why can a multi-key request be problematic in a cluster? Keys may not be handled like a single local-key operation across cluster slots.

keyPoints: Use EXISTS to test whether a key or a group of keys is present.
The integer reply is the count of supplied keys currently found.
A repeated existing key contributes separately for every appearance in the argument list.
Runtime grows linearly with the number of key names passed.
The command syntax requires at least one key and permits additional keys.
gotchas: Repeated key names are not deduplicated: an existing key contributes to the returned count on every occurrence.
Multi-key checks can behave differently in a Redis Cluster, so consult the cluster guidance before relying on them across slots.

EXPIRE.summary: Sets a relative expiration timeout, in seconds, on a key. When the timeout elapses, Redis automatically deletes the key.
EXPIRE.explanation: EXPIRE assigns a relative timeout, in seconds, to an existing key. Redis automatically removes the key after the timeout; calling EXPIRE again replaces the current timeout, while conditional options can restrict when the replacement occurs.
EXPIRE.syntax: EXPIRE key seconds [NX | XX | GT | LT]

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The key whose expiration should be set.

parameters.name: seconds
parameters.description: The time to live, in seconds.

parameters.name: condition
parameters.description: Optional condition: NX, XX, GT, or LT.

EXPIRE.returns: An integer reply: 1 if the timeout was set, or 0 if the key does not exist or the requested condition is not satisfied.

example.title: Cache a session for five minutes
example.code:
SET session:123 user-42
EXPIRE session:123 300 NX
TTL session:123
example.explanation: Creates a five-minute cache entry only when the key has no existing expiration, then checks its remaining lifetime.

useCases.title: Expire sessions
useCases.scenario: Session and authentication state

useCases.title: Bound cache lifetime
useCases.scenario: Cached API responses or computed results

useCases.title: Clean up temporary keys
useCases.scenario: Temporary locks or coordination markers

interview.question: What does EXPIRE do and what does it return?
interview.answer: EXPIRE takes a key and a relative lifetime in seconds, then returns 1 when the timeout is set or 0 when it is not. A missing key therefore produces 0.
interview.followUp: How would you apply a timeout only when the key has none? Use the NX option: EXPIRE key seconds NX.

interview.question: What happens when EXPIRE is called on a key that already has a timeout?
interview.answer: A later EXPIRE normally replaces the key's existing timeout with the new number of seconds. NX, XX, GT, and LT constrain whether that replacement is allowed.
interview.followUp: Which option updates only a longer existing timeout? GT permits the change only when the new timeout is greater than the current one.

interview.question: What precision does Redis use for key expiration?
interview.answer: The timeout is measured in seconds, but Redis expiration resolution is one millisecond. Redis also preserves expiration information across persistence and replication.
interview.followUp: Which commands provide millisecond-based expiration and inspection? PEXPIRE sets milliseconds, while PTTL reports the remaining lifetime in milliseconds.

keyPoints: EXPIRE sets a relative expiration period measured in seconds.
Once the lifetime elapses, Redis automatically deletes the key.
Calling EXPIRE again on an expiring key is supported.
A subsequent EXPIRE replaces the previous time-to-live with the new value.
Expiration remains through ordinary value-preserving operations but can be cleared by deletion or overwrite.
Although EXPIRE accepts seconds, Redis internally resolves expiration to one millisecond.
Expiration metadata is included in replication and disk persistence.
gotchas: Commands that delete or overwrite a key's value can remove its expiration, so updating a cached value may make it persistent.
A key with an expiration is considered volatile in Redis terminology.
EXPIRE does not create a missing key; the command's timeout is ineffective unless the target key already exists.

EXPIREAT.summary: Sets a key's expiration to an absolute Unix timestamp in seconds. Optional NX, XX, GT, or LT conditions control when the deadline may be changed.
EXPIREAT.explanation: EXPIREAT assigns a key an expiration deadline expressed as an absolute Unix timestamp in seconds rather than as a relative duration. Optional conditions can restrict whether Redis changes the deadline; a timestamp in the past removes the key immediately.
EXPIREAT.syntax: EXPIREAT key unix-time-seconds [NX | XX | GT | LT]

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The key whose expiration is being changed.

parameters.name: unix-time-seconds
parameters.description: Absolute expiration time as a Unix timestamp in seconds.

parameters.name: condition
parameters.description: Optional mutually exclusive condition: NX, XX, GT, or LT.

EXPIREAT.returns: Integer 1 if the timeout was set; integer 0 if it was not set, such as when the key does not exist or a supplied condition prevents the operation.

example.title: Set an absolute expiration
example.code:
SET session:user:42 "active"
EXPIREAT session:user:42 4102444800
TTL session:user:42
example.explanation: Sets a key, assigns it an absolute expiration time in Unix seconds, then checks its remaining TTL.

useCases.title: Absolute deadline coordination
useCases.scenario: Coordinate expiration with an externally calculated deadline shared across services.

useCases.title: Expiration preservation
useCases.scenario: Restore or migrate data while preserving an expiration time represented as an epoch timestamp.

useCases.title: Bounded deadline updates
useCases.scenario: Prevent a refresh from shortening or extending a deadline by using LT or GT.

interview.question: What does EXPIREAT do, and what does it return?
interview.answer: EXPIREAT sets a key's expiration using an absolute Unix timestamp in seconds. It returns 1 when the expiration is set and 0 when the key is missing or the requested condition prevents the change.
interview.followUp: How would you apply a deadline only if the key already has one? Use the XX option, which skips the update when the key is persistent.

interview.question: How do NX and XX change EXPIREAT behavior?
interview.answer: NX applies the deadline only when the key currently has no expiration. XX applies it only when the key already has an expiration; these conditional modes cannot be combined.
interview.followUp: Which option ensures a new deadline is later than the current one? GT; a persistent key is treated as having an infinite TTL for this comparison.

interview.question: How does EXPIREAT differ from EXPIRE?
interview.answer: The timestamp is measured in seconds since January 1, 1970, unlike EXPIRE, which accepts a relative number of seconds. A deadline in the past deletes the key immediately.
interview.followUp: What operational event differs for a past timestamp? Redis deletes the key and generates a del event rather than an expire event.

keyPoints: The deadline is an absolute epoch time in seconds, not a duration counted from the command's execution.
NX makes the command conditional on the key currently lacking an expiration.
XX limits the update to keys that already have a configured expiration.
GT changes the deadline only when the requested expiration is later than the existing one.
LT changes the deadline only when the requested expiration is earlier than the existing one.
A successful expiration update returns integer 1.
gotchas: Passing a past timestamp does not merely create an already-expired deadline; Redis deletes the key immediately.
Use at most one of NX, XX, GT, or LT in a command.
When using GT, a key without an existing expiration is considered to have an infinite current TTL, so a finite new deadline will not be greater.

FCALL.summary: FCALL invokes a function that is stored in Redis. You provide its name, the number of keys, optional key names, and optional extra arguments.
FCALL.explanation: FCALL runs a function already loaded into Redis. It passes the declared keys to the function's `KEYS` collection and the remaining values to its `ARGV` collection. The function decides what result Redis returns.

parameters.name: function
parameters.description: Name of the loaded function to invoke.

parameters.name: numkeys
parameters.description: Number of key names that follow.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Key names accessed by the function. Provide exactly `numkeys` keys.

parameters.name: arg
parameters.description: Extra values passed to the function.

FCALL.returns: The return value produced by the invoked function.

example.title: Call a Redis function
example.code: FUNCTION LOAD "#!lua name=mylib\nredis.register_function('myfunc', function(keys, args) return args[1] end)"\nFCALL myfunc 0 hello
example.explanation: This creates a library with `myfunc`, then calls it with no keys and one argument.

useCases.title: Call a stored function
useCases.scenario: Run reusable server-side logic that has been loaded into Redis.

useCases.title: Pass keys and arguments
useCases.scenario: Give a function Redis key names and separate non-key input values.

useCases.title: Return computed data
useCases.scenario: Use one command to execute logic and receive its function-defined result.

interview.question: What does FCALL do?
interview.answer: FCALL invokes a named function that has already been loaded into Redis. Its work and runtime cost depend on that function.
interview.followUp: How do you pass data to the function? Declare the key count, place that many key names first, and place other values after them.

interview.question: What is the purpose of numkeys?
interview.answer: `numkeys` tells Redis how many following arguments are keys. Redis provides those key names through Lua `KEYS`; additional arguments are provided through Lua `ARGV`.
interview.followUp: What happens if the count is wrong? The command does not provide the function with the intended key and argument split.

interview.question: What does FCALL return?
interview.answer: The command returns whatever value the invoked function returns. The documentation does not define one fixed return type for FCALL.
interview.followUp: How can you run a read-only function? Redis documents the related `FCALL_RO` command for that purpose.

keyPoints: FCALL invokes a function by name.
Its time complexity depends on the function it runs.
List accessed key names after `numkeys`; the function receives them through Lua `KEYS`.
Values after the keys become additional arguments in Lua `ARGV`.
The function controls the command's return value.
FCALL was added in Redis Open Source 7.0.0.
gotchas: The number of key names must match `numkeys` exactly.

FLUSHDB.summary: FLUSHDB removes all keys from the currently selected Redis database. Use ASYNC or SYNC to choose asynchronous or synchronous flushing.
FLUSHDB.explanation: FLUSHDB removes every key from the currently selected Redis database. It runs synchronously by default unless configuration changes the default, and ASYNC or SYNC can explicitly choose the execution mode.

parameters.name: ASYNC | SYNC
parameters.description: Optional flush mode: ASYNC performs asynchronous deletion; SYNC performs synchronous deletion. The default is controlled by lazyfree-lazy-user-flush.

example.title: Asynchronously clear the selected database
example.code: redis-cli FLUSHDB ASYNC
example.explanation: Removes the keys that existed in the selected database when the asynchronous flush began; keys added afterward are retained.

useCases.title: Reset test data
useCases.scenario: Clear an isolated logical database during development or testing.
