useCases.title: Invalidate a cache database
useCases.scenario: Remove all cached entries from the selected database when invalidating a cache namespace.

useCases.title: Asynchronous bulk cleanup
useCases.scenario: Choose nonblocking deletion for a large keyspace when immediate completion is unnecessary.

interview.question: What does FLUSHDB do, and what does it return?
interview.answer: FLUSHDB deletes all keys in the currently selected database and returns the simple string reply OK. Its time complexity is O(N), where N is the number of keys in that database.
interview.followUp: What does ASYNC change? It starts an asynchronous flush and only targets keys present when the command was invoked; later-created keys remain.

interview.question: How do SYNC, ASYNC, and the default mode differ?
interview.answer: The syntax is FLUSHDB [ASYNC | SYNC]. ASYNC performs the flush asynchronously, while SYNC performs it synchronously; without an option, the default is controlled by lazyfree-lazy-user-flush.
interview.followUp: How could the default behavior change without changing the command text? Set lazyfree-lazy-user-flush to yes, which makes the default asynchronous starting with Redis 6.2.

interview.question: How does FLUSHDB behave in Redis Cluster?
interview.answer: Redis Cluster supports only database ID zero, so FLUSHDB is identical to FLUSHALL there. In a non-clustered server, it affects the currently selected database.
interview.followUp: Why should cluster scope be treated carefully? The command's effective scope is the cluster's supported database context rather than one of several selectable logical databases.

keyPoints: The command clears every key in the logical database selected by the connection.
The documentation states that FLUSHDB never fails.
Unless configuration changes the default, the server completes the deletion synchronously.
From Redis 6.2 onward, lazyfree-lazy-user-flush=yes changes an unspecified mode to asynchronous.
The optional mode explicitly chooses asynchronous or synchronous flushing.
Its time complexity grows linearly with the number of keys in the selected database.
gotchas: With ASYNC, keys created after the command starts are not removed.
Stored functions are not removed by FLUSHDB.
In Redis Cluster, FLUSHDB has the same scope as FLUSHALL because only database 0 exists.

FUNCTION.summary: FUNCTION is a container for Redis function commands. Use FUNCTION HELP to list its available subcommands.
FUNCTION.explanation: FUNCTION groups commands for managing Redis function libraries. Use a subcommand such as LOAD, LIST, DELETE, DUMP, RESTORE, FLUSH, KILL, or STATS. Use FUNCTION HELP to see the available subcommands.

example.title: Show FUNCTION subcommands
example.code: FUNCTION HELP
example.explanation: Ask Redis to list the available FUNCTION subcommands.

useCases.title: List subcommands
useCases.scenario: You need to discover which function-management operations Redis supports.

useCases.title: Manage function libraries
useCases.scenario: You need to work with Redis libraries and their functions.

useCases.title: Inspect command support
useCases.scenario: You need to connect command-line tooling to Redis function features.

interview.question: What is FUNCTION used for?
interview.answer: FUNCTION is a container for commands that manage Redis function libraries. It has been available since Redis Open Source 7.0.0.
interview.followUp: How can you discover its subcommands? Call FUNCTION HELP.

interview.question: What is the time complexity of FUNCTION?
interview.answer: The command itself has no single fixed operation. Its time complexity depends on the selected subcommand.
interview.followUp: Which subcommands can remove functions? FUNCTION DELETE removes one library, while FUNCTION FLUSH removes all libraries and functions.

interview.question: How do you find available FUNCTION subcommands?
interview.answer: Use FUNCTION HELP to request the list of available function commands. Then choose the needed subcommand.
interview.followUp: Which related command invokes a loaded function? FCALL invokes a function, and FCALL_RO invokes a read-only function.

keyPoints: FUNCTION groups commands for Redis functions.
Redis added FUNCTION in Redis Open Source 7.0.0.
The cost depends on which FUNCTION subcommand you run.
FUNCTION belongs to the @slow ACL category.
Run FUNCTION HELP to list the available FUNCTION commands.
gotchas: FUNCTION is not one operation. Choose a specific subcommand, such as LOAD or LIST.

GEOADD.summary: Adds one or more members to a Redis geospatial index. Each member has a longitude, latitude, and name; the key is created if it does not exist.
GEOADD.explanation: GEOADD stores each member with a longitude and latitude in a geospatial index. Redis stores the index as a sorted set, so later commands such as GEOSEARCH can find members in a circle or box. Coordinates must use longitude first, then latitude.
GEOADD.syntax: GEOADD key [NX | XX] [CH] longitude latitude member [longitude latitude member ...]

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The sorted-set key used for the geospatial index. Redis creates it if needed.

parameters.name: condition
parameters.description: Optional. NX adds only new members; XX updates only existing members.

parameters.name: change
parameters.description: Optional. Count all changed members instead of only newly added members.

parameters.name: data
parameters.description: One or more triples. Each triple contains longitude, latitude, and member name.

GEOADD.returns: An integer. Normally it is the number of new members added. With CH, it is the number of members added or updated.

example.title: Add locations and search nearby
example.code:
GEOADD bikes:rentable -122.27652 37.805186 station:1
GEOADD bikes:rentable -122.2674626 37.8062344 station:2
GEOSEARCH bikes:rentable FROMLONLAT -122.27652 37.805186 BYRADIUS 5 km
example.explanation: This adds two bike stations, then finds stations within 5 kilometers of the first station.

useCases.title: Build a location index
useCases.scenario: Store places, vehicles, stores, or other named points for later geographic queries.

useCases.title: Bulk-load locations
useCases.scenario: Add many coordinates in one command when loading or synchronizing location data.

useCases.title: Update existing locations
useCases.scenario: Update the position of a member only when it already exists.

useCases.title: Insert new locations only
useCases.scenario: Prevent an existing location from being overwritten while accepting new locations.

interview.question: What does GEOADD do?
interview.answer: GEOADD adds one or more members to a geospatial index. Each member has a longitude and latitude, and Redis creates the key when it does not exist.
interview.followUp: What data structure stores the index? Redis stores it as a sorted set whose scores contain geohash data.

interview.question: What does GEOADD return?
interview.answer: Without options, the integer reply counts only new members. Updating the coordinates of an existing member does not increase that count.
interview.followUp: How can the reply include coordinate updates? Add CH; then the count includes new members and existing members whose coordinates changed.

interview.question: How do NX, XX, and CH affect GEOADD?
interview.answer: NX adds only members that do not already exist. XX updates only members that already exist and never adds new ones.
interview.followUp: What does CH change? It makes the reply count all changed members, including both additions and coordinate updates.

keyPoints: GEOADD can add several locations in one command. Redis creates the key when it is missing.
XX allows coordinate updates for existing members, but it does not create new members.
CH changes the reply count from new members only to every member that was added or had its coordinates changed.
The command accepts geographic coordinates as a longitude and latitude pair.
Adding each item costs O(log(N)), where N is the number of entries in the sorted set.
gotchas: Pass coordinates as longitude followed by latitude. Reversing them can produce the wrong location or an invalid coordinate.
Redis uses a spherical Earth model and the Haversine formula. Distance results can have errors of up to 0.5%, so use another system when exact distance matters.

GEOSEARCH.summary: GEOSEARCH finds members in a Redis geospatial index inside a circle or box. It can return names, ordering, limits, coordinates, distances, or geohash scores.
GEOSEARCH.explanation: GEOSEARCH reads a geospatial index and finds members inside a circle or rectangle. You choose the search center from a stored member or longitude and latitude, then choose a radius or box size. Optional flags sort results, limit their number, or add coordinates, distance, or the raw geohash score.
GEOSEARCH.syntax: GEOSEARCH key <FROMMEMBER member | FROMLONLAT longitude latitude> <BYRADIUS radius <M | KM | FT | MI> | BYBOX width height <M | KM | FT | MI>> [ASC | DESC] [COUNT count [ANY]] [WITHCOORD] [WITHDIST] [WITHHASH]

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The sorted set that contains the geospatial index.

parameters.name: from
parameters.description: Use a stored member, or provide the center longitude and latitude.

parameters.name: area
parameters.type: BYRADIUS radius unit | BYBOX width height unit
parameters.description: Use a circle radius or a box width and height, with a distance unit.

parameters.name: order
parameters.description: Optional result order: nearest first with ASC or farthest first with DESC.

parameters.name: count
parameters.description: Optional maximum result count. ANY may allow an early stop.

parameters.name: with
parameters.description: Optional flags that add coordinates, distances, or geohash scores.

GEOSEARCH.returns: Without a WITH option, an array of matching member names. With WITHCOORD, WITHDIST, or WITHHASH, an array of arrays containing the requested values for each member.

example.title: Find nearby places
example.code:
GEOADD places 13.361389 38.115556 Palermo
GEOADD places 15.087269 37.502669 Catania
GEOSEARCH places FROMLONLAT 15 37 BYRADIUS 200 km ASC WITHDIST
example.explanation: This stores two places, then returns places within 200 kilometers, ordered from nearest to farthest, with each distance included.

useCases.title: Nearby results
useCases.scenario: Find stores, vehicles, or other points close to a user's location.

useCases.title: Map-area search
useCases.scenario: Search all indexed members inside a rectangular service or map area.

useCases.title: Distance-aware results
useCases.scenario: Return distances so an application can show results from nearest to farthest.

interview.question: What does GEOSEARCH do?
interview.answer: GEOSEARCH finds members in a circle or box within a geospatial index. It can use a stored member or explicit longitude and latitude as the starting point.
interview.followUp: How would you return only the nearest five members? Add ASC and COUNT 5.

interview.question: How do circle and box searches differ?
interview.answer: BYRADIUS takes a radius and a unit. BYBOX takes width, height, and a unit; both can use meters, kilometers, feet, or miles.
interview.followUp: Can the search center be a member instead of coordinates? Yes. Use FROMMEMBER followed by the member name.

interview.question: What extra result data can GEOSEARCH return?
interview.answer: The command returns member names unless a WITH option is used. WITHCOORD adds coordinates, WITHDIST adds distance, and WITHHASH adds the raw 52-bit geohash score.
interview.followUp: What is the command complexity? It is O(N+log(M)), where N is the grid-aligned bounding-box candidates and M is the matching items.

keyPoints: It searches a geospatial index using either a circular area or a rectangular area.
The search center can be an existing member or a longitude and latitude pair.
Use BYRADIUS for a circle or BYBOX for a rectangle, with meters, kilometers, feet, or miles.
ASC and DESC control order. COUNT limits the number of returned members; ANY can stop early when enough results are found.
WITHCOORD adds each matching member's longitude and latitude.
WITHDIST adds each member's distance from the search center.
gotchas: Without a WITH option, the result contains only member names.
WITHDIST returns distances in the unit used by the search radius.
WITHCOORD returns longitude first and latitude second.

Geospatial.summary: Redis geospatial indexes store coordinates with named members. Search them by radius or bounding box to find nearby locations.
Geospatial.explanation: Redis stores longitude, latitude, and a member name in a geospatial index. Use GEOSEARCH to find members inside a circle or box; other commands can return positions, distances, or geohashes.
Geospatial.syntax:
GEOADD key longitude latitude member [longitude latitude member ...]
GEOSEARCH key FROMMEMBER member | FROMLONLAT longitude latitude BYRADIUS radius unit | BYBOX width height unit

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The Redis key containing the geospatial index.

parameters.name: longitude
parameters.description: The longitude of the location.

parameters.name: latitude
parameters.description: The latitude of the location.

parameters.name: member
parameters.description: The name of the location member.

parameters.name: area
parameters.description: The search shape, such as a radius or box.

Geospatial.returns: Search commands return matching members. Optional flags can also return distances or coordinates.

example.title: Find nearby locations
example.code:
GEOADD bikes:rentable -122.27652 37.805186 station:1
GEOADD bikes:rentable -122.2674626 37.8062344 station:2
GEOSEARCH bikes:rentable FROMLONLAT -122.27652 37.805186 BYRADIUS 5 km WITHDIST
example.explanation: Adds two bike stations, then finds stations within 5 kilometers and includes their distances.

useCases.title: Nearby stations
useCases.scenario: Find bike rental stations near a user's current location.

useCases.title: Map area search
useCases.scenario: Find locations inside a geographic rectangle.

useCases.title: Distance checks
useCases.scenario: Measure the distance between two indexed places.

interview.question: How do you add and find nearby locations?
interview.answer: Use GEOADD with a key, longitude, latitude, and member name. Then use GEOSEARCH with a circle or box filter to find nearby members.
interview.followUp: How can a query return distances? Add WITHDIST to GEOSEARCH. You can also request coordinates with WITHCOORD.

interview.question: What search areas can GEOSEARCH use?
interview.answer: GEOSEARCH supports a radius or a rectangular box. A radius uses a center point and a distance unit; a box uses width and height.
interview.followUp: Which units are supported? The documented units include meters, kilometers, miles, and feet.

interview.question: What coordinate details must a Redis geospatial command use?
interview.answer: GEOADD takes longitude before latitude. GEOSEARCH can start from coordinates or from an existing member in the index.
interview.followUp: How would you get the stored position? Use GEOPOS for longitude and latitude, or GEOHASH for geohash strings.

keyPoints: A geospatial index stores locations and supports searches over those locations.
Use a distance circle or a bounding box to limit the search area.
GEOADD inserts one or more named locations into the index.
GEODIST calculates the distance between two indexed members.
GEOHASH returns the geohash representation for requested members.
GEOPOS retrieves the stored longitude and latitude for members.
gotchas: Do not treat this data type as a replacement for Redis Search. Redis Search supports more formats and query options.
GEOADD creates the key when the geospatial index does not already exist.

GET.summary: GET returns the string value stored at a key. It returns nil for a missing key and errors when the key contains a non-string value.
GET.explanation: GET looks up one key and returns its stored string value. A missing key produces nil, while a key containing a non-string value causes an error because GET supports strings only.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key whose string value should be retrieved.

GET.returns: The string value stored at the key; nil when the key does not exist; an error if the stored value is not a string.

example.title: Read a string value
example.code:
redis-cli SET user:42:name Ada
redis-cli GET user:42:name
# "Ada"
example.explanation: Stores a string and then retrieves it by key using the Redis command-line client.

useCases.title: Cache lookup
useCases.scenario: Read a cached string by its cache key.

useCases.title: Session and token retrieval
useCases.scenario: Fetch a previously stored session token or identifier.

useCases.title: Existence-aware reads
useCases.scenario: Check whether a string key currently has a value.

interview.question: What does GET return when the key does not exist, and what is its complexity?
interview.answer: GET has O(1) time complexity and belongs to the read, string, and fast ACL categories. It returns the string stored at the requested key, or nil when that key is absent.
interview.followUp: What happens when the key contains a list? GET returns an error because it only handles string values.

interview.question: What argument does GET require and what kind of reply does it produce?
interview.answer: The command accepts one required argument, key, which identifies the value to retrieve. The result is a bulk string reply when the key exists, or nil for a missing key.
interview.followUp: How would you retrieve a hash instead? Use a hash-specific command such as HGET, supplying the key and field.

interview.question: What is the command syntax and when was GET introduced?
interview.answer: GET is available since Redis Open Source 1.0.0. Its syntax is GET key, and it reads rather than modifies the stored value.
interview.followUp: How can a value be written before reading it? Use SET with the key and string value, then call GET with that key.

keyPoints: GET retrieves the value associated with the specified key.
A missing key is represented by a nil reply.
The command is intended for Redis String values, not every Redis data type.
Its ACL categories identify it as a read operation for strings with fast classification.
Redis introduced GET in Redis Open Source 1.0.0.
gotchas: GET cannot read a key whose value has another Redis data type; use the command appropriate for that type.

GETBIT.summary: GETBIT reads one bit at a zero-based offset in a Redis String. It returns 0 or 1.
GETBIT.explanation: Redis stores bitmap data inside a String. GETBIT reads the bit at a zero-based position. A missing key or a position past the string is treated as a zero-filled area, so the result is 0 there.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key that holds the String.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: The zero-based bit position to read.

GETBIT.returns: An integer reply: 0 or 1, representing the bit stored at the requested offset.

example.title: Read bitmap bits
example.code:
SETBIT user:123:flags 7 1
GETBIT user:123:flags 7
GETBIT user:123:flags 8
example.explanation: This sets bit 7, then reads bits 7 and 8. The results are 1 and 0.

useCases.title: Compact binary states
useCases.scenario: Store one yes-or-no state per numeric ID, such as whether a device checked in.

useCases.title: Permission flags
useCases.scenario: Represent permissions or other flags where each position has a defined meaning.

useCases.title: Read updated flags
useCases.scenario: Check a bit after another process records it with SETBIT.

interview.question: What does GETBIT do?
interview.answer: GETBIT reads one bit from the String stored at a key. It takes a key and a zero-based bit offset, and returns either 0 or 1.
interview.followUp: What happens if the offset is outside the stored value? Redis treats the missing area as zero-filled, so the result is 0.

interview.question: What are the arguments and return values?
interview.answer: The syntax is GETBIT key offset. The offset starts at zero, and the command returns the bit value at that position.
interview.followUp: How would you mark a bit before reading it? Use SETBIT with the same key, offset, and a value of 0 or 1.

interview.question: What is the time complexity?
interview.answer: GETBIT has O(1) time complexity. Redis classifies it as a read, bitmap, and fast command.
interview.followUp: How are Redis bitmaps represented? They are bit operations on the String type, not a separate data type.

keyPoints: GETBIT reads one bit from the String held by the key.
The offset is zero-based, so the first bit uses offset 0.
The result is an integer with only two possible values: 0 or 1.
The command runs in constant time, O(1).
Redis bitmaps use String values together with bit operations.
Redis added GETBIT in version 2.2.0.
gotchas: Reading beyond the current string length returns 0. The command does not need the string to contain that position.
A missing key behaves like an empty string, so GETBIT returns 0.

GETDEL.summary: GETDEL returns a string value and deletes its key in the same command. It returns nil when the key is missing or does not contain a string.
GETDEL.explanation: GETDEL atomically retrieves a key's string value and removes that key when the operation succeeds. If the key is absent or holds a non-string value, it returns a nil response and does not provide a value.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key to retrieve and then delete.

GETDEL.returns: Bulk string reply containing the key's value, or a nil reply when the key does not exist or its value is not a string.

example.title: Read and remove a session value
example.code:
SET session:42 "user-123"
GETDEL session:42
GET session:42
example.explanation: The first command stores a string, GETDEL returns it while deleting the key, and the final GET returns nil.

useCases.title: One-time token consumption
useCases.scenario: Consume one-time tokens, then remove them after successful retrieval.

useCases.title: Read-and-invalidate caching
useCases.scenario: Fetch a transient cache entry while ensuring it cannot be read again.

useCases.title: Single-use work items
useCases.scenario: Atomically take ownership of a temporary string-valued work item.

interview.question: What does GETDEL do?
interview.answer: GETDEL takes one key, returns its string value, and deletes the key on success. It combines retrieval and removal in one Redis command.
interview.followUp: What happens for a hash key? GETDEL returns nil because the value type is not a string, rather than returning the hash contents.

interview.question: What is the command syntax and input?
interview.answer: The syntax is `GETDEL key`. The key identifies the value to read and then delete.
interview.followUp: How would you delete several keys? Use DEL with multiple key arguments, because GETDEL accepts only one key.

interview.question: What replies can GETDEL return?
interview.answer: A bulk string reply contains the value. A nil response means the key is absent or its value is not a string.
interview.followUp: Why should a client not treat nil as an empty string? Redis uses nil to represent the missing or incompatible-type cases, while an existing empty string is still a string value.

keyPoints: GETDEL combines reading and deletion for one key.
Unlike GET, a successful GETDEL removes the key after retrieving its value.
The required argument is the key name whose value should be returned and removed.
For an existing string key, the result is the stored value as a bulk string.
gotchas: Deletion applies only when the key contains a string; a non-string value produces a nil response.
Missing keys and keys with another data type both return nil, so callers must distinguish nil from an empty string.

GETEX.summary: Returns a string value while optionally setting, changing, or removing the key's expiration. GETEX supports relative and absolute expiration forms and is a write command.
GETEX.explanation: GETEX reads the string stored at a key and can change that key's expiration in the same command. Choose one mutually exclusive option: a relative lifetime with EX or PX, an absolute expiration with EXAT or PXAT, or PERSIST to remove the existing lifetime.
GETEX.syntax: GETEX key [EX seconds | PX milliseconds | EXAT unix-time-seconds | PXAT unix-time-milliseconds | PERSIST]

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Name of the string key to retrieve.

parameters.name: EX seconds
parameters.description: Relative expiration duration in seconds.

parameters.name: PX milliseconds
parameters.description: Relative expiration duration in milliseconds.

parameters.name: EXAT unix-time-seconds
parameters.description: Absolute Unix expiration time in seconds.

parameters.name: PXAT unix-time-milliseconds
parameters.description: Absolute Unix expiration time in milliseconds.

parameters.name: PERSIST
parameters.description: Remove the key's associated TTL.

GETEX.returns: Bulk string reply containing the value of `key`; a nil reply if the key does not exist.

example.title: Read and refresh a cache entry
example.code:
SET session:42 "user-data"
GETEX session:42 EX 300
example.explanation: Stores a value, then reads it while assigning a five-minute expiration.

useCases.title: Cache entry refresh
useCases.scenario: Read a cached value and assign a fresh relative lifetime in one operation.

useCases.title: Relative expiration
useCases.scenario: Apply a millisecond-precision or second-precision deadline supplied by an application.

useCases.title: Absolute deadline
useCases.scenario: Use a shared Unix deadline when several processes must observe the same expiry instant.

useCases.title: Make a key persistent
useCases.scenario: Read a value while removing its existing TTL.

interview.question: What does GETEX do, and how does it differ from GET?
interview.answer: GETEX returns the string value for a key and optionally changes its expiration. Unlike GET, it is a write command because expiration metadata may be changed.
interview.followUp: Why might GETEX be useful in a cache? It can retrieve an entry and refresh or assign its lifetime in one command, avoiding a separate expiration update.

interview.question: What expiration modes does GETEX support?
interview.answer: EX sets a relative lifetime in seconds, while PX uses milliseconds. EXAT and PXAT instead specify absolute Unix expiration times; PERSIST removes the key's associated TTL.
interview.followUp: Which option is appropriate for a deadline shared across clients? EXAT or PXAT, because both represent an absolute expiration instant.

interview.question: What does GETEX return when the key is absent?
interview.answer: If the key exists, GETEX returns its string value. If it does not exist, the command returns a nil or null reply, depending on the client representation.
interview.followUp: What should application code do with a missing result? Treat it as a cache miss and avoid assuming the returned value is an empty string.

keyPoints: GETEX combines reading a key with optional expiration management.
EXAT sets expiration at an absolute Unix timestamp expressed in seconds.
PXAT sets expiration at an absolute Unix timestamp expressed in milliseconds.
gotchas: Only one expiration option may be supplied in a GETEX call.
Although it returns a value like GET, GETEX is classified as a write command because it can modify expiration metadata.
A missing key produces a nil reply rather than a string value.

GETRANGE.summary: Returns a substring of the Redis string stored at a key, using inclusive zero-based start and end offsets. Negative offsets count backward from the string's end.
GETRANGE.explanation: GETRANGE reads part of the string stored at a key. The start and end offsets are zero-based and inclusive; negative offsets count backward from the string's end, and bounds outside the value are clipped to its actual length.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key.

parameters.name: start
parameters.description: The zero-based starting offset; negative values count from the string's end.

parameters.name: end
parameters.description: The zero-based inclusive ending offset; negative values count from the string's end.

GETRANGE.returns: Bulk string reply containing the substring selected by the inclusive start and end offsets.

example.title: Read string substrings
example.explanation: Stores a string, then retrieves an inclusive prefix, suffix, and the complete value using zero-based and negative offsets.

useCases.title: Partial string reads
useCases.scenario: Read a fixed-width prefix or suffix from a stored string without retrieving the entire value.

useCases.title: Suffix inspection
useCases.scenario: Use negative offsets to inspect the tail of a string, such as its final characters.

useCases.title: Offset-based data access
useCases.scenario: Retrieve bounded sections of serialized or packed string data using known offsets.

interview.question: What does GETRANGE do and what is its syntax?
interview.answer: GETRANGE returns a substring from the string value at a key. Its syntax is `GETRANGE key start end`, and both offsets are zero-based and inclusive.
interview.followUp: How does it behave with negative indexes? Negative offsets count backward from the end: -1 is the last character and -2 is the penultimate.

interview.question: How do negative offsets work?
interview.answer: A negative start or end counts from the string's end. For example, `-3 -1` selects the final three characters.
interview.followUp: What happens if the requested range exceeds the value? Redis limits the range to the actual string length.

interview.question: What does GETRANGE return and how does its cost depend on the request?
interview.answer: The command returns a bulk string reply containing the selected substring. If the key does not contain a string value, the command is not applicable to that data type.
interview.followUp: What is the performance characteristic? The work is O(N), where N is the length of the returned substring.

keyPoints: GETRANGE extracts a portion of a Redis string without modifying the stored value.
The required `key` argument identifies the string to read.
`start` begins at character position zero for the first character.
`end` identifies the final included position and uses zero-based indexing.
Negative values allow suffix-oriented reads without first determining the string length.
The result is returned as a bulk string containing the selected data.
The command takes exactly one key and two integer offsets.
gotchas: The end index is included, so requesting 0 through 3 returns four characters when all positions exist.
Indexes beyond the string's boundaries are clipped rather than causing an error.

GETSET.summary: GETSET atomically replaces a key's string value and returns the value previously stored there. It is deprecated since Redis 6.2.0; new code should use SET with GET.
GETSET.explanation: GETSET performs an atomic replacement of a key's string value and returns the value that was there before. If the key is absent, it creates it and returns a nil reply; a successful replacement also removes any existing expiration.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The new value to set.

GETSET.returns: A bulk string containing the old value, or a nil reply if the key does not exist; an error is returned when the existing key is not a string.

example.title: Replace a value and retrieve the old one
example.code:
redis-cli SET mykey "Hello"
redis-cli GETSET mykey "World"
redis-cli GET mykey
example.explanation: The command replaces the existing string and prints its previous value; the final GET confirms the new value.

useCases.title: Read and reset a counter
useCases.scenario: A producer increments an event counter, while a consumer periodically reads and clears the accumulated count as one atomic operation.

useCases.title: Compatibility migration
useCases.scenario: A legacy Redis integration needs to preserve the atomic replace-and-return-old-value behavior during migration.

interview.question: What does GETSET do, and what does it return when the key is missing?
interview.answer: GETSET atomically writes a new string value and returns the old string value. If the key does not exist, it returns nil after creating the key.
interview.followUp: How should new code replace GETSET? Use SET with the GET option, which provides the replacement-and-return-old-value behavior while avoiding this deprecated command.

interview.question: What replies and errors can GETSET produce?
interview.answer: It returns a bulk string containing the prior value, or a nil reply when the key is absent. If the key exists with a non-string value, Redis returns an error.
interview.followUp: What happens to expiration? A successful replacement discards the key's previous TTL, so use an appropriate SET expiration option when migrating.

interview.question: Give a practical atomic use case for GETSET.
interview.answer: The command is atomic, so it is useful when a counter must be read and reset without an intervening update. A documented pattern increments a counter with INCR and resets it with GETSET mycounter "0".
interview.followUp: Why is SET GET preferable for new implementations? GETSET is deprecated as of Redis 6.2.0, while SET supports the GET option and additional expiration controls.

keyPoints: It combines replacement and retrieval of the previous string value into one atomic operation.
Its command form takes exactly one key and the replacement value.
The key argument identifies the string entry to replace.
The value argument becomes the key's new string content.
When an old value exists, the reply contains that previous value.
A missing key produces a nil reply after the new value is stored.
A useful pattern is to increment an event counter and atomically read-and-reset it.
gotchas: GETSET is deprecated from Redis 6.2.0 onward; use SET with the GET option for new code or migrations.
The operation fails if the existing key contains a non-string data type.
A successful update removes the key's previous TTL.

Hash.summary: Redis hashes store field-value pairs under one key. They suit simple, flat objects and support field reads, updates, deletion, numeric changes, queries, and individual field expiration.
Hash.explanation: A Redis hash stores field-value pairs under one Redis key. Use hash commands to read, change, remove, increment, and expire individual fields; field values are strings, but some commands treat them as numbers.
Hash.syntax:
HSET key field value [field value ...]
HGET key field
HMGET key field [field ...]
HINCRBY key field increment
HGETALL key

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The Redis key that contains the hash.

parameters.name: field
parameters.description: The field name inside the hash.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The string value stored for the field.

parameters.name: increment
parameters.description: An integer change applied by HINCRBY.

Hash.returns: Command-specific results include field values, integer counts, or status replies.

example.title: Basic hash operations
example.code:
HSET user:42 name Ada visits 0
HGET user:42 name
HINCRBY user:42 visits 1
HMGET user:42 name visits
example.explanation: This stores two fields, reads one field, increments a numeric field, and reads both fields in one command.

useCases.title: Simple objects
useCases.scenario: Store a user profile with fields such as name, email, and status.

useCases.title: Counters
useCases.scenario: Keep several counters together, such as views, likes, and errors.

useCases.title: Field-level expiration
useCases.scenario: Expire one field without expiring the whole object.

useCases.title: Searchable flat data
useCases.scenario: Index and query flat object fields with Redis Search.

interview.question: What is a Redis hash used for?
interview.answer: A hash is a collection of field-value pairs stored under one Redis key. It fits simple objects with a small number of flat fields.
interview.followUp: When would JSON be a better choice? Use JSON for deeply nested structures, arrays, or richer search features.

interview.question: How do you read and write hash fields?
interview.answer: HSET writes one or more fields, and HGET reads one field. HMGET reads several named fields in one command, which can reduce client-server round trips.
interview.followUp: How would you read every field? Use HGETALL, but remember that its cost grows with the number of fields.

interview.question: How do you update a counter in a hash?
interview.answer: HINCRBY changes an integer field by a specified amount. If the field does not exist, Redis treats its starting value as zero.
interview.followUp: How can a hash field expire? Use HEXPIRE for seconds, HPEXPIRE for milliseconds, or HEXPIREAT for an absolute time.

keyPoints: A hash groups related field-value pairs under one Redis key.
Hash commands support reading, writing, deleting, and changing fields.
HINCRBY is useful for integer counters and creates a missing counter at zero.
Redis supports expiration for individual fields, not only for the whole hash key.
gotchas: Hash values are stored as strings. Use numeric hash commands only when the field contains a valid number.
Use a hash for simple, mostly flat objects. Use JSON when the object needs nested fields or arrays.

HDEL.summary: HDEL deletes one or more fields from a Redis hash. It ignores missing fields, removes the hash when no fields remain, and returns the number of fields actually deleted.
HDEL.explanation: HDEL removes one or more named fields from the hash stored at a key. Missing fields do not affect the result, and Redis removes the key automatically when the last remaining field is deleted.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key that holds the hash.

parameters.name: field [field ...]
parameters.description: One or more fields to delete from the hash.

HDEL.returns: An integer: the number of fields removed, excluding requested fields that did not exist.

example.title: Remove fields from a hash
example.code:
HSET user:42 name "Ada" role "admin"
HDEL user:42 role name
HGETALL user:42
example.explanation: Creates two hash fields, removes both, then shows that the hash is empty and has been deleted.

useCases.title: Partial record updates
useCases.scenario: Remove obsolete or user-edited attributes from a hash without replacing the entire object.

useCases.title: Batch field removal
useCases.scenario: Delete several known hash fields in one request.

useCases.title: Automatic empty-hash cleanup
useCases.scenario: Clean up a hash and let Redis remove its key when the last field disappears.

interview.question: What does HDEL return?
interview.answer: HDEL removes the requested fields from a hash and returns the number of fields actually removed. Requested fields that were absent are excluded from that count.
interview.followUp: What happens when the final field is removed? Redis deletes the hash key, so subsequent access treats it as nonexistent.

interview.question: What is the HDEL command syntax?
interview.answer: Its syntax is `HDEL key field [field ...]`. The command accepts one hash key and one or more fields in a single operation.
interview.followUp: How would you remove fields from several unrelated hashes? Issue a separate HDEL command for each hash key; HDEL operates on one key per invocation.

interview.question: What is HDEL's time complexity?
interview.answer: HDEL has linear complexity in the number of fields supplied for deletion, shown as O(N) in the command example. It is classified as a write and hash command.
interview.followUp: What determines N here? N is the number of fields passed to the command, not the total number of fields already stored in the hash.

keyPoints: Use HDEL to delete selected field-value pairs while leaving other fields in the same hash untouched.
Removing the final existing field also removes the parent hash key.
The command supports deleting multiple fields in one call.
The integer reply counts only fields that existed and were successfully removed.
Redis categorizes HDEL as a write operation on hashes and marks it as fast.
gotchas: Deleting a missing field is not an error and does not increase the returned count.
A missing hash key produces a zero result rather than an error.

HELLO.summary: HELLO performs a Redis connection handshake. It can select RESP2 or RESP3, authenticate the connection, set its name, and return server and connection details.
HELLO.explanation: HELLO performs a connection handshake. It can select RESP2 or RESP3, authenticate the connection, and set its name in one command. It also returns server and connection details such as the Redis version, protocol, connection ID, mode, role, and loaded modules.

parameters.name: protover
parameters.description: The RESP protocol version to select. Use 2 or 3. Required when another option is present.

parameters.name: AUTH username password
parameters.description: Optional authentication credentials: a username and password.

parameters.name: SETNAME clientname
parameters.description: The name to assign to the current connection.

HELLO.returns: A list of current server and connection properties, including protocol, version, connection ID, mode, role, and modules.

example.title: Switch protocol and authenticate
example.code: redis-cli HELLO 3 AUTH default secret SETNAME app-client
example.explanation: This changes the connection to RESP3, authenticates it, and names the connection.

useCases.title: Select RESP3
useCases.scenario: A client needs structured RESP3 replies instead of RESP2 replies.

useCases.title: Authenticate during connection setup
useCases.scenario: A new connection needs credentials during setup.

useCases.title: Name a connection
useCases.scenario: Operators need to identify a connection in Redis client tools.

useCases.title: Inspect connection details
useCases.scenario: A client needs server and connection metadata after connecting.

interview.question: What does HELLO do?
interview.answer: HELLO is a connection handshake command. It can change the connection between RESP2 and RESP3, authenticate it, and set a client name.
interview.followUp: How does a client request RESP3? Send HELLO 3. The reply uses RESP3 data types.

interview.question: What arguments does HELLO accept?
interview.answer: The syntax is HELLO [protover [AUTH username password] [SETNAME clientname]]. protover must be 2 or 3, and it is required when AUTH or SETNAME is included.
interview.followUp: Can AUTH be used without first calling AUTH separately? Yes. HELLO can authenticate while selecting the protocol.

interview.question: What does HELLO return?
interview.answer: HELLO returns server and connection properties, including the Redis version, protocol number, connection ID, mode, role, and loaded modules. Its time complexity is O(1).
interview.followUp: What changes when RESP3 is selected? Replies can use more meaningful types, such as a map for HGETALL instead of an array.

keyPoints: HELLO starts a handshake with the Redis server.
Redis supports RESP2 and RESP3 from Redis 6 onward.
A new connection starts in RESP2 mode.
Set protover to 2 or 3 to choose the protocol.
AUTH can authenticate while the command changes the protocol.
SETNAME assigns a name to the current connection.
The command returns current server and connection properties.
gotchas: You must provide protover when using AUTH or SETNAME.
Use the username default with the older requirepass authentication method.
With no arguments, HELLO reports the current connection context in Redis 6.2 and later.

HEXISTS.summary: Checks whether a field exists in a Redis hash. It returns 1 for an existing field and 0 when the field or hash key is absent.
HEXISTS.explanation: HEXISTS tests whether one field is present in the hash stored at a key. It returns 1 when the field exists and 0 when either the field is absent or the key does not exist; using a non-hash key produces a wrong-type error.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key that holds the hash.

parameters.name: field
parameters.description: The field to check for existence.

HEXISTS.returns: Integer reply: 1 if the hash contains the field; 0 if it does not contain the field or the key does not exist.

example.title: Check hash-field existence
example.code:
HSET user:42 name "Ada"
HEXISTS user:42 name
HEXISTS user:42 email
example.explanation: Creates a hash field, then checks two fields; Redis returns 1 for the existing name and 0 for the absent email.

useCases.title: Presence checks
useCases.scenario: Validate whether an optional attribute has been stored before reading or updating it.

useCases.title: Conditional hash handling
useCases.scenario: Avoid treating a missing hash field as an existing value in application logic.

useCases.title: Record inspection
useCases.scenario: Test membership of feature flags, user attributes, or other hash-backed records.

interview.question: What does HEXISTS do?
interview.answer: HEXISTS takes a hash key and one field name. It returns 1 when that field exists in the hash, otherwise 0, including when the key is missing.
interview.followUp: What is its time complexity? It is O(1), so checking one field does not require scanning the hash.

interview.question: What arguments does HEXISTS require?
interview.answer: The command accepts exactly two arguments after the command name: the key containing the hash and the field to test. Its syntax is HEXISTS key field.
interview.followUp: How would you check several fields? Issue separate HEXISTS commands or use a pipelined client operation; HEXISTS itself checks one field per invocation.

interview.question: How should the return value be interpreted?
interview.answer: A result of 0 is ambiguous: the hash may not contain the field, or the key may not exist. A result of 1 means the field is present in the hash.
interview.followUp: What happens if the key stores a string, list, or another non-hash type? Redis reports a wrong-type error rather than returning 0 or 1.

keyPoints: Tests one named field in the hash associated with the supplied key.
The key argument identifies the Redis hash to inspect.
The field argument is the hash-field name whose presence is tested.
Redis returns integer 0 when the field is absent.
Redis returns integer 1 when the field exists.
The command has a fixed two-argument signature: a hash key followed by a field.
gotchas: A missing key produces the same 0 result as a hash that lacks the requested field.
The command's documented result is an integer reply, not the field's stored value.

HGET.summary: Returns the value of one field in a Redis hash. If the field or its hash key does not exist, Redis returns nil/null.
HGET.explanation: HGET looks up one field in the hash stored at the specified key. Redis returns that field's string value when present; otherwise it returns a nil or null response when the field or key is absent.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key that holds the hash.

parameters.name: field
parameters.description: The field whose value to retrieve.

HGET.returns: A bulk string containing the field value, or a nil/null reply if the field is absent or the key does not exist.

example.title: Read a hash field
example.code:
HSET user:42 name "Ada"
HGET user:42 name
HGET user:42 email
example.explanation: Stores a hash field, retrieves an existing value, then demonstrates the nil result for a missing field.

useCases.title: Cache field lookup
useCases.scenario: Read one attribute from a cached object stored as a Redis hash.

useCases.title: Targeted application reads
useCases.scenario: Fetch a single counter, status, or metadata field without reading the complete hash.

useCases.title: Presence checks
useCases.scenario: Check whether a hash field exists by distinguishing a value response from nil/null.

interview.question: What does HGET do, and what does it return when the field is missing?
interview.answer: HGET reads one field from a Redis hash using the key and field arguments. Its average time complexity is O(1), and it returns a bulk string when the field exists or nil when it does not.
interview.followUp: How would you read several fields? Use HMGET, which returns an array of values in the same order as the requested fields.

interview.question: What is the syntax and purpose of each argument?
interview.answer: The command syntax is HGET key field. The key identifies the hash, and field identifies the single hash field whose value should be retrieved.
interview.followUp: What happens if the key contains a non-hash value? Redis reports a WRONGTYPE error rather than treating the value as a hash.

interview.question: Why is HGET efficient for single-field reads?
interview.answer: HGET has O(1) complexity because it retrieves one hash field. It is therefore suitable for targeted reads when an application needs a single attribute rather than the whole hash.
interview.followUp: What command retrieves every field and value? HGETALL does so, but its cost grows with the size of the hash.

keyPoints: HGET retrieves exactly one field value from a Redis hash.
The key selects the hash, while the field selects the value inside it.
An existing field is returned as a bulk string value.
Redis signals absence with a nil/null reply when either the field or hash key is missing.
The command is categorized as a read operation for hashes and as fast.
gotchas: A missing field and a missing hash key both produce a nil/null response, so callers must handle absence explicitly.

HGETALL.summary: Returns every field and value in the hash stored at a key. The operation is O(N), where N is the number of fields.
HGETALL.explanation: HGETALL reads the hash stored at the specified key and returns every field together with its value. The response represents each field immediately followed by its value, so the flat reply contains twice as many elements as the hash has fields.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key that holds the hash.

HGETALL.returns: An array containing all field names and values in the hash; each field is followed by its value. If the hash is empty or the key does not exist, the result is empty.

example.title: Read a complete hash
example.code:
HSET user:42 name Ada language Redis
HGETALL user:42
example.explanation: Creates a hash and returns its complete field-value mapping.

useCases.title: Inspect a hash
useCases.scenario: A diagnostic or administration tool needs to display the complete contents of a hash.

useCases.title: Load a complete cached record
useCases.scenario: An application needs to materialize all attributes associated with one cached entity.

useCases.title: Export hash contents
useCases.scenario: A migration or synchronization job must enumerate every field-value pair for a hash.

interview.question: What does HGETALL return and what is its complexity?
interview.answer: HGETALL takes one key and returns all fields and values in the hash stored there. Its time complexity is O(N), where N is the hash size.
interview.followUp: When should a client avoid it for a large hash? Use field-specific reads such as HMGET when only a subset is needed, because HGETALL processes every field.

interview.question: What is the command syntax and role of key?
interview.answer: The command syntax is HGETALL key. The key identifies the hash whose complete contents Redis should return.
interview.followUp: What happens when the key does not hold a hash? Redis reports a wrong-type error rather than treating another data type as a hash.

interview.question: When was HGETALL introduced, and how does its cost scale?
interview.answer: HGETALL was introduced in Redis 2.0.0. It is a read operation for hashes and is classified as a slow command because its work scales with the number of fields.
interview.followUp: How can an application reduce work when it needs selected fields? Issue HMGET with the required field names instead of retrieving the complete hash.

keyPoints: It retrieves the complete contents of the hash identified by key.
The returned sequence alternates each field name with that field's value.
Execution cost grows linearly with the number of fields in the hash.
The only required argument is the key containing the target hash.
The command is categorized as a hash read operation with slow, size-dependent work.
gotchas: The raw Redis reply is a flat sequence, not alternating nested field-value objects; its element count is twice the number of fields.

HINCRBY.summary: HINCRBY adds a signed integer to a field in a Redis hash and returns the updated value. Missing hashes and fields are created automatically, with a missing field starting at zero.
HINCRBY.explanation: HINCRBY adds a signed integer to a field in a Redis hash and returns the field's new value. Redis creates the hash when its key is absent and treats an absent field as zero before applying the increment; values must fit a signed 64-bit integer.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key that holds the hash.

parameters.name: field
parameters.description: The field whose value to increment.

parameters.name: increment
parameters.description: The integer amount to add to the field's value.

HINCRBY.returns: An integer reply containing the field's value after the increment operation.

example.title: Increment and decrement a hash counter
example.code:
HSET counters page_views 10
HINCRBY counters page_views 1
HINCRBY counters page_views -2
HGET counters page_views
example.explanation: Creates a numeric hash field, increments it, decrements it, then reads the resulting value.

useCases.title: Event counters
useCases.scenario: Track page views, API requests, downloads, or other event totals in a hash.

useCases.title: Quantity updates
useCases.scenario: Adjust inventory or balance-like integer quantities by positive or negative amounts.

useCases.title: Grouped metrics
useCases.scenario: Maintain several related integer counters under one Redis hash key.

interview.question: What does HINCRBY do?
interview.answer: HINCRBY takes a hash key, a field name, and a signed integer increment. It returns the field value after applying the operation.
interview.followUp: What happens when either the hash key or field is missing? Redis creates the hash if the key is absent and initializes the missing field to zero.

interview.question: Can HINCRBY decrement a value?
interview.answer: The command supports negative increments, so it can decrement a counter as well as increment one. The returned integer is the updated field value.
interview.followUp: How would you decrement by 10? Use `HINCRBY key field -10`.

interview.question: What are HINCRBY's complexity and numeric limits?
interview.answer: HINCRBY has O(1) time complexity. The increment argument and resulting value are constrained to signed 64-bit integers.
interview.followUp: What should be used for decimal values? Use the separate HINCRBYFLOAT command, which is intended for floating-point hash fields.

keyPoints: It updates one hash field by adding the supplied integer increment.
A missing hash key is automatically created as part of the operation.
A missing field starts at zero before the increment is applied.
Positive and negative increments support both increasing and decreasing counters.
The response is the field's new integer value, not the previous value.
gotchas: The increment and resulting value must remain within the signed 64-bit integer range.

HKEYS.summary: HKEYS returns all field names in the hash stored at a key. It returns an empty list when the key does not exist and has O(N) complexity based on the hash size.
HKEYS.explanation: HKEYS reads the hash stored at a key and returns every field name without returning field values. It performs work proportional to the number of fields, and a missing key produces an empty list.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The Redis key that stores the hash whose field names should be returned.

HKEYS.returns: An array containing the hash's field names; it is empty if the key does not exist.

example.title: List hash fields
example.explanation: Creates a hash, then retrieves only its field names with HKEYS.

useCases.title: Inspect available hash fields
useCases.scenario: An application needs to discover which attributes are present before fetching selected values.

useCases.title: Expose cached object schema
useCases.scenario: A cache stores an object as a Redis hash and a UI or API needs its attribute names.

useCases.title: Audit hash contents
useCases.scenario: A maintenance task checks the fields currently stored in a hash without retrieving their values.

interview.question: What does HKEYS return?
interview.answer: HKEYS takes one hash key and returns an array containing all field names in that hash. It does not return the associated values.
interview.followUp: What is its complexity? It is O(N), where N is the number of fields in the hash, so it may be expensive for large hashes.

interview.question: What is the syntax of HKEYS?
interview.answer: The command is HKEYS key. The key identifies the Redis hash whose field names should be listed.
interview.followUp: How would you retrieve both names and values? Use HGETALL, while HKEYS is appropriate when only names are needed.

interview.question: What are HKEYS's complexity and missing-key behaviors?
interview.answer: HKEYS has O(N) time complexity, with N equal to the hash size. The result is an array reply, or an empty list when the key does not exist.
interview.followUp: What should a client do when the result is empty? Treat it as either a missing key or a hash with no remaining fields, depending on application context.

keyPoints: HKEYS lists every field name belonging to the hash at the supplied key.
Runtime grows linearly with the number of fields in the hash.
Its sole argument is the key containing the target hash.
Clients receive the result as an array-like list of field names.
Redis Open Source has supported HKEYS since version 2.0.0.
gotchas: A nonexistent key is not an error; Redis returns an empty list.

HLEN.summary: HLEN returns the number of fields in a Redis hash. It runs in O(1) time and returns 0 when the key does not exist.
HLEN.explanation: HLEN takes the key of a Redis hash and returns how many fields it currently contains. The count is constant-time, and a missing key behaves like an empty hash, so the result is 0; using a key with another data type produces a wrong-type error.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key that holds the hash.

HLEN.returns: The number of fields in the hash, or 0 when the key does not exist.

example.title: Count hash fields
example.code:
HSET user:42 name Ada language Redis
HLEN user:42
example.explanation: Creates two fields, then returns their count: 2.

useCases.title: Presence and emptiness checks
useCases.scenario: Check whether a hash contains any fields without retrieving its contents.

useCases.title: Hash cardinality metrics
useCases.scenario: Track the number of attributes, counters, or members represented by a hash.

interview.question: What does HLEN return, and what is its time complexity?
interview.answer: HLEN returns the number of fields stored in the hash at the supplied key. Its command complexity is O(1), so the count does not require scanning every field.
interview.followUp: What happens when the key is absent? Redis returns 0, treating the missing key as an empty hash.

interview.question: What is the syntax and required argument for HLEN?
interview.answer: The syntax is `HLEN key`. The key identifies the Redis hash whose field count should be returned.
interview.followUp: How would you count values rather than fields? Use a command such as HVALS to retrieve the values, but that operation is O(N).

interview.question: When was HLEN introduced, and what does its result represent?
interview.answer: HLEN was introduced in Redis 2.0.0 and returns a long integer containing the number of hash fields. It is categorized as a read, hash, and fast command.
interview.followUp: What should a client do if the key contains a string instead of a hash? Handle the WRONGTYPE response and correct the key's data-model usage.

keyPoints: HLEN is a read operation for hashes and is marked fast.
Its single argument is the key containing the hash.
The response is an integer field count, with zero for a nonexistent key.
Redis introduced HLEN in version 2.0.0.
gotchas: A missing key returns 0, not an error, because Redis treats it as an empty hash.
HLEN counts fields, not the total size of field names and values.

HMGET.summary: Returns the values of multiple fields from a Redis hash, preserving field order and representing missing fields with nil.
HMGET.explanation: HMGET reads several fields from the hash stored at key in one command. Redis returns one result for each requested field, preserving request order and using a nil value when a field is absent.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key that holds the hash.

parameters.name: field [field ...]
parameters.description: One or more fields whose values to retrieve.

HMGET.returns: An array containing one value for each requested field, in request order; an absent field yields nil.

example.title: Read selected hash fields
example.code:
redis-cli HSET user:42 name Ada role engineer
redis-cli HMGET user:42 name role missing
example.explanation: The result contains values aligned with the requested fields; the missing field produces a nil entry.

useCases.title: Selective hash reads
useCases.scenario: Read a selected subset of attributes from a hash without fetching unrelated fields.

useCases.title: Batch field retrieval
useCases.scenario: Fetch several values in one command to reduce client-server round trips.

interview.question: What does HMGET do, and what is its complexity?
interview.answer: HMGET retrieves multiple fields from one Redis hash using a single command. Its time complexity is O(N), where N is the number of requested fields.
interview.followUp: How does it differ from HGETALL? HGETALL returns every field and value, while HMGET limits the response to the explicitly requested fields.

interview.question: In what order does HMGET return values?
interview.answer: The returned values follow the same order as the fields in the request. This lets callers associate each result with its corresponding input field by position.
interview.followUp: What happens for an absent field? Redis places a nil value at that field's corresponding result position.

interview.question: What are HMGET's required arguments and missing-field behavior?
interview.answer: The key must identify a hash, and the command requires at least one field name. Asking for a field that is not present returns nil rather than failing the entire command.
interview.followUp: What if the key contains another Redis data type? The command reports a wrong-type error because HMGET operates on hashes.

keyPoints: HMGET retrieves multiple values from a single hash.
The first argument identifies the hash to read.
The command accepts one or more field names after the key.
Execution cost grows linearly with the number of requested fields.
Results correspond positionally to the requested field order.

HRANDFIELD.summary: Returns one or more randomly selected fields from a hash. Positive counts select distinct fields up to the hash size; negative counts allow repeats, and WITHVALUES also returns the selected values.
HRANDFIELD.explanation: HRANDFIELD samples fields from the hash at key. Without count it returns one field; a positive count requests distinct fields up to the hash size, while a negative count requests exactly the absolute count and permits repeats. WITHVALUES adds each selected field's value and requires count.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key that holds the hash.

parameters.name: count
parameters.description: The number of fields to return. Positive values request up to that many distinct fields; negative values request exactly the absolute value and may repeat fields. If omitted, one field is returned.

parameters.name: WITHVALUES
parameters.description: Also return the value of each selected field; usable only with count.

HRANDFIELD.returns: A single field when count is omitted; otherwise an array of fields, or fields and values when count and WITHVALUES are both used. A negative count returns an empty array for an empty or missing hash.

example.title: Select random hash fields
example.code:
HSET coin heads 60 tails 40
HRANDFIELD coin
HRANDFIELD coin 2
HRANDFIELD coin -5 WITHVALUES
example.explanation: Creates a hash, selects one random field, selects up to two distinct fields, then requests five selections with their values; the final command may repeat fields.

useCases.title: Sample one candidate setting
useCases.scenario: Feature flags or configuration hashes

useCases.title: Choose several distinct options
useCases.scenario: Randomized menus and recommendations

useCases.title: Draw a fixed-size sample with replacement
useCases.scenario: Weighted or repeated trials represented by hash fields

useCases.title: Retrieve sampled fields with their values
useCases.scenario: Cache inspection or randomized diagnostics

interview.question: How does HRANDFIELD interpret positive and negative count values?
interview.answer: Without count, HRANDFIELD returns one random field. With a positive count, it returns up to count distinct fields, capped by the hash size.
interview.followUp: What changes for a negative count? It returns exactly the absolute count and can repeat fields.

interview.question: What does WITHVALUES do?
interview.answer: WITHVALUES makes the response include each selected field together with its associated value. The modifier must be used with count.
interview.followUp: How should a client handle the response shape? Branch on whether WITHVALUES was requested and parse field/value pairs accordingly.

interview.question: What happens when the hash does not exist?
interview.answer: A missing key behaves like an empty hash for sampling purposes. A negative count returns an empty array in that case, while a no-count request has no field to return.
interview.followUp: What ordering guarantee exists? The reply order is not truly random, so shuffle it in the client if required.

keyPoints: Calling the command with only a key samples one field from that hash.
A positive count produces distinct fields rather than repeated selections.
Positive-count results are capped by the number of fields actually stored.
Negative counts switch sampling to replacement, so duplicate fields are possible.
The number requested by a negative count is its absolute value.
WITHVALUES extends each selection with its hash value.
gotchas: Do not assume the returned order is randomized; shuffle the client-side result when ordering matters.
WITHVALUES cannot be used alone; it is valid only when count is supplied.
Negative counts normally produce the requested number of selections, but an empty or missing hash returns an empty array.

HSCAN.summary: HSCAN incrementally iterates through the fields of a Redis hash. It supports glob matching, a COUNT hint, and NOVALUES for returning field names without values.
HSCAN.explanation: HSCAN incrementally walks the fields of a hash. Begin with cursor 0, optionally filter field names with a glob pattern, suggest a batch size, or request names without values; continue using each returned cursor until it becomes 0.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Name of the key holding the hash.

parameters.name: cursor
parameters.description: Cursor for the current scan; begin with 0 and reuse the returned cursor.

parameters.name: MATCH pattern
parameters.description: Optional glob-style pattern for matching field names.

parameters.name: COUNT count
parameters.description: Optional hint for the number of fields returned per iteration; default 10.

parameters.name: NOVALUES
parameters.description: Optional flag that returns field names without values.

HSCAN.returns: A two-element array containing the next cursor and the scanned fields with values, or only fields when NOVALUES is used.

example.title: Scan matching hash fields
example.code:
HSET user:42 name Ada role engineer
HSCAN user:42 0 MATCH r* COUNT 10
example.explanation: Run the command repeatedly with the returned cursor until it is 0; the example filters hash fields beginning with r.

useCases.title: Incremental hash traversal
useCases.scenario: Enumerate a large hash in bounded batches without requesting every field at once.

useCases.title: Pattern-filtered inspection
useCases.scenario: Select only fields whose names match a glob-style naming pattern.

useCases.title: Field-only enumeration
useCases.scenario: Discover hash field names while avoiding value transfer.

interview.question: How does HSCAN iteration work?
interview.answer: HSCAN iterates a hash incrementally instead of returning the entire collection in one call. Start with cursor 0 and pass each returned cursor into the next call until the cursor returns to 0.
interview.followUp: How would you avoid blocking work on a large hash? Use repeated HSCAN calls and process each batch as it arrives, rather than using a single bulk retrieval operation.

interview.question: What do MATCH and COUNT do?
interview.answer: MATCH accepts a glob-style pattern and limits returned fields to matching names. COUNT supplies a suggested number of fields for an iteration, with a default of 10.
interview.followUp: Can MATCH guarantee that every call returns matching fields? No; filtering can produce an empty batch even while the cursor has not returned to 0.

interview.question: What does NOVALUES change?
interview.answer: Without NOVALUES, the response contains a cursor and scanned field/value pairs. With NOVALUES, Redis returns only field names; the option was introduced in Redis 7.4.
interview.followUp: When is NOVALUES useful? Use it when values are unnecessary, reducing the response data needed to enumerate hash fields.

keyPoints: The command takes a hash key and cursor, with optional MATCH, COUNT, and NOVALUES modifiers.
Initialize the scan with cursor 0 and continue with the cursor returned by Redis.
If COUNT is omitted, Redis uses 10 as the default iteration-size hint.
The reply has two top-level parts: the next cursor and the scanned results.
Normal results contain hash fields and their values as pairs.
Each individual HSCAN call has constant time complexity; completing a full iteration is O(N).
gotchas: MATCH filters field names using glob-style matching; it does not perform a general-purpose search.
COUNT is only a per-iteration hint, so a call may return fewer or more fields than requested.
Do not depend on the order of returned fields; collect or sort results when ordering matters.
NOVALUES changes the response shape by omitting values, so consumers must handle fields rather than field/value pairs.

HSET.summary: Creates or updates one or more fields in a Redis hash. It returns how many fields were newly added, excluding fields whose existing values were overwritten.
HSET.explanation: HSET writes one or more field-value pairs into the hash stored at a key. Existing fields are overwritten; if the key does not exist, Redis creates a new hash. The integer reply counts only fields that were newly added, not fields whose existing values were changed.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The Redis key containing the target hash.

parameters.name: field
parameters.description: The first hash field to set.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value assigned to the first field.

parameters.name: [field value ...]
parameters.description: Optional additional field-value pairs, repeated as needed.

HSET.returns: An integer equal to the number of fields newly added to the hash; updates to existing fields are not counted.

example.title: Create and inspect a hash
example.code:
HSET user:42 name "Ada" role "engineer"
HGETALL user:42
example.explanation: Creates or updates two fields, then reads the complete hash.

useCases.title: Model flat records
useCases.scenario: Store a compact record under one Redis key.

useCases.title: Partial updates
useCases.scenario: Change selected attributes without replacing the whole hash.

useCases.title: Multi-field writes
useCases.scenario: Initialize several related attributes in one command.

interview.question: What does HSET return?
interview.answer: HSET stores field-value pairs in a Redis hash and returns the number of fields that were newly created. Updating an existing field returns zero for that field, so the reply is not the total number of pairs written.
interview.followUp: How can several fields be written atomically from the command interface? Supply multiple field-value pairs in one HSET invocation; the command accepts repeated pairs after the first one.

interview.question: What happens when the target key does not exist?
interview.answer: If the key is absent, HSET creates a key containing a hash. If the key already contains a hash, the specified fields are added or modified.
interview.followUp: What should be checked when the key has another Redis data type? The command cannot operate on that incompatible type and should be treated as a wrong-type error.

interview.question: What is the HSET syntax?
interview.answer: The command accepts a key followed by one field and value, with optional additional field-value pairs. Its syntax is `HSET key field value [field value ...]`.
interview.followUp: Which command retrieves one field after writing it? HGET reads the value associated with a specified hash field.

keyPoints: Use HSET to add a field to a hash or change the value associated with an existing field.
The command maps each supplied field to the value immediately following it.
Repeated writes to the same field are replacement operations rather than merges.
gotchas: A missing key is initialized automatically as a hash.
Arguments must consist of at least one field-value pair; additional pairs can be supplied in the same command.

HVALS.summary: Returns all values stored in a Redis hash. Use it when field names are unnecessary; the result order is not guaranteed.
HVALS.explanation: HVALS reads the hash identified by key and returns the values of every field as an array. It does not return field names; use HGETALL when both fields and values are needed.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key that holds the hash.

HVALS.returns: An array containing all values in the hash; an absent key returns an empty array.

example.title: Read all hash values
example.code:
HSET myhash field1 "Hello"
HSET myhash field2 "World"
HVALS myhash
example.explanation: Stores two fields in a hash, then returns their values.

useCases.title: Extract hash values
useCases.scenario: An application needs every cached attribute value from a hash but does not need the attribute names.

useCases.title: Batch-read cached values
useCases.scenario: A service prepares a list of cached values for processing or display.

useCases.title: Order-independent verification
useCases.scenario: A test compares the contents of a hash independent of Redis's unspecified iteration order.

interview.question: What does HVALS return, and what is its complexity?
interview.answer: HVALS takes one hash key and returns all values stored in that hash. Its time complexity is O(N), where N is the number of hash fields.
interview.followUp: How would you retrieve field names as well? Use HGETALL, which returns both fields and values.

interview.question: What is the syntax and behavior for a missing key?
interview.answer: The command is `HVALS key`. The key must identify a hash; the result is an array of values, and an absent key produces an empty array.
interview.followUp: What should be done before calling HVALS if a key might contain another data type? Check or enforce the key's type, because a wrong type causes a Redis error.

interview.question: When should an application use HVALS instead of HGET?
interview.answer: HVALS is useful when only the values from a hash are needed, such as collecting cached record attributes without transferring field names. It is a read-only hash command.
interview.followUp: When would HGET be preferable? Use HGET when one known field is needed, avoiding a full O(N) scan.

keyPoints: HVALS retrieves every value from the hash named by the supplied key, without returning field names.
Its required argument is the key whose value is a Redis hash.
The command is read-only and does not modify the hash.
Execution cost grows linearly with the number of fields in the hash.
Redis classifies HVALS as a read operation on hashes and marks it as slow relative to constant-time commands.

HyperLogLog.summary: Redis HyperLogLog estimates the number of distinct values with low, bounded memory use. It trades exactness for a standard error rate of 0.81%.
HyperLogLog.explanation: A HyperLogLog stores a compact summary of values instead of every value. Redis hashes added items and uses that summary to estimate how many distinct items exist. Multiple HyperLogLogs can be merged to estimate the union of their distinct items.
HyperLogLog.syntax:
PFADD key [element ...]
PFCOUNT key [key ...]
PFMERGE destination source [source ...]

parameters.name: destination
parameters.description: Destination HyperLogLog key for PFMERGE.

parameters.name: elements
parameters.description: One or more values to add with PFADD.

parameters.name: source keys
parameters.description: One or more HyperLogLog keys to read or merge.

HyperLogLog.returns: PFADD returns 1 when at least one internal register changes, otherwise 0. PFCOUNT returns the estimated number of distinct values. PFMERGE returns OK.

example.title: Count distinct items
example.code:
PFADD bikes Hyperion Deimos Phoebe Quaoar
PFCOUNT bikes
PFADD commuter_bikes Salacia Mimas Quaoar
PFMERGE all_bikes bikes commuter_bikes
PFCOUNT all_bikes
example.explanation: This adds items to two HyperLogLogs, combines them, and estimates the total distinct items. The shared item Quaoar is counted once.

useCases.title: Space-efficient distinct counting
useCases.scenario: Estimate unique visitors, events, or other distinct values without storing each value.

useCases.title: Union of counts
useCases.scenario: Combine daily or per-group HyperLogLogs to estimate distinct values across their union.

interview.question: What problem does HyperLogLog solve?
interview.answer: HyperLogLog estimates the number of distinct values while using constant memory. Redis uses up to 12 KB and has a standard error rate of 0.81%.
interview.followUp: Why not use a set? A set gives an exact count, but its memory use grows with the number of distinct values.

interview.question: Which Redis commands operate on HyperLogLogs?
interview.answer: PFADD adds values and creates the key when needed. PFCOUNT returns the estimated distinct count. PFMERGE combines one or more HyperLogLogs into a destination key.
interview.followUp: What does PFMERGE count for a shared value? The shared value contributes once to the estimated union.

interview.question: What are the main time complexities?
interview.answer: PFCOUNT with one key is O(1) with a small average constant time. With multiple keys, it is O(N), where N is the number of keys. PFMERGE is O(N) for N HyperLogLogs.
