interview.followUp: Why can multi-key operations need extra deployment care? In sharded environments, the keys must be placed on the same shard.

keyPoints: HyperLogLog estimates the cardinality, or number of distinct values, rather than storing an exact set.
Redis uses at most 12 KB in the worst case and has a standard error rate of 0.81%.
PFADD adds one or more values and creates the HyperLogLog key when that key is missing.
PFCOUNT returns the estimated number of distinct values represented by one or more keys.
PFMERGE writes a combined HyperLogLog to one destination key.
Its memory use stays bounded instead of growing in proportion to the number of values counted.
gotchas: PFMERGE does not produce an exact distinct count. Its result is an estimate across the source HyperLogLogs.
PFCOUNT across multiple keys and PFMERGE use multiple keys. In a sharded setup, place those keys on the same shard.

INCR.summary: Increments the integer stored at a key by one. A missing key starts at zero, so the first call returns one.
INCR.explanation: INCR reads the string stored at key as a signed integer, adds one, stores the result back, and returns the new value. If the key is missing, Redis treats it as zero first. The operation is atomic and works in constant time, but fails when the existing value is not a valid integer string or exceeds the signed 64-bit range.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key whose integer value is incremented.

INCR.returns: The new integer value after incrementing, returned as an integer reply; an error is returned for an invalid type or non-integer-representable string.

example.title: Increment a page-view counter
example.code: redis-cli INCR page_views
example.explanation: Atomically increments the counter and prints its new integer value; a missing key starts at zero and therefore returns 1 on the first call.

useCases.title: Event counters
useCases.scenario: Track page views, jobs, logins, or other event totals.

useCases.title: Sequence generation
useCases.scenario: Assign sequential numbers to requests or generated items.

useCases.title: Atomic unit increments
useCases.scenario: Maintain simple per-key quantities that change one unit at a time.

interview.question: What does INCR do when its key does not exist?
interview.answer: INCR atomically adds one to the integer represented by a string key and returns the resulting value. A missing key is treated as zero, so the first increment returns one.
interview.followUp: What happens when the key contains a list? Redis returns a wrong-type error because INCR operates on string values, not list values.

interview.question: What is the time complexity of INCR, and why is it useful for counters?
interview.answer: The command has O(1) time complexity. It updates the value in one Redis command, making it suitable for counters that need atomic increments.
interview.followUp: How would you increment by an arbitrary integer? Use INCRBY with the key and the desired increment.

interview.question: What value formats can INCR process?
interview.answer: INCR parses the stored string as a signed integer, increments it by one, stores the new integer as the key's value, and returns that integer. Values must fit within the signed 64-bit range.
interview.followUp: How can a fractional counter be changed? Use INCRBYFLOAT, which is the related command for floating-point increments.

keyPoints: INCR increases the integer value associated with the specified key by exactly one.
A missing key is initialized to zero before the increment, so the resulting value is one.
The supported numeric range is the signed 64-bit integer range.
Redis categorizes INCR as a write command for string values with fast performance.
A common use is maintaining counters by issuing INCR whenever an event occurs.
gotchas: The key must contain an integer-representable string value; other data types and non-integer strings produce an error.
The counter cannot exceed the signed 64-bit integer range.

INCRBY.summary: INCRBY adds an integer increment to a key's integer value and returns the updated value. Missing keys begin at zero, while wrong types, non-integer strings, and out-of-range values cause errors.
INCRBY.explanation: INCRBY adds a signed integer increment to the integer value held by a key and returns the resulting value. A missing key is treated as zero before the addition; invalid types, non-integer strings, and values outside the signed 64-bit range produce errors.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key.

parameters.name: increment
parameters.description: The integer amount to add to the value.

INCRBY.returns: Integer reply: the value of the key after the increment.

example.title: Increment a counter
example.code:
redis> SET mykey "10"
OK
redis> INCRBY mykey 5
(integer) 15
example.explanation: Adds 5 to the integer stored in mykey and returns the updated value.

useCases.title: Counters
useCases.scenario: Maintain a request, job, or event total that changes by an arbitrary integer amount.

useCases.title: Decrements
useCases.scenario: Apply a negative increment to reduce a stored integer.

useCases.title: Lazy initialization
useCases.scenario: Create a counter lazily without initializing it first.

interview.question: What does INCRBY do when the key does not exist?
interview.answer: INCRBY atomically adds the supplied integer to the integer stored at the key and returns the new value. If the key is absent, Redis first treats it as zero.
interview.followUp: What happens when the key contains a list? Redis returns a wrong-type error because INCRBY requires an integer-compatible string value.

interview.question: What is the command syntax and return value?
interview.answer: The command takes a key and an integer increment: INCRBY key increment. Its return is an integer reply containing the value after the increment.
interview.followUp: How would you decrement a counter? Supply a negative increment, provided the resulting value remains within the supported signed 64-bit range.

interview.question: What constraints apply to the stored value and result?
interview.answer: INCRBY works with signed 64-bit integers and rejects values that cannot be represented as integers. It also rejects keys containing values of the wrong Redis type.
interview.followUp: What value is returned after a successful update? Redis returns the key's value after applying the increment, rather than the increment itself.

keyPoints: Adds the specified integer amount to the number stored under the key.
A missing key starts at zero, so the first INCRBY can create a counter.
The increment argument is the integer quantity applied to the stored value.
A successful call returns the updated counter value.
Both the stored integer and resulting arithmetic are constrained to signed 64-bit integers.
gotchas: The target must hold a Redis string representing an integer; other Redis types cause an error.
Numeric text must be representable as an integer, not arbitrary numeric or floating-point text.
The operation cannot represent results outside the signed 64-bit integer range.

INCRBYFLOAT.summary: Adds a floating-point number to the numeric string stored at a Redis key and returns the updated value as a string. Missing keys start at zero, and negative increments decrement the value.
INCRBYFLOAT.explanation: INCRBYFLOAT parses the string stored at a key as a double-precision floating-point number, adds the supplied increment, stores the new value back at the same key, and returns that value as a string. A missing key starts at zero; a negative increment performs subtraction.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key.

parameters.name: increment
parameters.description: The floating-point amount to add to the value. A negative value decrements the value instead.

INCRBYFLOAT.returns: Bulk string reply containing the value of the key after the increment.

example.title: Increment and decrement a Redis string value
example.code:
redis-cli SET mykey 10.50
redis-cli INCRBYFLOAT mykey 0.1
# "10.6"
redis-cli INCRBYFLOAT mykey -5
# "5.6"
example.explanation: The command adds 0.1, then subtracts 5 by using a negative increment.

useCases.title: Atomic floating-point counters
useCases.scenario: Maintain a decimal-valued counter such as a score, balance, or measurement without client-side read-modify-write logic.

useCases.title: Decrementing decimal values
useCases.scenario: Apply a reduction using a negative increment while retaining the same command and key representation.

useCases.title: Server-side numeric updates
useCases.scenario: Update a shared numeric value with one Redis command so competing clients do not need separate GET and SET steps.

interview.question: What does INCRBYFLOAT do when the key does not exist?
interview.answer: It adds the floating-point increment to the value at key and returns the resulting value as a string. If the key is absent, Redis initializes it to zero first.
interview.followUp: What does a negative increment do? It decrements the stored value, because the operation is ordinary addition with a negative operand.

interview.question: What are the syntax and validation requirements?
interview.answer: The syntax is INCRBYFLOAT key increment. Both the existing value and increment must be parseable as double-precision floating-point numbers, and the key must hold a string.
interview.followUp: What is the complexity? The command runs in O(1), as documented in the Redis command reference.

interview.question: What does the command return, and how is the result represented?
interview.answer: On success, Redis stores the updated number at the key and returns it as a bulk string. The returned formatting uses fixed precision of 17 digits after the decimal point.
interview.followUp: How is it persisted and replicated? Redis propagates it as a SET operation to avoid inconsistencies from differing floating-point implementations.

keyPoints: Adds the specified floating-point increment to a numeric string stored at the key.
A missing key is treated as zero before addition.
Negative increments support decrementing without a separate command.
Success replaces the old string with the newly calculated value.
The response is the post-increment value, returned as a bulk string.
Redis propagates and appends the resulting state as SET for deterministic behavior.
gotchas: The command fails when the key contains a non-string value or when either the stored value or increment cannot be parsed as a double-precision floating-point number.
Do not assume the textual result reflects the exact internal precision; output formatting is fixed to 17 digits after the decimal point.
Replication and AOF represent the operation as SET, rather than preserving the original INCRBYFLOAT command.

INFO.summary: INFO returns Redis server information and statistics. You can request the default sections or select specific sections.
INFO.explanation: Redis returns server information as sections containing named fields and values. With no section, it uses the default sections. You can request one or more sections, or use special names such as all and everything.

parameters.name: section
parameters.description: One or more information sections, such as server, clients, memory, all, default, or everything. Optional.

INFO.returns: A bulk reply containing server information and statistics. Client libraries may parse it into a string or structured key-value data.

example.title: Read memory information
example.code: INFO memory
example.explanation: This asks Redis for memory information only.

useCases.title: Inspect the server
useCases.scenario: Check Redis version, mode, and general server details.

useCases.title: Monitor server state
useCases.scenario: Review memory, persistence, CPU, or replication measurements.

useCases.title: Study command behavior
useCases.scenario: Collect command counts, latency percentiles, or error counts.

interview.question: What does the INFO command do?
interview.answer: INFO returns information and statistics about the Redis server. Its time complexity is O(1), and its syntax is INFO followed by zero or more section names.
interview.followUp: How can you request all available sections? Use INFO everything, which includes all sections and module-generated sections.

interview.question: How do you limit INFO output?
interview.answer: A section name limits the output to one area, such as memory, clients, or replication. Multiple section names can be supplied.
interview.followUp: What does INFO all exclude? It excludes module-generated sections; INFO everything includes them.

interview.question: How should software parse INFO output?
interview.answer: The output can change between Redis versions. A client should skip unknown properties and handle missing fields instead of assuming every field exists.
interview.followUp: Why is this useful for monitoring tools? It lets them keep working when Redis adds or removes fields.

keyPoints: INFO reports information and statistics about the Redis server.
The command accepts zero or more section names after INFO.
The server section contains general Redis server information.
The memory section reports information about memory consumption.
The all option returns all regular sections but leaves out module-generated sections.
The everything option includes all sections and module sections.
gotchas: Fields can change between Redis versions. Ignore fields you do not know, and handle missing fields safely.
Calling INFO without a section does not request every section. It uses the default set.

KEYS.summary: Returns every key name matching a glob-style pattern. Because it can block the Redis server while producing the complete result, reserve it for debugging and exceptional administrative tasks.
KEYS.explanation: KEYS scans the database for every key name matching a glob-style pattern and returns the matches as an array. Pattern characters can select exact names, prefixes, suffixes, or single-character variations, but the command runs synchronously and can block the server while collecting results.

parameters.name: pattern
parameters.description: A glob-style pattern used to match key names.

KEYS.returns: An array reply containing all key names that match the pattern.

example.title: Find keys by prefix
example.code:
redis-cli SET user:1 Alice
redis-cli SET user:2 Bob
redis-cli KEYS 'user:*'
example.explanation: Creates two sample keys, then lists keys whose names begin with user:.

useCases.title: Debug key naming
useCases.scenario: Inspecting a development database

useCases.title: Special keyspace operations
useCases.scenario: Renaming or restructuring a keyspace during maintenance

useCases.title: Targeted inspection
useCases.scenario: Checking whether keys with a naming prefix exist

interview.question: What does the KEYS command do?
interview.answer: KEYS takes one glob-style pattern and returns every key name matching it. For example, KEYS user:* matches keys whose names begin with user:.
interview.followUp: Why can KEYS harm latency? It blocks the Redis server while all matching keys are returned, so large databases can experience substantial pauses.

interview.question: How is KEYS pattern matching specified?
interview.answer: The pattern is the required argument and uses glob-style matching. A literal pattern matches one name, while wildcard patterns can match groups of names.
interview.followUp: What should replace KEYS for incremental traversal? SCAN is the documented alternative when iterating through a keyspace subset because it avoids requesting the entire result at once.

interview.question: When is KEYS appropriate?
interview.answer: KEYS is intended for debugging and special operations, such as changing keyspace layout. It should not be used in regular application code because it can block the server.
interview.followUp: How should a production application find a subset of keys? Prefer SCAN or an appropriate set-based design instead of scanning the full keyspace with KEYS.

keyPoints: The command returns matching key names rather than their values or metadata.
Its sole required argument is a glob-style pattern applied to key names.
Redis classifies KEYS as a keyspace read command that is slow and potentially dangerous.
A match can produce multiple keys, including an empty result when no name fits.
gotchas: Avoid KEYS on large databases or in latency-sensitive application paths because it blocks the server until the complete result is available.
Use it for debugging or exceptional keyspace operations rather than normal application logic.
Cluster deployments may not provide the same keyspace behavior as standalone Redis; consult the cluster guidance before relying on the result.

LINDEX.summary: LINDEX returns one element from a Redis list by position. Indexes start at 0; negative indexes count from the end.
LINDEX.explanation: LINDEX reads one element from a Redis list. Indexes start at zero, and negative indexes count backward from the end. If the index is outside the list, Redis returns a nil or null reply. If the key stores another data type, Redis returns an error.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key that stores the list.

parameters.name: index
parameters.description: The zero-based position to read. Negative values count from the tail; -1 is the last item.

LINDEX.returns: The requested element as a bulk string. For an out-of-range index, RESP2 returns a nil reply and RESP3 returns a null reply. A wrong data type produces an error.

example.title: Read list elements
example.code:
LPUSH mylist "World"
LPUSH mylist "Hello"
LINDEX mylist 0
LINDEX mylist -1
LINDEX mylist 3
example.explanation: The commands create a list, read its first and last elements, then request an index outside the list.

useCases.title: Inspect the list head
useCases.scenario: Read the first item without removing it.

useCases.title: Inspect the list tail
useCases.scenario: Read the newest or last item without changing the list.

useCases.title: Read by position
useCases.scenario: Fetch an item at a known position in a small list.

interview.question: What does LINDEX do?
interview.answer: LINDEX returns one list element using its position. Index 0 is the first element, and -1 is the last element.
interview.followUp: How do negative indexes work? They count from the list tail, so -2 selects the element before the last one.

interview.question: What is the time complexity of LINDEX?
interview.answer: Its time complexity is O(N), where N is the number of elements Redis must pass to reach the requested position. Reading either end is O(1).
interview.followUp: Which requests are fastest? Requests for index 0 and index -1 are O(1), because they access the first or last element.

interview.question: What arguments does LINDEX require?
interview.answer: The command is `LINDEX key index`. The key names the list, and index is an integer position.
interview.followUp: What happens for an invalid position? Redis returns nil in RESP2 or null in RESP3 when the index is out of range.

keyPoints: LINDEX reads one element from the list stored at a key.
Positions start at zero: index 0 is the first item and index 1 is the second.
Negative positions count from the end of the list.
Index -1 selects the last item; -2 selects the item before it.
Reading the first or last position takes constant time.
LINDEX is a read-only list command in the read, list, and slow ACL categories.
gotchas: The key must contain a list. Other data types cause a Redis error.
An index outside the list does not return an element; it returns a nil reply in RESP2.

LINSERT.summary: Inserts a value before or after a matching value in a Redis list. It returns the list length, 0 for a missing key, or -1 when the pivot is not found.
LINSERT.explanation: LINSERT searches the list stored at key for pivot. It adds element immediately before or after the first matching pivot, depending on the chosen position. If the key is missing, Redis does nothing. If the key has another data type, Redis returns an error.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The key containing the list.

parameters.name: where
parameters.description: Insert before or after the pivot.

parameters.name: pivot
parameters.description: The existing list value used as the reference.

parameters.name: element
parameters.description: The value to insert.

LINSERT.returns: An integer: the list length after insertion, 0 if the key does not exist, or -1 if the pivot is not found.

example.title: Insert before a list element
example.code:
RPUSH mylist "Hello" "World"
LINSERT mylist BEFORE "World" "There"
LRANGE mylist 0 -1
example.explanation: This adds "There" before "World", then reads the whole list.

useCases.title: Insert relative to a value
useCases.scenario: Add an item next to a known item in an ordered list.

useCases.title: Adjust list order
useCases.scenario: Build or update a small ordered queue when the insertion point is identified by its value.

useCases.title: Detect a missing pivot
useCases.scenario: Check whether the requested reference value exists by inspecting the integer result.

interview.question: What does LINSERT do?
interview.answer: LINSERT adds one element before or after a matching pivot in a Redis list. Its syntax is `LINSERT key BEFORE|AFTER pivot element`.
interview.followUp: What happens if the key is missing? Redis treats it as an empty list and returns 0 without inserting anything.

interview.question: What values can LINSERT return?
interview.answer: It returns the new list length after a successful insertion. It returns 0 when the key does not exist and -1 when the pivot is absent.
interview.followUp: How can an application distinguish a missing key from a missing pivot? Check for 0 versus -1 in the integer reply.

interview.question: What is the time complexity?
interview.answer: The operation is O(N), where N is the number of list elements Redis traverses before finding the pivot. Insertion near the head can be treated as O(1), while insertion near the tail is O(N).
interview.followUp: Why can a tail insertion be slower? Redis may scan most of the list before it reaches the pivot.

keyPoints: Use LINSERT to place a new list element relative to an existing value.
Choose BEFORE to place the new value on the pivot's left, or AFTER to place it on the right.
The pivot must be an existing value in the target list.
The element argument is the new value that Redis adds to the list.
A successful insertion reports the list's length after the change.
The scan cost depends on how many elements Redis checks before reaching the pivot.
Redis has supported this command since version 2.2.0.
gotchas: A missing key does not create a list or insert a value.
The command fails if the key contains a non-list value.
A return value of -1 means that the pivot was not found, so no insertion occurred.

LLEN.summary: Returns the number of elements in a Redis list. A missing key is treated as an empty list and returns 0.
LLEN.explanation: LLEN reads the number of items in the list stored at the given key. It does not change the list. A missing key acts like an empty list, so the command returns 0. If the key contains another data type, Redis returns an error.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The key that stores the list whose length you want to read.

LLEN.returns: An integer containing the list length. Redis returns 0 when the key does not exist.

example.title: Get a list length
example.code:
LPUSH mylist "World"
LPUSH mylist "Hello"
LLEN mylist
example.explanation: Adds two values to mylist, then returns its length: 2.

useCases.title: Read queue size
useCases.scenario: Check how many items are waiting in a Redis list.

useCases.title: Check for an empty list
useCases.scenario: Test whether a list contains any elements without retrieving them.

interview.question: What does LLEN do?
interview.answer: LLEN returns the number of elements in a list. It returns an integer reply, and its time complexity is O(1).
interview.followUp: What happens for a missing key? Redis treats the missing key as an empty list and returns 0.

interview.question: What is the syntax and required argument?
interview.answer: The command is `LLEN key`, where `key` names the list. It is a read-only list command.
interview.followUp: What if the key stores a string? Redis returns an error because the value is not a list.

interview.question: What does LLEN return?
interview.answer: LLEN returns an integer containing the list length in both RESP2 and RESP3. It does not return the list elements.
interview.followUp: How can you create a list for testing? Use LPUSH or another list-writing command, then call LLEN.

keyPoints: LLEN reports how many elements a list contains.
Its only argument is the key containing the list.
A missing key produces 0.
The result is an integer reply in RESP2.
The result is also an integer reply in RESP3.
LLEN runs in constant time, O(1).
gotchas: The key must hold a Redis list. LLEN fails when the key stores another data type.

LMOVE.summary: LMOVE atomically moves one item between Redis lists. It can pop from either end of one list and push to either end of another.
LMOVE.explanation: LMOVE atomically removes one item from either end of a source list and adds it to either end of a destination list. It returns the moved item. If both keys are the same, it rotates the list.

parameters.name: source
parameters.description: Key of the list from which Redis removes an item.

parameters.name: destination
parameters.description: Key of the list to which Redis adds the item.

parameters.name: wherefrom
parameters.description: End of `source` to pop from: `LEFT` or `RIGHT`.

parameters.name: whereto
parameters.description: End of `destination` to push to: `LEFT` or `RIGHT`.

LMOVE.returns: The moved element as a bulk string reply. If the source list does not exist, the result is nil.

example.title: Move a task to processing
example.code:
RPUSH tasks "email-1" "email-2"
LMOVE tasks processing RIGHT LEFT
LRANGE tasks 0 -1
LRANGE processing 0 -1
example.explanation: This takes the last task from `tasks` and puts it at the start of `processing`.

useCases.title: Reliable queue
useCases.scenario: Move a job from an input list to a processing list before handling it.

useCases.title: Circular list
useCases.scenario: Rotate one list so workers can process items repeatedly.

useCases.title: Queue and stack operations
useCases.scenario: Move items between list ends to implement queue or stack behavior.

interview.question: What does LMOVE do?
interview.answer: LMOVE removes an item from the selected end of `source` and pushes it to the selected end of `destination` as one atomic operation. It returns the moved item.
interview.followUp: How can it support reliable job processing? Move a job into a processing list, then remove it with LREM after successful processing. A monitor can retry items that remain too long.

interview.question: What do the two direction arguments mean?
interview.answer: The first direction chooses where to pop from `source`: LEFT means the head and RIGHT means the tail. The second chooses where to push in `destination`: LEFT means the head and RIGHT means the tail.
interview.followUp: What command matches the old RPOPLPUSH behavior? `LMOVE source destination RIGHT LEFT`.

interview.question: What happens when both keys are the same?
interview.answer: With the same source and destination key, LMOVE removes an item and adds it back to the chosen end. This can rotate a list; using the same direction for both sides is a no-op.
interview.followUp: How can several workers use this pattern? They can rotate the same list and receive different items without copying the whole list with LRANGE.

keyPoints: It returns the item that it moves.
The remove and push happen atomically.
LEFT selects the list head. RIGHT selects the list tail.
The last direction controls where the item enters the destination list.
If the move empties the source, Redis deletes that list key.
The command has constant time complexity.
gotchas: A missing source list returns nil and leaves all lists unchanged.
Use LMOVE instead of the deprecated RPOPLPUSH command.

LPOP.summary: Removes and returns elements from the beginning of a Redis list. It removes one element by default or up to count elements when count is supplied.
LPOP.explanation: LPOP removes elements from the beginning of the list stored at the specified key and returns what it removed. Without count it removes one element; with count it removes up to that many elements, limited by the list length.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key that holds the list.

parameters.name: count
parameters.description: The maximum number of elements to pop; omitted means one.

LPOP.returns: Without count, a bulk string containing the first element, or nil if the key does not exist. With count, an array containing up to count elements, or nil if the key does not exist.

example.title: Pop list elements from the left
example.code:
RPUSH tasks "build" "test" "deploy"
LPOP tasks
LPOP tasks 2
example.explanation: Adds three values, removes the oldest value, then removes up to two remaining values from the list.

useCases.title: FIFO queue consumption
useCases.scenario: Consume queued work in insertion order by appending with RPUSH and removing with LPOP.

useCases.title: Stack-style processing
useCases.scenario: Use LPUSH and LPOP together when processing the newest item first.

useCases.title: Batch consumption
useCases.scenario: Remove several ready items in one command when batch size is bounded by count.

interview.question: What does LPOP do, and what does count change?
interview.answer: LPOP removes and returns the first element of a list. With count omitted it returns one bulk string; with count supplied it returns up to count elements.
interview.followUp: How does the command behave when count exceeds the list length? It returns every remaining element, not an error.

interview.question: What is LPOP's time complexity?
interview.answer: The command operates on one list key and removes elements from its head. Its time complexity is O(N), where N is the number of elements returned.
interview.followUp: What alternative supports multiple candidate keys? LMPOP can pop from the first non-empty list among supplied keys.

interview.question: What happens for a missing key or an emptied list?
interview.answer: If the key does not exist, LPOP returns a nil reply. If the last element is popped, Redis removes the list key.
interview.followUp: How can a consumer wait for work instead of polling? BLPOP blocks the connection while the specified lists are empty.

keyPoints: LPOP atomically removes values from the list head and returns those values.
Omitting count makes the command remove exactly one element when available.
With count, the result contains no more than the requested number of elements.
If fewer elements exist than requested, Redis returns only the elements present.
The required key argument identifies the list to modify.
The optional count argument controls the maximum number removed.
Runtime grows with the number of elements returned.
gotchas: When the final list element is removed, Redis deletes the key.
A nonexistent key returns a nil reply rather than an empty list.

LPOS.summary: LPOS finds a value in a Redis list and returns its zero-based position. Options can select a match, return several positions, or limit the scan.
LPOS.explanation: LPOS searches a Redis list for a value and returns its zero-based position. By default it searches from the head and returns the first match. RANK chooses which match to start with, COUNT returns several positions, and MAXLEN limits how many list items are checked.
LPOS.syntax: LPOS key element [RANK rank] [COUNT num-matches] [MAXLEN len]

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The key containing the list to search.

parameters.name: element
parameters.description: The list value to find.

parameters.name: rank
parameters.description: The match rank to return. Positive values search from the head; negative values search from the tail.

parameters.name: num-matches
parameters.description: The number of matching positions to return. Zero returns all matches.

parameters.name: len
parameters.description: The maximum number of list items to compare. Zero scans the whole list.

LPOS.returns: Without COUNT, an integer containing one zero-based matching index, or nil when there is no match. With COUNT, an array of matching indexes, or an empty array when no match is found.

example.title: Find list positions
example.code:
RPUSH mylist a b c 1 2 3 c
LPOS mylist c
LPOS mylist c COUNT 0
LPOS mylist c RANK -1 COUNT 2
example.explanation: The first command returns 2. The second returns all matching indexes, [2,6,7]. The third returns up to two matches while searching from the tail.

useCases.title: Locate one list item
useCases.scenario: Find the first occurrence of a value in a list.

useCases.title: Find all duplicates
useCases.scenario: Return every position where a value occurs.

useCases.title: Bound the search
useCases.scenario: Avoid scanning a large list completely when an early match is expected.

interview.question: What does LPOS return by default?
interview.answer: LPOS returns the zero-based index of a matching list element. With no options, it scans from head to tail and returns the first match, or nil when there is no match.
interview.followUp: How do you return the second match? Use RANK 2. A negative rank starts the search from the tail.

interview.question: How do RANK and COUNT change LPOS?
interview.answer: RANK selects which matching occurrence to return. COUNT asks for multiple matching positions, and COUNT 0 requests all matches.
interview.followUp: What happens with RANK -1 COUNT 2? It searches from the tail and returns up to two matching positions in that search order.

interview.question: What is LPOS's time complexity?
interview.answer: The average complexity is O(N), where N is the list length. Searching near an end or providing MAXLEN can make the operation run in constant time.
interview.followUp: Why use MAXLEN? It bounds the number of comparisons, which limits the command's maximum work when an early match is expected.

keyPoints: LPOS searches a list and returns the position of a matching value.
Indexes start at 0, so the first list item has position 0.
RANK 1 selects the first match from the head; RANK -1 selects the first match from the tail.
COUNT limits the number of positions returned. COUNT 0 returns every match.
MAXLEN limits the number of list items LPOS compares.
The command was added in Redis Open Source 6.0.6.
LPOS is a read-only list command in the slow ACL category.
gotchas: The no-match result depends on COUNT: without COUNT, the result is nil; with COUNT, it is an empty array.
A negative RANK searches from the tail, but returned indexes still use the normal zero-based positions from the head.
MAXLEN 0 means scan without a comparison limit. It does not mean scan zero list items.

LPUSH.summary: LPUSH prepends one or more elements to a Redis list, creating the list when the key is absent. It returns the list's length after insertion.
LPUSH.explanation: LPUSH prepends one or more values to the list at the specified key. Redis creates the key as a list when it is absent; multiple arguments are inserted sequentially, so the rightmost supplied value becomes the first list item.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Name of the key that holds the list.

parameters.name: element [element ...]
parameters.description: One or more values to prepend to the list.

LPUSH.returns: Integer reply: the length of the list after the push operation.

example.title: Prepend values to a list
example.code:
LPUSH mylist "world"
LPUSH mylist "hello"
LRANGE mylist 0 -1
example.explanation: Adds two values at the list head, then reads the complete list to show the newest value first.

useCases.title: Recent-item feeds
useCases.scenario: Add newest items at the front of a list while retaining insertion history.

useCases.title: Queue production
useCases.scenario: Place work identifiers onto a list for later consumption by a worker.

useCases.title: LIFO stacks
useCases.scenario: Build stack-like behavior by pairing head insertion with head removal.

interview.question: What does LPUSH do and what does it return?
interview.answer: LPUSH adds one or more elements to the head of a list and returns the list's length afterward. If the key is absent, Redis creates the list automatically.
interview.followUp: How does LPUSH mylist a b c order the values? The resulting order is c, b, a because arguments are inserted one at a time from left to right at the head.

interview.question: What is the syntax and argument structure of LPUSH?
interview.answer: Its syntax is LPUSH key element [element ...]. The command accepts one or more elements, and the key identifies the target list.
interview.followUp: What happens when the key contains a string? Redis returns a type error because the existing value is not a list.

interview.question: What is LPUSH's complexity?
interview.answer: LPUSH has constant-time complexity for each element added, so a call adding multiple elements takes time proportional to the number of supplied elements. It is categorized as a write operation on a list.
interview.followUp: Which command provides the create-only-if-present behavior? LPUSHX prepends values only when the key already exists and contains a list.

keyPoints: LPUSH prepends every supplied element to the target list.
An absent key is initialized as an empty list before insertion.
The result is the list length after all insertions complete.
Each individual element insertion has constant-time complexity.
Redis classifies LPUSH as a write command for list data structures and marks it fast.
gotchas: The command fails if the key already contains a non-list value.
With multiple elements, insertion order is reversed in the resulting list: the last argument ends up at the head.

LRANGE.summary: Returns an inclusive range of elements from a Redis list. Start and stop use zero-based indexes, and negative indexes count from the list's tail.
LRANGE.explanation: LRANGE reads the elements between the supplied zero-based start and stop positions from a Redis list. Both boundaries are inclusive, negative positions count backward from the tail, and indexes outside the list are tolerated rather than treated as errors.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Name of the key that holds the list.

parameters.name: start
parameters.description: Zero-based starting index; negative indexes count from the tail.

parameters.name: stop
parameters.description: Inclusive zero-based ending index; negative indexes count from the tail.

LRANGE.returns: An array containing the selected list elements, or an empty array if the key does not exist.

example.title: Read a complete Redis list
example.code:
redis-cli RPUSH mylist one two three
redis-cli LRANGE mylist 0 -1
# 1) "one"
# 2) "two"
# 3) "three"
example.explanation: Adds three values, then reads the entire list with an inclusive range from the first element through the last.

useCases.title: List retrieval and pagination
useCases.scenario: Read all values in a list with 0 -1 or fetch a bounded slice for display.

useCases.title: Recent-item inspection
useCases.scenario: Inspect the newest entries by using a negative range such as -5 -1.

useCases.title: Queue monitoring
useCases.scenario: Read a queue segment without removing its jobs.

interview.question: How do LRANGE indexes work?
interview.answer: LRANGE returns a selected portion of a list using zero-based start and stop indexes. The stop index is inclusive, so 0 0 reads the first element and 0 -1 reads the whole list.
interview.followUp: How does it behave when indexes exceed the list? Out-of-range indexes do not cause errors; the result contains the overlapping elements, or is empty when the range does not overlap.

interview.question: What do negative indexes mean in LRANGE?
interview.answer: Negative indexes count from the tail: -1 identifies the last element, -2 the previous one, and so forth. This makes 0 -1 a convenient full-list read.
interview.followUp: What happens if the key is absent? Redis returns an empty array.

interview.question: What is LRANGE's time complexity?
interview.answer: The command has O(S+N) complexity, where S is the distance from the relevant list end to the start offset and N is the number of returned elements. Reading a large range therefore costs more than reading a small one.
interview.followUp: Which list operation can prepare the example list? RPUSH appends values to the list, after which LRANGE can read them.

keyPoints: LRANGE selects and returns elements from the list associated with the specified key.
Both positions use zero-based indexing, with the first list element at position zero.
The stop boundary is included in the returned range.
A negative position measures backward from the list's final element.
Runtime is O(S+N), combining the traversal distance to the start with the number of returned items.
gotchas: Indexes beyond the list boundaries are accepted; they simply select whatever portion overlaps the list.
A start position after the list's end produces no elements.
A missing key returns an empty array rather than an error.

LREM.summary: Removes matching elements from a Redis list. The count value controls how many matches to remove and which end to scan from.
LREM.explanation: LREM removes matching values from a Redis list. A positive count searches from the head, a negative count searches from the tail, and zero removes every match. The command removes no more than the requested number unless count is zero.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The key that stores the list.

parameters.name: count
parameters.description: A positive number removes from the head, a negative number from the tail, and zero removes all matches.

parameters.name: element
parameters.description: The list value to remove.

LREM.returns: An integer: the number of removed elements.

example.title: Remove one matching value
example.code:
RPUSH tasks "write" "test" "write"
LREM tasks 1 "write"
LRANGE tasks 0 -1
example.explanation: Adds three values, removes the first matching value from the head side, then reads the remaining list.

useCases.title: Delete the first matching item
useCases.scenario: Remove one occurrence while keeping later duplicates.

useCases.title: Delete from the tail
useCases.scenario: Remove recent duplicates from the end of a list.

useCases.title: Remove all matches
useCases.scenario: Clean every occurrence of an unwanted value.

interview.question: How does count change LREM behavior?
interview.answer: LREM removes matching values from a list. With a positive count it scans from head to tail; with a negative count it scans from tail to head; zero removes every match.
interview.followUp: How do you remove only the last two matching values? Use a count of -2, such as LREM mylist -2 hello.

interview.question: What does LREM return?
interview.answer: The command returns an integer containing the number of elements it removed. A missing key behaves like an empty list, so the result is 0.
interview.followUp: What result should code expect after trying to remove a value from a missing key? It should handle integer 0 as a normal result, not as an error.

interview.question: What is the time complexity of LREM?
interview.answer: Its time complexity is O(N+M), where N is the list length and M is the number of removed elements. It is a write command for Redis lists.
interview.followUp: Why can count 0 be more expensive than a small positive count? It may inspect the full list because it removes all matching values.

keyPoints: LREM removes matching list values, up to the number given by count.
A positive count removes matches while scanning from the list head toward its tail.
A negative count scans from the tail toward the head.
A count of zero removes every matching value in the list.
The result is the number of values that LREM actually removed.
Runtime depends on the list length and the number of removed values.
gotchas: If the key does not exist, Redis treats it as an empty list and returns 0.
If the operation removes the list's final element, Redis deletes the key.
The sign of count controls the search direction, not only the number of elements removed.

LSET.summary: LSET replaces an existing value in a Redis list at a specified index. Indexes start at zero, and negative indexes count from the end.
LSET.explanation: LSET replaces one item in a Redis list. Give the list key, the item's zero-based position, and its new value. A negative position starts counting from the end. The command fails when the position is outside the list.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The Redis key containing the list.

parameters.name: index
parameters.description: The zero-based item position. Negative values count from the tail.

parameters.name: element
parameters.description: The replacement value for the selected item.

LSET.returns: A simple string reply: `OK` on success.

example.title: Replace list items
example.code:
RPUSH mylist "one" "two" "three"
LSET mylist 0 "four"
LSET mylist -2 "five"
LRANGE mylist 0 -1
example.explanation: Creates a list, changes its first item and then changes the second-to-last item.

useCases.title: Update one list item
useCases.scenario: A list stores ordered values and one value must be corrected without changing the other positions.

useCases.title: Change an item from the tail
useCases.scenario: A program knows the position of an item relative to the end of a list.

useCases.title: Edit in place
useCases.scenario: A service needs to replace a list value while keeping the list length unchanged.

interview.question: What does LSET do?
interview.answer: LSET changes the value at one position in a Redis list. Its syntax is `LSET key index element`, and it returns `OK` when the change succeeds.
interview.followUp: What happens with a negative index? It counts from the list's tail, so `-1` means the last item.

interview.question: How are LSET indexes interpreted?
interview.answer: The index is zero-based, so index `0` selects the first item. Negative indexes count backward from the end of the list.
interview.followUp: How would you change the final item? Use index `-1`, provided the list is not empty.

interview.question: What is the time complexity of LSET?
interview.answer: The general time complexity is O(N), where N is the list length. Setting the first or last item is O(1).
interview.followUp: Which indexes can use the O(1) case? Index `0` and index `-1` select the first and last items, respectively.

keyPoints: LSET updates one existing list element at a chosen position.
Indexes start at zero, so the first list item uses index 0.
A negative index selects an item by counting from the end of the list.
The key argument identifies the Redis list to modify.
The element argument supplies the replacement value.
Changing the first or last item takes constant time; other positions use O(N) time in general.
gotchas: The index must point to an existing list item. LSET does not add a new item when the index is outside the list.

LTRIM.summary: Trims a Redis list to an inclusive index range. It supports zero-based and negative indexes, and deletes the key when the resulting list is empty.
LTRIM.explanation: LTRIM changes a Redis list in place so only the inclusive index range from start through stop remains. Indexes begin at zero; negative indexes count backward from the tail. Indexes outside the list do not cause an error. If the range is empty, Redis removes the key.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The key containing the list.

parameters.name: start
parameters.description: The zero-based first index to keep. Negative indexes count from the tail.

parameters.name: stop
parameters.description: The zero-based last index to keep, inclusive. Negative indexes count from the tail.

example.title: Keep a fixed-size list
example.code:
RPUSH recent "event-1"
RPUSH recent "event-2"
RPUSH recent "event-3"
LTRIM recent 0 1
LRANGE recent 0 -1
example.explanation: Adds three values, then keeps only indexes 0 and 1. The final command shows the two remaining values.

useCases.title: Bounded list
useCases.scenario: Keep only the newest fixed number of events, logs, or messages.

useCases.title: Recent-item buffer
useCases.scenario: Add an item and remove older items so the list stays at a fixed maximum size.

useCases.title: List range trimming
useCases.scenario: Keep only a selected section of an existing list by index.

interview.question: What does LTRIM do?
interview.answer: LTRIM keeps the inclusive range from start to stop. Both indexes are zero-based, and negative values count from the list tail.
interview.followUp: What happens when the range is invalid? If start is greater than stop, Redis removes the key because the resulting list is empty.

interview.question: What is the syntax and return value?
interview.answer: The command is LTRIM key start stop. It returns the simple string reply OK in both RESP2 and RESP3.
interview.followUp: What does an out-of-range stop do? Redis treats a stop beyond the list end as the last element.

interview.question: How can LTRIM bound a list?
interview.answer: A common bounded-list pattern pushes an item and then runs LTRIM with 0 99. This keeps at most 100 elements.
interview.followUp: What is the usual complexity of that pattern? It is O(1) on average when only one item is removed from the tail.

keyPoints: start and stop use zero-based positions. Index 0 is the list head.
Negative indexes count from the tail: -1 is last, -2 is second to last.
key is the name of the Redis key containing the list.
stop is inclusive, so the element at that index remains when it is in range.
Use a push command followed by LTRIM key 0 99 to cap a list at 100 elements.
The general time complexity is O(N), where N is the number of removed elements.
gotchas: If start is greater than stop, the list becomes empty and Redis deletes the key.
A stop index beyond the list end is treated as the last element.
With the common push-then-trim pattern, the operation is O(1) on average because usually one tail element is removed.

MEMORY.summary: MEMORY USAGE estimates how many bytes a key and its value use in RAM. For aggregate values, it can sample nested values to estimate the total size.
MEMORY.explanation: MEMORY USAGE estimates the RAM needed for a key, its value, and related administrative overhead. For aggregate values, Redis can sample nested values and use their average to estimate the total; use SAMPLES 0 to inspect all nested values.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The key whose RAM usage Redis should estimate.

parameters.name: count
parameters.description: Optional number of nested values to sample for aggregate types. Use 0 to sample all.

MEMORY.returns: The estimated memory usage in bytes for the key and its value, or a null result when the key does not exist.

example.title: Measure a key's memory use
example.code:
redis-cli SET user:1 Alice
redis-cli MEMORY USAGE user:1
redis-cli MEMORY USAGE user:1 SAMPLES 0
example.explanation: Stores a key, then reports its memory use. The last command samples every nested value when the value is an aggregate.

useCases.title: Investigate memory usage
useCases.scenario: Find keys that consume more RAM than expected.

useCases.title: Compare data layouts
useCases.scenario: Compare the cost of different key or value designs.

useCases.title: Inspect all nested values
useCases.scenario: Measure a complete aggregate when an exact nested scan is needed.

interview.question: What does MEMORY USAGE report?
interview.answer: MEMORY USAGE returns an estimate of the bytes needed to store a key and its value in RAM. It also counts data structures and administrative overhead.
interview.followUp: What does SAMPLES control? For aggregate values, it sets how many nested values Redis samples; SAMPLES 0 samples all nested values.

interview.question: What is the syntax and what are the arguments?
interview.answer: The command syntax is MEMORY USAGE key [SAMPLES count]. The key is required, while SAMPLES and its count are optional.
interview.followUp: What is the default sample count? Redis uses five samples unless SAMPLES 0 or another count is supplied.

interview.question: How does sampling affect command cost?
interview.answer: Its time complexity is O(N), where N is the number of samples. A larger sample count can therefore require more work.
interview.followUp: How can you inspect every nested value? Use SAMPLES 0, but expect the work to depend on the full nested collection.

keyPoints: Use MEMORY USAGE to estimate how much RAM one key and its value need.
SAMPLES applies to nested or aggregate data types.
Redis averages sampled nested values to estimate the aggregate's total size.
SAMPLES 0 checks every nested value; otherwise the default is five samples.
The command's work grows with the number of samples.
gotchas: The result includes administrative overhead, not only the stored data.
For aggregate values, the default sample count is five, so the estimate may not inspect every nested value.
Memory figures can differ on active-active Redis Software or Redis Cloud databases.

MGET.summary: MGET atomically retrieves the string values of one or more keys in a single command. Missing keys and keys holding non-string values return nil in their corresponding result positions.
MGET.explanation: MGET atomically reads the string values for one or more keys and returns them as an array aligned with the requested key order. A missing key or a key containing a non-string value contributes nil, so the command does not fail for those cases.

parameters.name: key [key ...]
parameters.description: One or more keys whose string values should be retrieved.

MGET.returns: An array of values corresponding to the specified keys; missing keys and keys that do not hold strings return nil.

example.title: Read several string keys
example.code:
redis-cli SET user:1 Alice
redis-cli SET user:2 Bob
redis-cli MGET user:1 user:2 user:3
example.explanation: The command returns the values in key order; the missing key produces nil.

useCases.title: Batch cache reads
useCases.scenario: Read several cached string fields in one request.

useCases.title: Lower read latency
useCases.scenario: Fetch a group of independent values while reducing client-server round trips.

useCases.title: Aligned multi-key results
useCases.scenario: Preserve the association between requested keys and returned values by using the response positions.

interview.question: What does MGET do, and what does it return?
interview.answer: MGET accepts one or more keys and returns an array containing the corresponding values. Results preserve the input-key order, and missing or non-string keys contribute nil.
interview.followUp: What is its time complexity? It is O(N), where N is the number of keys retrieved.

interview.question: Why use MGET instead of issuing several GET commands?
interview.answer: MGET is atomic as a command: Redis returns the string values for all requested keys in one operation. It is useful when several independent string values must be read with fewer client-server round trips.
interview.followUp: How would you reduce latency further for many unrelated requests? Compare MGET with pipelining, while considering the key distribution and the deployment's clustering behavior.

interview.question: What happens when one requested key is missing or has the wrong type?
interview.answer: MGET is intended for string values. If a requested key is absent or does not contain a string, its position in the returned array is nil rather than causing the whole command to fail.
interview.followUp: How should an application distinguish an absent key from a non-string key? Use an additional type-aware check such as TYPE when that distinction matters, because MGET itself reports nil for both cases.

keyPoints: Use MGET to retrieve multiple Redis string values in one atomic command.
The response contains one result for every supplied key.
Missing keys and non-string keys do not abort the complete multi-key read.
Redis classifies MGET as a read operation for string data and marks it fast.
Execution cost grows linearly with the number of requested keys.
gotchas: A missing key and a key with a non-string data type both produce nil, which can make those cases indistinguishable from the returned value alone.
Cluster configuration affects multi-key behavior; verify the documented clustering rules before assuming every requested key is handled identically.

MSET.summary: MSET atomically assigns string values to one or more keys in a single command. Existing values are overwritten, and a successful command returns OK.
MSET.explanation: MSET accepts one or more key-value pairs and writes every pair as a single atomic operation. Existing values are replaced, and the command returns OK when the operation completes successfully.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: A key whose string value will be written.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The string value assigned to the preceding key.

parameters.name: key value ...
parameters.description: Additional key-value pairs; at least one pair is required.

example.title: Set multiple string keys
example.code:
MSET user:1 Alice user:2 Bob
GET user:1
GET user:2
example.explanation: Stores two string values in one command, then reads them back.

useCases.title: Batch cache population
useCases.scenario: Write several related cache entries while reducing client-server round trips.

useCases.title: Atomic multi-key update
useCases.scenario: Replace a group of string values so readers see either the old or complete new state.

useCases.title: Bulk initialization
useCases.scenario: Initialize multiple independent string keys in one request.

interview.question: What does MSET do, and is it atomic?
interview.answer: MSET writes multiple string key-value pairs in one command and replaces values that already exist. It is atomic, so clients cannot observe only part of the batch.
interview.followUp: How does its complexity scale? It is O(N), where N is the number of keys being set.

interview.question: What is MSET's syntax and return value?
interview.answer: The command takes alternating keys and values: MSET key value [key value ...]. It returns the simple string reply OK because the command cannot fail under its documented conditions.
interview.followUp: What would you use to avoid overwriting existing keys? MSETNX, which provides conditional multi-key creation.

interview.question: What should you consider when using MSET with Redis Cluster?
interview.answer: MSET is useful for reducing round trips when several string values must be written together. In clustered deployments, however, its multi-key behavior varies, so key placement must be considered.
interview.followUp: What cluster constraint should be investigated? Whether the participating keys can be handled together according to Redis cluster multi-key operation rules.

keyPoints: MSET writes each supplied key with its corresponding string value.
If a key already exists, its previous value is replaced.
The complete batch becomes visible atomically rather than as separate updates.
Readers cannot observe a partially applied MSET batch.
Execution cost grows linearly with the number of key-value pairs.
A successful invocation returns OK.
gotchas: In clustered Redis, multi-key behavior can differ; consult the multi-key operations guidance when keys may be distributed across hash slots.
MSET overwrites existing values; use MSETNX when conditional, no-overwrite behavior is required.

MULTI.summary: MULTI starts a Redis transaction and queues later commands on the current connection. EXEC runs the queued commands atomically, while DISCARD cancels them.
MULTI.explanation: MULTI switches the current connection into transaction mode. Commands sent afterward are queued rather than run immediately, and EXEC later runs the queued commands as one atomic batch; DISCARD can instead clear the queue and leave transaction mode.

example.title: Queue and execute a transaction
example.code:
MULTI
SET cache:user:42 "Ada"
INCR stats:users
EXEC
example.explanation: Starts a transaction, queues two commands, then executes them atomically with EXEC.

useCases.title: Atomic grouped updates
useCases.scenario: Update several related keys as one uninterrupted operation.

useCases.title: Transaction batching
useCases.scenario: Batch commands that must be committed together.

useCases.title: Optimistic concurrency control
useCases.scenario: Pair with WATCH when writes depend on a prior read.

interview.question: What does MULTI do?
interview.answer: MULTI marks the beginning of a Redis transaction and changes the connection into transaction mode. Subsequent commands are queued, and EXEC executes them as a group.
interview.followUp: How can a client cancel the transaction? Send DISCARD; it removes the queued commands and restores the connection to normal mode.

interview.question: What replies should a client expect after MULTI?
interview.answer: MULTI itself returns the simple string reply OK. Commands issued after MULTI normally return QUEUED because Redis schedules them for execution at EXEC.
interview.followUp: When are the commands' actual results available? EXEC returns the results after the queued commands run.

interview.question: What are MULTI's syntax, complexity, and introduction version?
interview.answer: MULTI has O(1) time complexity and was introduced in Redis Open Source 1.2.0. Its syntax is simply MULTI, with no arguments.
interview.followUp: Which related commands complete or cancel the transaction? EXEC commits the queued commands, while DISCARD aborts them.

keyPoints: MULTI begins a transaction on the current client connection.
Commands after MULTI wait in a queue and are executed together when EXEC is called.
A successful MULTI command acknowledges entry into transaction mode with OK.
EXEC is the commit point that causes Redis to run the queued commands.
The command has no client API method signature documented on its command-reference page.
gotchas: Clustered deployments can impose different transaction behavior, so verify the multi-key transaction constraints for the topology in use.
Do not expect queued commands to return their normal results before EXEC; their immediate replies indicate that they were queued.
Use DISCARD to abandon the queued commands instead of executing them.

PERSIST.summary: Removes the existing expiration from a key, making it persistent. Returns 1 when a timeout was removed, otherwise 0.
PERSIST.explanation: PERSIST removes the expiration associated with a key. The key remains present and becomes persistent; the command reports whether an expiration was actually removed.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key.

PERSIST.returns: Integer reply: 1 if the timeout has been removed; 0 if the key does not exist or does not have an associated timeout.

example.title: Remove a key expiration
example.code:
redis-cli SET session:123 "active"
redis-cli EXPIRE session:123 300
redis-cli PERSIST session:123
redis-cli TTL session:123
example.explanation: The final TTL is -1, showing that the key no longer has an expiration.

useCases.title: Promote a cache entry to persistent
useCases.scenario: A cache entry must survive beyond its previously assigned TTL.

useCases.title: Keep selected application state
useCases.scenario: A session or configuration key should remain available indefinitely after a condition is met.

useCases.title: Cancel expiration
useCases.scenario: Application logic needs to cancel a scheduled key expiration.

interview.question: What does PERSIST do, and what does it return?
interview.answer: PERSIST key removes the key's existing timeout, changing it from volatile to persistent. It returns 1 when a timeout was removed and 0 when the key is missing or has no timeout.
interview.followUp: How can you verify the result? Use TTL: it returns -1 for an existing key with no associated timeout.

interview.question: What are PERSIST's complexity and required argument?
interview.answer: The command has O(1) time complexity. It takes one required argument, key, which identifies the key whose expiration should be removed.
interview.followUp: What is the command syntax? PERSIST key.

interview.question: Does PERSIST delete or modify the key's value?
interview.answer: PERSIST changes expiration metadata; it does not delete the key or alter its value. After successful removal, the key remains available without an associated timeout.
interview.followUp: What happens if the key already has no timeout? The command returns 0 and leaves that state unchanged.

keyPoints: PERSIST removes the current expiration and makes the key persistent.
Once its timeout is removed, the key will not expire because it has no associated timeout.
A return value of 1 confirms that PERSIST removed the timeout.
The command returns 0 when the named key is absent.
PERSIST completes in constant time.
Its required argument is the key name whose expiration should be removed.
gotchas: A return value of 0 does not distinguish between a missing key and an existing key without an expiration.

PEXPIRE.summary: Sets a key's expiration timeout in milliseconds. Optional NX, XX, GT, and LT modes conditionally control whether the timeout is applied.
PEXPIRE.explanation: PEXPIRE assigns a timeout to an existing key in milliseconds. Redis removes the key after the timeout elapses; optional mutually exclusive modes restrict setting the expiry based on whether an expiry exists or how the new timeout compares with the current one.
PEXPIRE.syntax: PEXPIRE key milliseconds [NX | XX | GT | LT]

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Key whose timeout is modified.

parameters.name: milliseconds
parameters.description: Timeout duration, in milliseconds.

parameters.name: mode
parameters.description: Optional mutually exclusive condition: NX, XX, GT, or LT.

PEXPIRE.returns: Integer reply: 1 if the timeout was set; 0 if it was not set, including when the key does not exist or an option condition fails.

example.title: Set a millisecond expiration
example.code:
SET session:42 "active"
PEXPIRE session:42 1500
PTTL session:42
example.explanation: Stores a value, assigns a 1.5-second expiration, then reads the remaining lifetime in milliseconds.

useCases.title: Apply precise cache expiration
useCases.scenario: Session and cache entries need sub-second or exact millisecond lifetimes.

useCases.title: Conditionally initialize a timeout
useCases.scenario: A write should establish an expiry only if another operation has not already set one.

useCases.title: Adjust an existing expiration
useCases.scenario: A refresh should extend or shorten an existing lifetime only under a chosen comparison.

interview.question: What does PEXPIRE do, and what does it return?
interview.answer: PEXPIRE sets a key's time-to-live using milliseconds rather than seconds. It returns 1 when the timeout is applied and 0 when it is not, such as when the key does not exist.
interview.followUp: How would you verify millisecond precision? Use PTTL after setting the timeout; it reports the remaining lifetime in milliseconds.

interview.question: Explain the NX, XX, GT, and LT options.
interview.answer: NX applies the timeout only if the key currently has no expiry, while XX requires an existing expiry. GT applies it only when the new timeout is greater than the current one, and LT requires it to be less.
interview.followUp: What happens if these modes are combined? The options are mutually exclusive, so they must be supplied individually.

interview.question: When is an expired key removed and when are expiration events generated?
interview.answer: A positive timeout causes the key to expire after the specified duration. Redis can remove expired keys when accessed or through background expiration, so expiration-related events are not guaranteed to occur exactly when the TTL reaches zero.
interview.followUp: What event accompanies a negative timeout? Redis deletes the key immediately and emits only a del event, rather than an expire event.

keyPoints: PEXPIRE is the millisecond-granularity counterpart of EXPIRE.
The key argument identifies the key whose lifetime should be changed.
The milliseconds argument specifies the duration before expiration.
NX protects an already-expiring key by applying the timeout only when no expiry exists.
XX requires the target key to already have an expiration.
GT allows replacement only when the new expiration is later than the current expiration.
LT allows replacement only when the new expiration is earlier than the current expiration.
gotchas: NX, XX, GT, and LT cannot be combined.
With GT, a key without an expiry is considered to have an infinite current TTL, so a finite new expiry does not replace it.
A missing key or a condition that fails returns 0 rather than applying an expiry.

PFADD.summary: PFADD adds items to a HyperLogLog key. It creates the key if it does not exist and reports whether the estimated cardinality changed.
PFADD.explanation: PFADD records one or more items in a HyperLogLog stored at a key. Redis creates the HyperLogLog when the key is missing. The structure estimates how many different items were added; use PFCOUNT to read that estimate.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the HyperLogLog key.

parameters.name: element [element ...]
parameters.description: One or more items to add. This argument is optional.

PFADD.returns: An integer: 1 if at least one HyperLogLog internal register changed; otherwise 0.

example.title: Add items and count them
example.code:
PFADD visitors alice bob carol
PFCOUNT visitors
example.explanation: Adds three names, then reads the estimated number of unique names.

useCases.title: Estimate unique items
useCases.scenario: Track approximate unique visitors, devices, or events while using less memory than storing every item.

useCases.title: Batch observations
useCases.scenario: Add several observations to one HyperLogLog in a single command.

useCases.title: Initialize a key
useCases.scenario: Create an empty HyperLogLog before later updates.

interview.question: What does PFADD return?
interview.answer: PFADD adds items to a HyperLogLog. It returns 1 when at least one internal register changes, and 0 when no register changes.
interview.followUp: What does a return value of 0 prove? It only says that no internal register changed. It does not by itself prove that every supplied item was already seen.

interview.question: What is the syntax of PFADD?
interview.answer: The command syntax is PFADD key [element [element ...]]. The key identifies the HyperLogLog, and the elements are the values to add.
interview.followUp: What happens when the element list is empty? Redis creates the structure only if the key does not already exist.

interview.question: When would you use PFADD?
interview.answer: PFADD is used when a memory-saving estimate of unique items is enough. Add items with PFADD, read the estimate with PFCOUNT, and combine structures with PFMERGE when needed.
interview.followUp: How is the count different from a set count? A HyperLogLog estimates cardinality, while a set stores the actual unique members.

keyPoints: PFADD writes items to a HyperLogLog and creates the key when needed.
A return value of 1 means the estimated unique-item count changed.
A return value of 0 means no internal register changed.
The documented complexity is O(1) for adding each element.
The required key argument names the HyperLogLog to update.
You can provide one or more elements after the key.
Use PFCOUNT to retrieve the current estimate of unique items.
gotchas: Calling PFADD with only a key does not add an item. It creates the HyperLogLog only when the key does not exist; otherwise it does nothing.

PFCOUNT.summary: PFCOUNT estimates the number of unique values in one or more HyperLogLog keys. With multiple keys, it estimates the size of their union.
PFCOUNT.explanation: PFCOUNT reads one or more HyperLogLog keys. With one key, it returns that key's estimated unique-element count. With several keys, it estimates the count of their union by merging them temporarily.

parameters.name: key [key ...]
parameters.description: One or more Redis keys containing HyperLogLog structures. With multiple keys, Redis estimates the union.

PFCOUNT.returns: An integer containing the approximated number of unique elements observed through PFADD.

example.title: Count unique values
example.code:
PFADD daily_queries "redis" "cache" "redis"
PFCOUNT daily_queries
example.explanation: Add values to a HyperLogLog, then return its estimated number of unique values.

useCases.title: Daily unique counts
useCases.scenario: Count unique search queries during a day without storing every query.

useCases.title: Combined estimates
useCases.scenario: Estimate unique users or events across several HyperLogLogs.

useCases.title: Memory-efficient counting
useCases.scenario: Track large-scale distinct values with low memory use.

interview.question: What does PFCOUNT return?
interview.answer: PFCOUNT returns an estimated number of unique elements stored in one or more HyperLogLogs. With multiple keys, it returns the estimated cardinality of their union.
interview.followUp: Why can two keys with overlapping values still produce a union count? HyperLogLog merging combines their registers, so shared values are not simply added twice.

interview.question: What is its time complexity?
interview.answer: A single-key call has constant time complexity, with a small average constant. For multiple keys, the complexity is O(N), where N is the number of keys, and the constant is larger.
interview.followUp: Why is the multi-key case slower? Redis performs an on-the-fly merge and cannot cache the resulting union cardinality.

interview.question: How accurate and memory-efficient is PFCOUNT?
interview.answer: The result is approximate, not exact. Redis documents a standard error of 0.81%, while each HyperLogLog uses about 12 KB plus a small amount for its key.
interview.followUp: When is this useful? It is suitable for large unique-count estimates, such as daily search-query counts, when exact membership storage would use more memory.

keyPoints: PFCOUNT estimates how many different values were added to HyperLogLog key(s).
A missing single key returns 0.
Several keys are counted as one combined set, so the result estimates their union.
The estimate has a documented standard error of 0.81%.
A HyperLogLog provides unique counting without storing every value.
PFCOUNT was added in Redis Open Source 2.8.9.
gotchas: PFCOUNT can change the HyperLogLog internally to store a cached count, so treat it as technically a write command.
Counting several keys can be much slower because Redis merges them during the command and cannot cache the union count.
Check Redis cluster multi-key rules before calling PFCOUNT with keys that may be on different slots.

PFMERGE.summary: PFMERGE combines one or more HyperLogLogs into a destination key. It produces an approximate count of unique items across the merged data.
PFMERGE.explanation: PFMERGE combines HyperLogLog values into the destination key. The destination is included in the merge, along with every source key. The result estimates the number of unique items across the inputs, so it does not store the original items.

parameters.name: destkey
parameters.description: The HyperLogLog key that stores the merged result. Its current value is also part of the merge.

parameters.name: sourcekey
parameters.description: One or more HyperLogLog keys to combine with the destination.

example.title: Merge HyperLogLogs
example.code:
PFADD bikes Hyperion Deimos Phoebe Quaoar
PFADD commuter_bikes Salacia Mimas Quaoar
PFMERGE all_bikes bikes commuter_bikes
PFCOUNT all_bikes
example.explanation: Adds items to two HyperLogLogs, combines them, then reads the estimated number of unique items.

useCases.title: Combine separate counters
useCases.scenario: You track unique users, devices, or events in separate HyperLogLogs and need one estimate for all of them.

useCases.title: Build a combined estimate
useCases.scenario: You need to preserve a daily or regional HyperLogLog while adding data from other keys.

useCases.title: Estimate overall cardinality
useCases.scenario: You want a space-efficient estimate of unique values across several groups.

interview.question: What does PFMERGE do?
interview.answer: PFMERGE writes one or more HyperLogLog values into a destination key. Its syntax is PFMERGE destkey [sourcekey [sourcekey ...]]. The command returns OK when it succeeds.
interview.followUp: What happens if the destination already has data? The destination is included in the merge, so its existing HyperLogLog data contributes to the result.

interview.question: What is the time complexity?
interview.answer: Its time complexity is O(N), where N is the number of HyperLogLogs merged. The documentation also notes that the constant factors are high.
interview.followUp: How would you reduce the work? Merge fewer source HyperLogLogs in each call, because the work grows with the number of inputs.

interview.question: Is the merged count exact?
interview.answer: A HyperLogLog estimates set cardinality rather than storing the actual members. PFMERGE therefore produces an approximate count of unique items across the merged HyperLogLogs.
interview.followUp: How can you read the estimate? Run PFCOUNT on the destination key after the merge.

keyPoints: The command combines HyperLogLog values into one destination key.
destkey is the key that receives the merged HyperLogLog.
You can provide one or more source keys after the destination key.
Existing data in the destination participates in the merge.
The work grows with the number of HyperLogLogs, and each merge can have a large constant cost.
A successful command returns the simple string OK.
gotchas: In a Redis cluster, multi-key behavior can differ. Check the cluster rules before merging keys.

PING.summary: PING returns PONG or echoes an optional message. Use it to check a Redis connection, test whether the server can serve data, or measure latency.
PING.explanation: PING asks Redis for a liveliness response. Without a message, Redis returns PONG. With a message, Redis returns the same message. You can use it to check a connection, check whether the server can serve data, or measure latency.

parameters.name: message
parameters.description: Optional text that Redis returns instead of PONG.

PING.returns: With no message, a simple string reply: PONG. With a message, a bulk string containing that message. For a subscribed RESP2 client, an array containing lowercase pong and the message or an empty bulk string.

example.title: Check a Redis connection
example.code:
redis-cli PING
redis-cli PING "hello world"
example.explanation: The first command checks the server and prints PONG. The second sends a message and prints that message.

useCases.title: Check connection liveness
useCases.scenario: A health check needs to confirm that a Redis connection responds.

useCases.title: Check server readiness
useCases.scenario: An application needs to detect whether Redis is ready to serve data.

useCases.title: Measure latency
useCases.scenario: A network or deployment test needs round-trip timing.
