interview.question: What does Redis PING return?
interview.answer: PING has constant O(1) time complexity. With no argument it returns the simple string PONG. With a message, it returns that message as a bulk string.
interview.followUp: What happens for a subscribed RESP2 client? It receives a two-item array: lowercase pong first, then the supplied message or an empty bulk string.

interview.question: When would you use PING?
interview.answer: Use PING to test whether a connection is alive, check whether the server can serve data, or measure latency. It is a connection command.
interview.followUp: Can PING prove that every read will succeed? No. It checks the server response, but the documented cases show it can return an error when the server cannot currently serve data.

interview.question: What is the syntax and protocol behavior of PING?
interview.answer: The syntax is PING [message], where message is optional. Redis added this command in version 1.0.0.
interview.followUp: How does RESP3 differ in subscribed mode? RESP3 clients keep the standard PING reply even while subscribed.

keyPoints: Run PING without an argument to receive PONG.
An optional message is returned unchanged as a bulk string.
Use PING as a basic connection liveness check.
PING can show whether the server is currently able to serve data.
RESP3 keeps the normal PING response even for subscribed clients.
gotchas: A subscribed RESP2 client receives an array instead of the normal reply. Its first item is lowercase pong, and its second item is the message or an empty string.
A successful connection does not always mean Redis can serve data. PING can return an error while data is loading or when the connection uses a stale replica.

PSUBSCRIBE.summary: PSUBSCRIBE subscribes a client to one or more glob-style channel patterns. It delivers messages published on channels whose names match those patterns.
PSUBSCRIBE.explanation: PSUBSCRIBE puts a client into subscribed mode for one or more channel-name patterns. Redis delivers messages published on channels that match those patterns. In RESP2, the client should then use only subscription-related commands, PING, RESET, or QUIT; RESP3 allows other commands while subscribed.

parameters.name: pattern [pattern ...]
parameters.description: One or more glob-style channel-name patterns. Matching published channels deliver messages to the client.

PSUBSCRIBE.returns: No ordinary return value. Redis pushes one `psubscribe` confirmation message for each pattern when the subscription succeeds.

example.title: Subscribe to matching channels
example.code: PSUBSCRIBE news:*
example.explanation: Subscribes the client to every channel whose name starts with `news:`. Redis sends matching published messages to this client.

useCases.title: Watch a channel family
useCases.scenario: A service needs events from channels such as `orders:created` and `orders:paid` without subscribing to each channel separately.

useCases.title: Monitor related channels
useCases.scenario: A monitoring client listens to channels with names that follow a shared prefix.

useCases.title: Combine multiple patterns
useCases.scenario: A client needs one subscription for several channel naming patterns.

interview.question: What does PSUBSCRIBE do?
interview.answer: PSUBSCRIBE subscribes a client to one or more glob-style channel patterns. Redis sends the client messages published to channels whose names match at least one pattern.
interview.followUp: How does pattern matching work? The pattern can use `?` for one character, `*` for any sequence, and bracket expressions such as `[ae]`.

interview.question: What are the syntax and time complexity?
interview.answer: Its syntax is `PSUBSCRIBE pattern [pattern ...]`. The command takes at least one pattern, and its time complexity is O(N), where N is the number of patterns.
interview.followUp: Why does adding patterns affect the command cost? Redis processes each supplied pattern, so the work grows with the number of patterns.

interview.question: What does a successful PSUBSCRIBE return?
interview.answer: In RESP2 and RESP3, the command has no ordinary returned value. Redis pushes a `psubscribe` confirmation for each pattern after a successful subscription.
interview.followUp: How can a client leave subscribed mode? It can use `RESET`, available for this purpose starting in Redis 6.2.0, or unsubscribe and then stop subscribing.

keyPoints: Use it to receive messages from many channels through one pattern-based subscription.
The command requires at least one pattern and accepts multiple patterns in one call.
The `?` wildcard matches exactly one character.
The `*` wildcard matches a sequence of characters, including an empty sequence.
A bracket expression matches one character from the listed set.
Redis 6.2.0 added RESET as a way to leave subscribed mode.
gotchas: After subscribing, a RESP2 client cannot normally send unrelated commands. It may use subscription commands, PING, RESET, or QUIT.
Pattern characters have special meanings. Escape them when the channel name must contain them literally.
A successful command has no normal return value. Redis instead pushes one confirmation message for each pattern.

PTTL.summary: Returns the remaining expiration time of a key in milliseconds. It distinguishes an existing key without expiration (-1) from a missing key (-2).
PTTL.explanation: PTTL takes one key and reports how long that key will remain before expiration, measured in milliseconds. A nonnegative result is the remaining lifetime; -1 distinguishes an existing key without expiration from -2, which means the key does not exist.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key whose remaining expiration should be returned.

PTTL.returns: An integer: the remaining TTL in milliseconds; -1 if the key exists without an associated expiration; or -2 if the key does not exist.

example.title: Inspect a millisecond expiration
example.code:
SET session:42 "user-123" PX 30000
PTTL session:42
example.explanation: Stores a session with a 30-second millisecond expiration, then reads its remaining lifetime.

useCases.title: Read cache freshness
useCases.scenario: A cache client needs to expose or calculate how long a cached entry remains valid with millisecond precision.

useCases.title: Calculate retry timing
useCases.scenario: A rate limiter needs the remaining lockout interval to tell a client when retrying may be reasonable.

useCases.title: Inspect key lifecycle
useCases.scenario: An operations check verifies whether a key has an expiration and observes its remaining duration.

interview.question: What does PTTL measure, and how does it differ from TTL?
interview.answer: PTTL returns the remaining time to live for a key in milliseconds. Unlike TTL, which reports seconds, PTTL uses millisecond units.
interview.followUp: How would you distinguish a missing key from a persistent key? Check for -2 for a missing key and -1 for an existing key without an expiration.

interview.question: What are PTTL's argument and time complexity?
interview.answer: The command accepts one required argument: the key whose expiration is being inspected. Its time complexity is O(1), making the lookup constant time.
interview.followUp: What should a caller do when the result is nonnegative? Treat it as the remaining lifetime in milliseconds, while remembering that it can decrease immediately after the read.

interview.question: What values can PTTL return?
interview.answer: PTTL returns an integer reply: a nonnegative TTL in milliseconds, -1 when the key exists without an expiration, or -2 when the key does not exist. These meanings apply to both RESP2 and RESP3.
interview.followUp: Which command can establish a millisecond expiration before checking it? PEXPIRE sets a relative timeout with millisecond precision.

keyPoints: PTTL reports a key's remaining expiration interval using milliseconds.
The required key argument identifies which Redis key to inspect.
Use PTTL when millisecond units are needed; TTL provides the corresponding value in seconds.
The command has been available since Redis Open Source 2.6.0.
PTTL performs a constant-time expiration lookup.
gotchas: Do not interpret every negative result as the same condition: -2 means the key is absent.
An existing persistent key returns -1, so callers should handle it separately from a missing key.

PUBLISH.summary: PUBLISH sends a message to a channel for delivery to its current subscribers. It returns the number of clients that received the message.
PUBLISH.explanation: PUBLISH sends a message to every client currently subscribed to the specified channel. In a Redis Cluster, Redis forwards the publication as needed, but the returned count includes only clients connected to the publisher's node.

parameters.name: channel
parameters.description: Channel to publish the message to.

parameters.name: message
parameters.description: Message to publish.

PUBLISH.returns: Integer reply: the number of clients that the message was sent to.

example.title: Publish to a channel
example.code:
redis-cli SUBSCRIBE news
redis-cli PUBLISH news "Redis update"
example.explanation: Run the subscriber in one terminal and the publisher in another; the publisher receives the number of clients that received the message.

useCases.title: Real-time notifications
useCases.scenario: Broadcast an event to all currently connected consumers of a topic.

useCases.title: Job completion signaling
useCases.scenario: Signal a waiting service that an operation completed without polling.

useCases.title: Event fan-out
useCases.scenario: Fan out a serialized application event to active listeners.

interview.question: What does PUBLISH do, and what does it return?
interview.answer: PUBLISH takes a channel and a message, then returns an integer representing the number of clients that received it. The command does not require subscribers to exist.
interview.followUp: How does this count behave in a cluster? It includes only clients connected to the same node as the publishing client.

interview.question: What are PUBLISH's arguments?
interview.answer: The command uses the syntax `PUBLISH channel message`. The channel identifies the publication topic, while the message is the payload delivered to subscribers.
interview.followUp: How can clients receive pattern-based publications? They can use PSUBSCRIBE; Redis sends those deliveries as pattern-matching messages.

interview.question: What is the time complexity of PUBLISH?
interview.answer: PUBLISH has time complexity O(N+M), where N is the number of clients subscribed to the receiving channel and M is the total number of subscribed patterns.
interview.followUp: What delivery guarantee does Redis Pub/Sub provide? At-most-once delivery: a message is delivered once if at all.

keyPoints: PUBLISH broadcasts the supplied payload on one named channel.
Cluster clients may issue PUBLISH against any node.
Redis Cluster routes publications so subscribers can connect through any node.
The integer response reports how many clients received the publication.
Its cost grows with direct subscribers and subscribed patterns.
PUBLISH has been available since Redis Open Source 2.0.0.
gotchas: In a Redis Cluster, the integer reply does not count subscribers connected to other nodes.

RANDOMKEY.summary: Returns a random key name from the currently selected Redis database. An empty database returns no key.
RANDOMKEY.explanation: Redis looks in the currently selected database and chooses a key at random. The command does not change data. An empty database produces a null result, while a database with keys produces the selected key name.
RANDOMKEY.returns: A random key name as a bulk string. If the selected database is empty, the result is nil in RESP2 or null in RESP3.

example.title: Get a random key
example.code: RANDOMKEY
example.explanation: Returns one key chosen at random from the selected database. It returns nothing when that database has no keys.

useCases.title: Sample one existing key without listing all keys.
useCases.scenario: Testing or inspection

useCases.title: Check whether the selected database contains a key.
useCases.scenario: Keyspace checks

interview.question: What does RANDOMKEY do, and what is its time complexity?
interview.answer: RANDOMKEY returns a randomly selected key name from the currently selected database. It has constant time complexity, O(1).
interview.followUp: How does it behave on an empty database? It returns a nil reply in RESP2 or a null reply in RESP3.

interview.question: Does RANDOMKEY change data?
interview.answer: The command takes no arguments, so its syntax is simply RANDOMKEY. It is read-only and does not modify the database.
interview.followUp: Which ACL categories apply? The documentation lists @keyspace, @read, and @slow.

interview.question: What does RANDOMKEY return when keys exist?
interview.answer: A database containing keys returns a bulk string reply containing one key name. The result is from the database selected by the connection.
interview.followUp: What should a client do with the result? Check for a null value before using the returned key name.

keyPoints: It selects the key from the database currently selected by the connection.
With data present, the result is a bulk string containing a key name.
Redis has supported this command since version 1.0.0.
The command has constant time complexity, written as O(1).
Its ACL categories are @keyspace, @read, and @slow.
gotchas: Handle a null or nil result when the selected database has no keys.

RENAME.summary: Renames a key to a new name, replacing the destination if it already exists. In Redis Cluster, both names must belong to the same hash slot.
RENAME.explanation: RENAME moves an existing key from key to newkey and returns success. If the destination already exists, Redis replaces it; in clustered deployments, both names must map to the same hash slot.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The key to rename.

parameters.name: newkey
parameters.description: The new key name. An existing key with this name is overwritten.

RENAME.returns: Simple string: OK on success; an error when the source key does not exist.

example.title: Rename a key
example.code:
SET user:42 "Ada"
RENAME user:42 user:99
GET user:99
example.explanation: Stores a value, moves the key to a new name, then reads it through the new name.

useCases.title: Migrate a key name
useCases.scenario: Change a cache key after a namespace or identifier migration without rewriting its stored value.

useCases.title: Promote staged data
useCases.scenario: Publish a completed temporary value under its final key name.

useCases.title: Cluster-compatible renaming
useCases.scenario: Move a key within a cluster when both names share a hash tag and slot.

interview.question: What does RENAME do when the source key is missing?
interview.answer: RENAME changes the name of an existing key and returns a simple string success response. If the source key does not exist, Redis returns an error.
interview.followUp: What happens when the destination exists? Redis overwrites it through an implicit DEL, which can add latency for a very large value.

interview.question: What is RENAME's time complexity, and what performance caveat applies?
interview.answer: The command has O(1) time complexity in the usual case. However, replacing an existing destination can incur deletion work that is not represented by the nominal rename complexity.
interview.followUp: How would you avoid an unconditional overwrite? Use RENAMENX, which renames only when the target name does not already exist.

interview.question: What restriction applies to RENAME in cluster mode?
interview.answer: In Redis Cluster, the source and destination must be assigned to the same hash slot. Keys using the same hash tag can be designed to satisfy that requirement.
interview.followUp: Why does this matter? Multi-key operations cannot reliably coordinate keys placed in different cluster slots.

keyPoints: The command transfers the key's existing value and associated data to the new name.
A missing source key causes the command to fail rather than creating the destination.
The destination name is not preserved when it already refers to another key.
RENAME has been available since Redis Open Source 1.0.0.
The documented normal-case complexity is constant time.
gotchas: The destination is replaced without a protection check, so use RENAMENX when overwriting an existing destination would be unsafe.
Replacing a large destination can trigger an implicit deletion and add latency.
Cluster deployments require compatible hash slots, typically achieved by using the same hash tag in both names.

RESTORE.summary: RESTORE creates a key by deserializing a serialized value produced by DUMP. It can apply a relative or absolute expiration and optionally replace an existing key or initialize eviction metadata.
RESTORE.explanation: RESTORE deserializes a value produced by DUMP and creates the specified key. A TTL of zero means no expiration; otherwise Redis interprets the TTL as milliseconds, or as an absolute Unix-millisecond expiration time when ABSTTL is supplied.
RESTORE.syntax: RESTORE key ttl serialized-value [REPLACE] [ABSTTL] [IDLETIME seconds] [FREQ frequency]

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Name of the destination key to create.

parameters.name: ttl
parameters.description: Expiration in milliseconds; zero means no expiration. With ABSTTL, it is an absolute Unix timestamp in milliseconds.

parameters.name: serialized-value
parameters.description: Serialized value produced by DUMP.

parameters.name: REPLACE
parameters.description: Replace the destination if it exists.

parameters.name: ABSTTL
parameters.description: Interpret ttl as an absolute Unix timestamp in milliseconds.

parameters.name: IDLETIME seconds
parameters.description: Set idle time for LRU eviction, in seconds.

parameters.name: FREQ frequency
parameters.description: Set the access-frequency counter for LFU eviction.

RESTORE.returns: A simple string status reply, normally OK on success; errors are returned for a busy destination without REPLACE or invalid serialized data.

example.title: Copy a serialized key
example.explanation: Serializes one key with DUMP and recreates it under another name with a 60-second relative expiration.

useCases.title: Key migration or duplication
useCases.scenario: Move or copy a value between key names after obtaining its serialized representation with DUMP.

useCases.title: Cache restoration with expiration
useCases.scenario: Recreate cached data while preserving a relative lifetime or supplying an absolute expiration deadline.

useCases.title: Eviction metadata initialization
useCases.scenario: Restore data while initializing idle time or access frequency used by an eviction policy.

interview.question: What does RESTORE do?
interview.answer: RESTORE creates a key by deserializing a serialized value, normally one returned by DUMP. Its TTL argument is expressed in milliseconds, and zero creates the key without expiration.
interview.followUp: How would you preserve an absolute expiration timestamp? Use ABSTTL, which makes the TTL argument an absolute Unix timestamp in milliseconds rather than a relative duration.

interview.question: How do you restore over an existing key?
interview.answer: By default, RESTORE fails when the destination key already exists. REPLACE changes that behavior by replacing the existing key.
interview.followUp: What happens if the destination does not exist but the payload is invalid? Redis validates the RDB version and checksum and returns an error when they do not match.

interview.question: What are IDLETIME and FREQ used for?
interview.answer: IDLETIME sets the restored key's idle time in seconds for LRU eviction, while FREQ sets its access-frequency counter for LFU eviction. These options let restoration initialize eviction-related metadata.
interview.followUp: When should ABSTTL be used instead of a relative TTL? Use it when the expiration is already represented as an absolute Unix timestamp in milliseconds, such as when preserving a shared deadline.

keyPoints: RESTORE reconstructs a Redis key from an opaque serialized representation, typically generated by DUMP.
A zero TTL creates a persistent key rather than applying an expiration.
ABSTTL switches the TTL from a relative duration to an absolute expiration timestamp.
REPLACE allows restoration to overwrite an existing destination key.
IDLETIME initializes the restored key's idle time in seconds for LRU eviction behavior.
FREQ initializes the restored key's access-frequency counter for LFU eviction behavior.
gotchas: An existing destination key causes an error unless REPLACE is included.
Redis rejects payloads when the serialized data's RDB version or checksum validation fails.

RPOP.summary: RPOP removes and returns items from the end of a Redis list. It removes one item by default or up to a requested count.
RPOP.explanation: RPOP changes the list stored at key by removing items from its right end and returning them. With no count, it removes one item. With count, it removes up to that many items, limited by the current list length. If the operation removes the final item, Redis deletes the key.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key that stores the list.

parameters.name: count
parameters.description: Optional number of elements to remove. Without it, one element is removed.

RPOP.returns: Without count, the removed element, or nil when the key does not exist. With count, up to count removed elements, or nil when the key does not exist.

example.title: Remove items from the list tail
example.code:
RPUSH mylist one two three four five
RPOP mylist
RPOP mylist 2
LRANGE mylist 0 -1
example.explanation: The first command creates a list. The next command removes five. The count form then removes four and three. Two elements remain.

useCases.title: Use a list as a stack
useCases.scenario: Process the newest queued item first.

useCases.title: Batch removal
useCases.scenario: Remove several completed items from the tail in one command.

useCases.title: Queue consumption
useCases.scenario: Read and remove work in one atomic Redis command.

useCases.title: Tail cleanup
useCases.scenario: Keep only older items after taking recent entries.

interview.question: What does RPOP do?
interview.answer: RPOP removes and returns the last item in a Redis list. Its syntax is `RPOP key [count]`; without count it returns one item, and with count it returns up to that many items.
interview.followUp: How does the operation scale? Its complexity is O(N), where N is the number of returned items.

interview.question: What are RPOP's arguments?
interview.answer: The `key` identifies the list. The optional integer `count` sets the maximum number of items to remove from the list's end.
interview.followUp: What happens when count is larger than the list? Redis returns only the items that the list contains.

interview.question: What does RPOP return?
interview.answer: For one item, the reply is that item. For a count, the reply contains the removed items in tail-to-head order. If the key does not exist, the reply is nil.
interview.followUp: What happens after popping the last item? Redis deletes the list key.

keyPoints: RPOP both reads and deletes items at the right end of a list.
The command accepts a required key and an optional count.
The key must refer to the Redis list to change.
Count controls the maximum number of removed items.
RPOP has been available since Redis Open Source 1.0.0.
The time cost grows with the number of elements returned.
gotchas: Without count, the result is one value rather than a list of values.
A count is a maximum, so a shorter list returns fewer elements.
After the final item is removed, the list key no longer exists.

RPUSH.summary: Appends one or more values to the tail of a Redis list, creating the key when absent. It returns the list's new length.
RPUSH.explanation: RPUSH appends every supplied element to the right-hand end of the list at key. Redis creates the key as a list when it is absent; arguments are added from left to right, and a non-list value causes an error. The command returns the resulting list length.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key that holds the list.

parameters.name: element [element ...]
parameters.description: One or more values to append to the list.

RPUSH.returns: Integer reply: the length of the list after the push operation.

example.title: Append values and inspect the list
example.code:
redis-cli RPUSH mylist "hello" "world"
redis-cli LRANGE mylist 0 -1
example.explanation: Appends two values, then reads the complete list to verify their order.

useCases.title: Build an ordered list
useCases.scenario: Append events, jobs, or records while preserving insertion order.

useCases.title: Implement a queue
useCases.scenario: Add work at the tail and remove it from the head with LPOP or BLPOP.

useCases.title: Batch list appends
useCases.scenario: Add several related values in one command call.

interview.question: What does RPUSH do when its key does not exist?
interview.answer: RPUSH adds one or more values at the tail of a Redis list and returns the list length after the operation. If the key is missing, Redis creates the list first.
interview.followUp: How does a multi-element call affect complexity? Each added element takes constant time, so adding N elements in one call is O(N).

interview.question: Explain RPUSH's arguments and ordering.
interview.answer: The syntax is `RPUSH key element [element ...]`. `key` identifies the list, while the variadic element portion supplies one or more values to append.
interview.followUp: What ordering results from `RPUSH mylist a b c`? The list contains a, then b, then c, because values are appended left to right.

interview.question: What does RPUSH return, and when can it fail?
interview.answer: The command returns an integer representing the list's length after the push. A key containing a non-list value produces an error instead of being converted.
interview.followUp: Which command appends only when the list already exists? `RPUSHX` provides that conditional behavior.

keyPoints: All supplied values are appended to the list's tail.
A missing key is initialized as an empty list before values are added.
One invocation can append multiple values.
Multiple arguments preserve their left-to-right order in the resulting list.
The response is the list's new length.
gotchas: The command fails if the key already contains a non-list value.
With multiple values, their command-line order becomes their list order.

SADD.summary: SADD adds one or more unique members to a Redis set. It creates the set if needed and returns the number of newly added members.
SADD.explanation: SADD adds one or more members to the set stored at a key. It creates a new set when the key does not exist and ignores members that are already present. The command returns how many new members it added.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key that holds the set.

parameters.name: member [member ...]
parameters.description: One or more members to add to the set.

SADD.returns: An integer: the number of members added. Members that were already in the set are not counted.

example.title: Add members to a set
example.code:
SADD myset Hello World
SADD myset World
SMEMBERS myset
example.explanation: The first command adds two members. The second adds no new member because World is already present. SMEMBERS then returns the set members.

useCases.title: Keep unique items
useCases.scenario: Store unique values such as tags, IDs, or group members.

useCases.title: Track new additions
useCases.scenario: Add many values while knowing how many were new.

useCases.title: Prepare set data
useCases.scenario: Build a set before checking membership or running set operations.

interview.question: What does SADD do, and what does it return?
interview.answer: SADD adds one or more members to a set and returns the number of members that were newly added. Existing members do not increase this count.
interview.followUp: What happens when the key does not exist? Redis creates a new set before adding the members.

interview.question: What are SADD's arguments and time complexity?
interview.answer: The command takes a key and one or more members. Its time complexity is O(1) for each member, so adding N members in one call costs O(N).
interview.followUp: How does adding several members in one call affect the complexity? It remains linear in the number of supplied members.

interview.question: How does SADD handle duplicate members?
interview.answer: Redis sets contain unique members, so adding an existing member has no effect. SADD returns zero for that member and does not create a duplicate.
interview.followUp: How can you inspect the resulting set? Use SMEMBERS, but do not depend on member order.

keyPoints: SADD adds one or more members and creates the set key when it is missing.
Members already in the set are ignored.
The integer reply counts only newly added members.
Adding one member costs O(1). Adding N members in one call costs O(N).
The command needs at least one member after the key.
The key identifies the set that receives the members.
gotchas: The command fails if the key already stores a value of another Redis type.

SCAN.summary: SCAN incrementally iterates over key names in the currently selected Redis database. Continue with each returned cursor until it becomes 0, optionally filtering by pattern, count hint, or type.
SCAN.explanation: SCAN incrementally iterates key names in the currently selected database. Each call receives a cursor and returns a new cursor plus a batch of keys; continue until the cursor returns to 0, optionally constraining results with MATCH, COUNT, or TYPE.

parameters.name: cursor
parameters.description: Cursor position; use 0 to begin and the returned cursor for the next call.

parameters.name: MATCH pattern
parameters.description: Optional glob-style pattern used to filter returned key names.

parameters.name: COUNT count
parameters.description: Optional work-count hint for each call; it is not an exact result count.

parameters.name: TYPE type
parameters.description: Optional Redis data type used to restrict returned keys.

SCAN.returns: A two-element array containing the next cursor and an array of key names.

example.title: Iterate matching keys
example.explanation: Starts at cursor 0, repeatedly supplies the returned cursor, filters keys with MATCH, and stops when Redis returns cursor 0.

useCases.title: Incremental keyspace inspection
useCases.scenario: Traverse a large keyspace in bounded batches instead of requesting every key at once.

useCases.title: Pattern-based discovery
useCases.scenario: Find keys belonging to a namespace without using a blocking whole-keyspace command.

useCases.title: Type-restricted maintenance
useCases.scenario: Process only keys whose Redis data type is appropriate for an operation.

interview.question: How do you complete a SCAN iteration?
interview.answer: SCAN iterates keys in the selected database without requiring a key argument. Start with cursor 0, pass each returned cursor into the next call, and finish when it becomes 0.
interview.followUp: How would you avoid scanning keys of the wrong type? Use the optional TYPE argument, while remembering that matching and iteration behavior still apply.

interview.question: What do MATCH and COUNT do?
interview.answer: MATCH accepts a glob-style pattern and limits which returned keys are reported. COUNT suggests how much work Redis should do per call, but it does not guarantee the batch length.
interview.followUp: Why might MATCH return an empty batch? Matching is performed after Redis retrieves elements, so a batch may contain no matching keys.

interview.question: What is SCAN's complexity and what does it imply?
interview.answer: Each call has constant operation complexity, while completing an iteration is O(N), where N is the number of elements in the database. SCAN is therefore suitable for incremental traversal rather than one large blocking result.
interview.followUp: What property must production code handle? Results are not ordered and may repeat, so consumers should tolerate duplicates and avoid relying on order.

keyPoints: SCAN traverses key names in the currently selected Redis database.
Begin with cursor 0 and feed every returned cursor into the following call.
MATCH restricts reported keys to a glob-style pattern.
A call is O(1); a complete traversal is O(N).
gotchas: MATCH can produce empty batches because filtering happens after Redis fetches candidates.

SCARD.summary: SCARD returns the number of members in a Redis set. It returns 0 when the key does not exist.
SCARD.explanation: SCARD reads the set stored at the given key and returns how many members it contains. It does not change the set. If the key is missing, Redis returns zero.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key that holds the set.

SCARD.returns: An integer equal to the number of members in the set. It is 0 when the key does not exist.

example.title: Count set members
example.code:
SADD myset "Hello" "World"
SCARD myset
example.explanation: Adds two unique members to `myset`, then returns `2`.

useCases.title: Count unique items
useCases.scenario: Count unique values stored in a set without reading all members.

useCases.title: Check for an empty set
useCases.scenario: Check whether a set has any members by testing whether the result is zero.

useCases.title: Track set size
useCases.scenario: Measure the size of a set after adding values with SADD.

interview.question: What does SCARD do, and what is its time complexity?
interview.answer: SCARD returns the number of members in a Redis set. Its time complexity is O(1), so counting does not require scanning every member.
interview.followUp: How does SCARD behave for a missing key? Redis returns an integer reply of 0.

interview.question: What argument does SCARD require?
interview.answer: The command takes one key argument: the key that stores the set. Its syntax is `SCARD key`.
interview.followUp: What should the key contain? It should refer to a Redis set.

interview.question: What does SCARD return?
interview.answer: SCARD returns an integer representing the set cardinality, which means the number of elements in the set. The same integer result applies when the set is empty or the key does not exist, with a value of 0.
interview.followUp: How can you create members before counting them? Use SADD, then call SCARD on the same key.

keyPoints: SCARD counts the members in a set.
The key must identify the set to count.
The command runs in constant time.
SCARD is a read command in the set and fast ACL categories.
Redis added SCARD in version 1.0.0.
gotchas: A missing key is not an error. The result is 0.

SCRIPT.summary: SCRIPT is a container for managing Lua scripts in Redis. Use a SCRIPT subcommand to perform a specific management task.
SCRIPT.explanation: SCRIPT is a container for managing Lua scripts in Redis. It does not run one operation by itself; use a SCRIPT subcommand for a specific management task.

example.title: List SCRIPT subcommands
example.code: SCRIPT HELP
example.explanation: Asks Redis to list the available SCRIPT subcommands.

useCases.title: List subcommands
useCases.scenario: You need to discover which script-management operations Redis supports.

useCases.title: Manage scripts
useCases.scenario: You need to inspect or manage loaded Lua scripts.

useCases.title: Check access category
useCases.scenario: You need to connect command permissions to Redis ACL groups.

interview.question: What is SCRIPT in Redis?
interview.answer: SCRIPT groups commands used to manage Lua scripts. The page lists SCRIPT HELP as a way to view the available subcommands.
interview.followUp: How can you discover the available subcommands? Run SCRIPT HELP.

interview.question: When was SCRIPT introduced, and what is its complexity?
interview.answer: The command was added in Redis Open Source 2.6.0. Its time complexity depends on which subcommand you use.
interview.followUp: Why can one fixed complexity value not describe SCRIPT? Its subcommands perform different tasks.

interview.question: How do you learn which SCRIPT operations are available?
interview.answer: SCRIPT is a container command, so it needs a subcommand for a useful operation. The documentation lists management commands such as SCRIPT EXISTS, SCRIPT FLUSH, SCRIPT KILL, and SCRIPT LOAD.
interview.followUp: Which command helps inspect the available options? SCRIPT HELP lists them.

keyPoints: SCRIPT groups commands for managing Lua scripts.
Use SCRIPT HELP to list the available SCRIPT commands.
Redis added SCRIPT in version 2.6.0.
Redis places SCRIPT in the @slow ACL category.
Related scripting commands include EVAL, EVALSHA, and FCALL.
gotchas: The time cost is different for each SCRIPT subcommand.

SDIFF.summary: SDIFF returns members in the first set that are absent from all following sets. It reads the sets without changing them.
SDIFF.explanation: SDIFF compares sets from left to right. It returns members found in the first set but missing from every later set. It does not change any set. A missing key acts like an empty set.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The first set key. Its members are candidates for the result.

parameters.name: key ...
parameters.description: Zero or more additional set keys. Members found in these sets are excluded.

SDIFF.returns: The members of the resulting set. RESP2 uses an array reply; RESP3 uses a set reply.

example.title: Find members in one set but not another
example.code:
SADD users:all alice bob carol
SADD users:blocked bob
SDIFF users:all users:blocked
example.explanation: This returns members in users:all that are absent from users:blocked, such as alice and carol.

useCases.title: Find a set difference
useCases.scenario: Remove users who already have a feature from the full user set.

useCases.title: Apply exclusion sets
useCases.scenario: Compare an allowlist with one or more exclusion lists.

useCases.title: Compare memberships
useCases.scenario: Check which tags or permissions are unique to a primary group.

interview.question: What does SDIFF calculate?
interview.answer: SDIFF returns the members of the first set that do not occur in any later set. With A = {a,b,c} and B = {b}, SDIFF A B returns {a,c}.
interview.followUp: What happens if a later key does not exist? Redis treats that key as an empty set, so it does not remove any members.

interview.question: How are the arguments interpreted?
interview.answer: The command needs at least one key, using the form SDIFF key [key ...]. The first key is the source set; all remaining keys are exclusion sets.
interview.followUp: How does the result differ from SDIFFSTORE? SDIFF returns the members, while SDIFFSTORE saves the result in a destination set.

interview.question: What are the cost and return formats?
interview.answer: Its time complexity is O(N), where N is the total number of elements across all supplied sets. RESP2 returns an array, while RESP3 returns a set.
interview.followUp: Why might RESP3 be useful here? A set reply directly represents the result as unordered unique members.

keyPoints: SDIFF computes a set difference across multiple keys.
Only members from the first set can appear in the result. Any match in a later set removes that member.
A missing key is treated as an empty set.
The work grows with the combined number of elements in all input sets.
With RESP2, the result is returned as an array of members.
With RESP3, the result is returned as a set.
The command has been available since Redis Open Source 1.0.0.
gotchas: In a Redis cluster, behavior can differ for multi-key operations. Check cluster rules before using keys on different nodes.

SELECT.summary: SELECT changes the logical Redis database for the current connection. It uses a zero-based database index.
SELECT.explanation: SELECT changes the logical Redis database used by the current connection. The database number starts at zero, and a new connection starts in database zero. The selected database belongs to the connection, so a client must select it again after reconnecting.

parameters.name: index
parameters.description: Zero-based integer of the logical database to select.

SELECT.returns: A simple string reply: OK, in RESP2 and RESP3.

example.title: Select a database and use it
example.code:
redis-cli
127.0.0.1:6379> SELECT 2
OK
127.0.0.1:6379[2]> SET theme dark
OK
127.0.0.1:6379[2]> GET theme
dark
example.explanation: This switches the connection to database 2, then stores and reads a key there.

useCases.title: Separate keys for one application
useCases.scenario: One application needs separate key spaces within one Redis instance.

useCases.title: Restore the selected database
useCases.scenario: A client reconnects after selecting a non-default database.

interview.question: What does SELECT do?
interview.answer: SELECT changes the logical database for the current connection. Its argument is a zero-based integer, and the command runs in O(1) time.
interview.followUp: What happens after reconnecting? The client must select the desired database again because the selected database is connection-specific.

interview.question: How is the database index interpreted?
interview.answer: The index is zero-based, so SELECT 0 chooses the first database. New connections already use database zero.
interview.followUp: How can you inspect the database used by a connection? CLIENT LIST shows the selected database for each client.

interview.question: Can SELECT be used with Redis Cluster?
interview.answer: Redis Cluster supports only database zero, so SELECT is unavailable there. Multiple databases would not fit the cluster design for atomic operations on one database.
interview.followUp: How should separate applications be organized in a cluster? Use separate key namespaces or separate deployments rather than SELECT-based databases.

keyPoints: The command switches the connection to the database identified by a zero-based integer.
A connection begins in database zero unless it selects another database.
Logical databases share the same RDB or AOF persistence file.
The same key name can exist separately in different logical databases.
The selected database belongs to the connection, not to the key or client application globally.
CLIENT LIST can show which database each connection currently uses.
gotchas: Redis Cluster supports only database zero, so SELECT cannot be used there.
Redis Software and Redis Cloud do not provide shared logical databases; SELECT is accepted only for compatibility and does not change the database.

Set.summary: Redis sets are unordered collections of unique strings. They support fast membership checks and set operations such as intersection, union, and difference.
Set.explanation: A Redis set stores unique strings without keeping them in a defined order. You can add or remove members, check membership, count members, list members, and combine sets with intersection, union, or difference operations.
Set.syntax:
SADD key member [member ...]
SISMEMBER key member
SMISMEMBER key member [member ...]
SCARD key
SMEMBERS key
SINTER key [key ...]
SUNION key [key ...]
SDIFF key [key ...]

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The Redis key that identifies the set.

parameters.name: member
parameters.description: One or more string members to add or test.

parameters.name: set
parameters.description: One or more set keys used by set algebra commands.

Set.returns: Set commands return command-specific results, such as a count, membership result, or set of members.

example.title: Basic set operations
example.code:
SADD colors red blue
SISMEMBER colors red
SCARD colors
SMEMBERS colors
example.explanation: This adds two unique members, checks whether one member exists, counts the members, and returns all members.

useCases.title: Unique collections
useCases.scenario: Store unique values such as user IDs, product IDs, or event names.

useCases.title: Membership checks
useCases.scenario: Check quickly whether a value belongs to a group or feature set.

useCases.title: Set relationships
useCases.scenario: Compare groups to find shared, combined, or excluded members.

interview.question: What is a Redis set?
interview.answer: A Redis set is an unordered collection of unique strings. Adding the same member again does not create a duplicate.
interview.followUp: How would you find common members? Use SINTER with the set keys.

interview.question: Which commands support common set operations?
interview.answer: Use SADD to add members. Use SISMEMBER to test one member, SMISMEMBER to test several, and SCARD to count members.
interview.followUp: Why use SMISMEMBER? It checks several values in one command, which can reduce client-server round trips.

interview.question: How do Redis set algebra commands differ?
interview.answer: SINTER returns members shared by all input sets. SUNION returns members from any input set. SDIFF returns members in the first set that are absent from the remaining sets.
interview.followUp: What should you check when using SDIFF? Check the argument order because changing it changes the result.

keyPoints: Sets contain strings, remove duplicates, and do not preserve a meaningful order.
Adding, removing, and checking one member are constant-time operations.
SADD keeps one copy when the same member is added more than once.
SISMEMBER is suitable for fast membership checks.
SMISMEMBER checks several candidate members in one command.
SINTER calculates the intersection of multiple sets.
gotchas: SMEMBERS does not return members in a guaranteed order.
SDIFF depends on the order of its set arguments.

SET.summary: Sets a key to a string, creating it or replacing its current value. Conditions, expiration controls, and GET support conditional writes, lifetimes, and retrieval of the previous string.
SET.explanation: SET writes a string value to a key, creating it when absent or replacing its existing value regardless of the existing type. Optional conditions control whether the write occurs, while expiration options assign or preserve a lifetime; GET can return the previous string value instead of the normal status response.
SET.syntax: SET key value [NX | XX | IFEQ ifeq-value | IFNE ifne-value | IFDEQ ifdeq-digest | IFDNE ifdne-digest] [GET] [EX seconds | PX milliseconds | EXAT unix-time-seconds | PXAT unix-time-milliseconds | KEEPTTL]

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Name of the key.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The string value to set.

SET.returns: Without GET, OK on success; with NX or XX when the condition fails, nil; with GET, the old string or nil. An error occurs with GET if the existing value is not a string.

example.title: Conditional write with expiration
example.code:
SET session:user:42 active EX 300 NX
GET session:user:42
example.explanation: Creates the key only when absent and sets a five-minute expiration.

useCases.title: Insert-if-absent initialization
useCases.scenario: Create a value only when no value is present, avoiding an overwrite.

useCases.title: Expiring cache values
useCases.scenario: Attach a lifetime directly to a cache entry during the write.

useCases.title: Conditional updates
useCases.scenario: Replace an existing value only when the key is already present.

interview.question: What does SET do when the key already exists?
interview.answer: SET stores a string at the specified key. It creates a missing key and overwrites an existing value regardless of its type; a successful ordinary write returns OK.
interview.followUp: How can a write be conditional? Use NX for an absent key or XX for an existing key, with the condition options mutually exclusive.

interview.question: How does SET control expiration?
interview.answer: EX and PX specify relative expiration in seconds or milliseconds. EXAT and PXAT specify absolute Unix expiration times, while KEEPTTL preserves the existing lifetime.
interview.followUp: What happens if multiple expiration options are supplied? They are mutually exclusive, so the command must select only one.

interview.question: What does the GET option change?
interview.answer: GET makes SET return the old string stored at the key, or nil when the key did not exist. If the existing value is not a string, Redis returns an error and aborts SET.
interview.followUp: Does GET make SET type-safe for other Redis data types? No; it errors on a non-string existing value rather than converting or replacing it.

keyPoints: SET writes string data even when the key currently contains another Redis data type.
A missing key is created by a successful unconditional SET.
NX turns SET into an insert-only operation.
XX prevents SET from creating a new key.
GET changes the reply to the prior string value, or nil for an absent key.
EX assigns a positive whole-number lifetime measured in seconds.
gotchas: Use at most one condition option in a command.
Expiration options are mutually exclusive; choose one lifetime behavior.
With GET, a non-string existing value causes an error rather than returning it.
A successful overwrite removes the old expiry unless KEEPTTL is used.

SETBIT.summary: SETBIT sets or clears one bit in a Redis String. It creates the key when missing and returns the bit's previous value.
SETBIT.explanation: SETBIT changes one bit in the string stored at a key. The offset starts at zero, and the value must be 0 or 1. Redis creates the key when needed and adds zero-filled space when the offset is beyond the current string.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key that holds the String.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: The zero-based bit position. It must be at least 0 and less than 2^32.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The bit to store: 0 or 1.

SETBIT.returns: An integer containing the bit value that was stored at the offset before the command ran.

example.title: Mark and check a user
example.code:
SETBIT users:online 123 1
GETBIT users:online 123
GETBIT users:online 456
example.explanation: This marks user 123 as online, then checks users 123 and 456.

useCases.title: Binary status tracking
useCases.scenario: Track whether numbered users, devices, or sensors have performed an event.

useCases.title: Compact permissions
useCases.scenario: Store permissions where each bit represents one allowed action.

useCases.title: Compact integer sets
useCases.scenario: Represent a set whose members are integer IDs from 0 to N.

interview.question: What does SETBIT do and return?
interview.answer: SETBIT sets one bit in a Redis string and returns the bit that was stored at that offset before the change. It creates the key if it does not exist.
interview.followUp: What happens when the offset is past the current string? Redis grows the string and fills the new bits with zero.

interview.question: What are the valid offset and value ranges?
interview.answer: The offset is zero-based and must be from 0 through 2^32 - 1. The value must be either 0 or 1.
interview.followUp: Why is the maximum offset limited? The limit keeps the bitmap within a 512 MB string.

interview.question: How are Redis bitmaps represented?
interview.answer: A bitmap uses Redis String storage. Each byte represents eight consecutive bit offsets, so normal string commands such as GET and SET can also access its bytes.
interview.followUp: How could a client initialize many bits efficiently? Encode the desired bits as bytes and use one SET command instead of many SETBIT calls.

keyPoints: SETBIT changes one bit and creates the key when it is missing.
Use value 1 to set the bit or 0 to clear it.
Offsets begin at zero.
The command has constant time complexity.
The result is the old value of the selected bit.
Redis stores bitmaps as binary-safe Strings, not as a separate data type.
gotchas: The offset cannot be negative or reach 2^32. This limits a bitmap to 512 MB.
Bits added before the requested offset start as zero.
Setting the last possible bit on a new or small string can temporarily block the server.

SETEX.summary: SETEX stores a string at a key and gives it a timeout in seconds. It is deprecated in favor of SET with the EX option.
SETEX.explanation: SETEX writes a string to the specified key and assigns an expiration measured in seconds. It replaces an existing value and is functionally the same as SET with the EX option; invalid seconds cause an error.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key.

parameters.name: seconds
parameters.description: The time to live, in seconds.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value to set.

SETEX.returns: Simple string reply: OK when the operation succeeds.

example.title: Cache a value with a timeout
example.code:
redis-cli SETEX cache:user:42 60 '{"name":"Ada"}'
redis-cli TTL cache:user:42
redis-cli GET cache:user:42
example.explanation: Stores a JSON string for 60 seconds, then checks its remaining lifetime and reads the value.

useCases.title: Expiring cache entries
useCases.scenario: Cache a serialized response with a bounded lifetime so stale data disappears automatically.

useCases.title: Temporary credentials
useCases.scenario: Store a short-lived token or session value without requiring a separate expiration command.

useCases.title: Self-expiring coordination data
useCases.scenario: Set a safety timeout on a transient coordination key.

interview.question: What does SETEX do and what is its complexity?
interview.answer: SETEX takes a key, a lifetime in seconds, and a string value. It sets the value and expiration together in one operation, with O(1) complexity.
interview.followUp: How should new code express the same operation? Use SET key value EX seconds, which is the documented replacement.

interview.question: What are SETEX's arguments?
interview.answer: The syntax is SETEX key seconds value. The seconds argument is the key's time to live, and the value is the string stored under the key.
interview.followUp: What happens if seconds is invalid? Redis returns an error rather than applying the command.

interview.question: What happens when the key already exists?
interview.answer: An existing key is overwritten with the supplied string and receives the specified expiration. The command creates the key when it does not already exist.
interview.followUp: How can the remaining lifetime be inspected? Use TTL on the key after SETEX.

keyPoints: SETEX stores a string and schedules the key to expire after the requested number of seconds.
Its behavior can be expressed with SET followed by the EX expiration option.
The key argument identifies the Redis key to create or replace.
The seconds argument specifies how long the key remains available.
The value argument supplies the string stored by the command.
SETEX creates the target key when no key with that name currently exists.
gotchas: SETEX is deprecated; use SET with EX for new code or migrations.
The seconds argument must be valid; otherwise Redis returns an error.

SETNX.summary: Sets a string value only when a key does not already exist. It returns 1 when the key is created and 0 when no write occurs; SET with NX is the recommended replacement for new code.
SETNX.explanation: SETNX attempts to store a string value only when the named key is absent. It performs no write when the key already exists and reports whether the write occurred with an integer result.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The value to set, only if the key does not already exist.

SETNX.returns: Integer reply: 1 if the key was set; 0 if the key was not set.

example.title: Set only when absent
example.code:
SETNX mykey "Hello"
SETNX mykey "World"
GET mykey
example.explanation: The first command creates the key and returns 1; the second does nothing and returns 0, so GET still returns Hello.

useCases.title: Conditional initialization
useCases.scenario: Prevent a one-time initialization value from being overwritten when multiple clients race to create the same key.

useCases.title: Simple locking primitive
useCases.scenario: Claim a key as a basic coordination marker so only the client receiving 1 proceeds.

useCases.title: Duplicate detection
useCases.scenario: Use the return code to distinguish the first insertion from later duplicate attempts.

interview.question: What does SETNX do?
interview.answer: SETNX stores the supplied string only if the key does not exist. It returns 1 when it creates the key and 0 when the key already exists.
interview.followUp: How should new code express the same condition? Use SET with the NX option, which is the documented replacement for SETNX.

interview.question: What are SETNX's arguments and behavior when the key already exists?
interview.answer: The command takes exactly a key and a value: SETNX key value. The value is written only when the key is absent; an existing key is left unchanged.
interview.followUp: What happens if the existing key contains a different data type? SETNX performs a presence check and does not replace the existing value.

interview.question: How has SETNX historically been used for locking?
interview.answer: A successful result of 1 indicates that the client acquired the lock key; a result of 0 means another client already holds it. The documented pattern releases the lock with DEL.
interview.followUp: What limitation should be considered for a production lock? A robust design needs an expiration and ownership-safe release strategy rather than relying only on a bare SETNX key.

keyPoints: It conditionally creates a key with a string value.
An existing key remains unchanged, including its current value.
The name describes its set-if-absent semantics.
The integer result is 0 when the conditional write does not happen.
The integer result is 1 when the command creates the key.
The historical locking pattern stores a future validity timestamp as the lock value.
gotchas: SETNX is deprecated; for new code, prefer SET with the NX option.
A lock implemented with SETNX requires an explicit DEL release step, so the lock key must be managed carefully.

SETRANGE.summary: Overwrites part of a Redis string from a specified zero-based offset. It pads with zero bytes when necessary and returns the string's resulting length.
SETRANGE.explanation: SETRANGE replaces bytes in the string stored at a key, beginning at a zero-based offset and continuing for the length of the supplied value. If the key is missing, Redis treats it as an empty string; if the offset extends past the current value, Redis inserts zero-byte padding before writing. The command returns the resulting string length.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: The zero-based offset at which to start overwriting. The string is zero-padded if the offset is beyond the current length.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The string to write at the offset.

SETRANGE.returns: Integer reply: the length of the string after it was modified by the command.

example.title: Overwrite part of a string
example.code:
SET key1 "Hello World"
SETRANGE key1 6 "Redis"
GET key1
example.explanation: Writes "Redis" starting at byte offset 6, then reads the resulting string: "Hello Redis".

useCases.title: Random-access string storage
useCases.scenario: Treat a Redis string as a byte-addressable sequence and update a region without replacing the entire value.

useCases.title: Dense byte arrays
useCases.scenario: Store compact per-entity byte values in a large string, using offsets as positions.

useCases.title: Range-based string updates
useCases.scenario: Combine with GETRANGE to read and update fixed regions of a string.

interview.question: What does SETRANGE do, and what does it return?
interview.answer: SETRANGE uses a zero-based offset and overwrites the existing string for the entire length of the new value. If the write extends beyond the current end, Redis pads the gap with zero bytes and returns the final string length.
interview.followUp: What happens when the key does not exist? Redis treats it as an empty string, creates the string, and places the supplied value at the requested offset.

interview.question: Explain SETRANGE's arguments.
interview.answer: The command's syntax is `SETRANGE key offset value`. `key` identifies the string, `offset` is the zero-based starting position, and `value` is the string written there.
interview.followUp: How should an offset beyond the existing value be interpreted? It causes zero-byte padding before the new value is stored.

interview.question: What is SETRANGE's time complexity?
interview.answer: The documented complexity is O(1), excluding the time needed to copy the new string in place. When the value being copied is longer, the complexity is O(M), where M is its length.
interview.followUp: What storage pattern does Redis documentation associate with SETRANGE and GETRANGE? They can treat strings as linear arrays with O(1) random access.

keyPoints: It modifies an existing Redis string in place, beginning at the supplied position.
The overwrite spans every byte in the replacement value.
Offsets count from zero, so the first byte is position 0.
The result is the string's length after the write, not the number of bytes changed.
Together with GETRANGE, it supports array-like random access over string data.
For a non-small replacement, runtime grows with the replacement value's length.
gotchas: The offset cannot exceed 536870911 because Redis strings are limited to 512 MB.
Writing beyond the current end enlarges the string and inserts zero bytes between the old content and the new value.
A missing key is created as a string large enough to contain the value at the requested offset.

SINTER.summary: SINTER returns the members shared by multiple Redis sets. It reads the sets and does not store or modify the result.
SINTER.explanation: SINTER checks several Redis sets and returns the members found in every set. It does not change any set. A missing key acts like an empty set, so the result is empty if any input key is missing.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The first set key to include in the intersection.

parameters.name: key ...
parameters.description: Zero or more additional set keys. Every supplied set contributes to the intersection.

SINTER.returns: RESP2 returns an array containing the resulting members. RESP3 returns a set containing the resulting members.

example.title: Find shared set members
example.code:
SADD key1 a b c
SADD key2 c d e
SINTER key1 key2
example.explanation: The result contains only the member shared by both sets.

useCases.title: Find common members
useCases.scenario: Find users, permissions, or items that belong to every selected group.

useCases.title: Filter by several sets
useCases.scenario: Compare several collections and keep only values present in all of them.

useCases.title: Read-only set comparison
useCases.scenario: Check a shared membership result without changing the source sets.

interview.question: What does SINTER do?
interview.answer: SINTER returns the members common to all supplied sets. It accepts one or more set keys and leaves the source sets unchanged.
interview.followUp: What happens if one key is missing? Redis treats it as an empty set, so the result has no members.

interview.question: What is the time complexity?
interview.answer: The worst-case complexity is O(N*M). N is the size of the smallest set, and M is the number of sets.
interview.followUp: How can input choice affect work? Starting from a smaller set can reduce the number of membership checks.

interview.question: What does SINTER return?
interview.answer: With RESP2, the command returns an array. With RESP3, it returns a set. Both contain the members in the intersection.
interview.followUp: Which command stores the result? SINTERSTORE writes the intersection to a Redis key instead of returning it directly.

keyPoints: The result contains members present in every input set.
The command needs at least one key and accepts additional keys.
SINTER has been available since Redis Open Source 1.0.0.
Worst-case work depends on the smallest set and the number of input sets.
Redis classifies SINTER as a read, set, and slow command.
RESP2 returns the result members in an array.
gotchas: A missing key makes the intersection empty.
Check Redis cluster multi-key rules before using keys across cluster slots.

SISMEMBER.summary: SISMEMBER checks whether a member belongs to a Redis set. It returns 1 if present and 0 if absent or if the key does not exist.
SISMEMBER.explanation: SISMEMBER checks one value in the set stored at a key. It returns 1 when the value is present. It returns 0 when the value is absent or the key does not exist. The check takes constant time.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The key that holds the set.

parameters.name: member
parameters.description: The member to check.

SISMEMBER.returns: An integer reply: 1 when the member is in the set; 0 when it is absent or the key does not exist.

example.title: Check set membership
example.code:
SADD myset one
SISMEMBER myset one
SISMEMBER myset two
example.explanation: The first command adds `one`. The next command returns `1` because `one` is present. The last returns `0` because `two` is absent.

useCases.title: Test membership
useCases.scenario: Check whether an item is already stored before taking an action.

useCases.title: Query unique items
useCases.scenario: Track unique values such as identifiers or tags and query them quickly.

useCases.title: Check set relationships
useCases.scenario: Check access or relationship membership represented by a set.

interview.question: What does SISMEMBER return?
interview.answer: SISMEMBER checks whether one member belongs to the set at the given key. It returns integer 1 for a member and integer 0 for a non-member or a missing key.
interview.followUp: How can several members be checked? Use SMISMEMBER, which checks multiple members in one command and returns one result for each member.

interview.question: What is the time complexity of SISMEMBER?
interview.answer: Its time complexity is O(1). It reads the set and performs one membership lookup.
interview.followUp: What is the complexity of checking multiple members with SMISMEMBER? The documentation lists it as O(N), where N is the number of members checked.

interview.question: What arguments does SISMEMBER require?
interview.answer: The command has two required arguments: the set key and the member to check. Its syntax is `SISMEMBER key member`.
interview.followUp: What happens if the key stores another data type? Redis commands require the expected data type, so a wrong type causes a command error.

keyPoints: Use SISMEMBER to test whether one value belongs to a Redis set.
The key argument identifies the Redis key containing the set.
The member argument is the value whose presence you want to test.
A result of 1 means the member is in the set.
Each membership check has constant time complexity.
SISMEMBER has been available since Redis Open Source 1.0.0.
gotchas: A missing key returns 0, just like a member that is not in the set. These two cases cannot be distinguished from this reply alone.

SMEMBERS.summary: Returns every member of the set stored at a key. The result contains the set's complete, unordered membership.
SMEMBERS.explanation: SMEMBERS reads the complete set stored at the specified key and returns its members as an unordered collection. It is equivalent to running SINTER with that one key, and its work grows linearly with the set size.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The key containing the set whose members should be returned.

SMEMBERS.returns: All members of the set at the key; RESP2 represents them as an array reply, while RESP3 represents them as a set reply.

example.title: Read all set members
example.code:
SADD myset "Hello" "World"
SMEMBERS myset
example.explanation: Adds two values to a Redis set, then retrieves every member.

useCases.title: Read set membership
useCases.scenario: Inspect the current contents of a set during application logic or debugging.

useCases.title: Materialize a set
useCases.scenario: Load all participants, tags, or identifiers represented by a set when the collection is suitably small.

useCases.title: Support set-based workflows
useCases.scenario: Compare a set's full contents with another collection after retrieving its members.

interview.question: What does SMEMBERS return, and what is its complexity?
interview.answer: SMEMBERS returns all members held by the set at a key. Its time complexity is O(N), where N is the set cardinality.
interview.followUp: How would you read a very large set incrementally? Use SSCAN, which iterates through set members in batches instead of retrieving the entire collection at once.

interview.question: What argument does SMEMBERS require, and what does the reply look like?
interview.answer: The command takes one required argument: the key containing the set. The result is an array in RESP2 and a set in RESP3.
interview.followUp: Does SMEMBERS sort its output? No; set membership has no ordering guarantee, so consumers should not depend on result order.

interview.question: When was SMEMBERS introduced and what kind of operation is it?
interview.answer: SMEMBERS is a read-only set command that returns every member stored at the supplied key. It has been available since Redis Open Source 1.0.0.
interview.followUp: What happens if the key contains a non-set value? Redis reports a wrong-type error rather than treating the value as a set.

keyPoints: Use SMEMBERS to retrieve the complete membership of a Redis set.
Its sole argument is the key whose value is the target set.
The command has existed since Redis Open Source 1.0.0.
Redis classifies SMEMBERS as a read operation for set data and marks it as slow.
gotchas: SMEMBERS does not impose ordering; treat the result as a set rather than relying on element positions.
Retrieving a large set can be expensive because the command processes every member.

SMISMEMBER.summary: SMISMEMBER checks whether multiple values belong to a Redis set. It returns one result per value, in the same order as the input.
SMISMEMBER.explanation: SMISMEMBER checks several values against the set stored at a key. It returns one result for each value, in the same order as the input. A result is 1 when the value is in the set and 0 when it is absent or the key does not exist.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key that holds the set.

parameters.name: member [member ...]
parameters.description: One or more set members to check.

SMISMEMBER.returns: An array containing one 1 or 0 result for each requested member, in input order.

example.title: Check several set members
example.code:
SADD myset "one"
SMISMEMBER myset "one" "notamember"
example.explanation: Adds one member, then checks two members. Redis returns 1 for "one" and 0 for "notamember".

useCases.title: Batch membership checks
useCases.scenario: Check several permissions, tags, or identifiers against one set in a single command.

useCases.title: Ordered lookup results
useCases.scenario: Keep returned results aligned with the submitted values for later processing.

interview.question: What does SMISMEMBER do?
interview.answer: SMISMEMBER checks multiple values in one command. It returns an array with one result per value, in request order.
interview.followUp: How does it behave when the key is missing? It returns 0 for each checked value.

interview.question: What arguments does SMISMEMBER require?
interview.answer: The first argument is the key holding the set. It must be followed by one or more members to check.
interview.followUp: What happens if no member is supplied? The command does not match its required syntax, which requires at least one member.

interview.question: What is the time complexity?
interview.answer: Its time complexity is O(N), where N is the number of members checked. It is intended for checking several members together.
interview.followUp: How can a client use the results safely? Match each returned value with the input member at the same position.

keyPoints: Use SMISMEMBER to test several values against one Redis set.
Each requested member gets its own membership result.
The result positions follow the order of the input members.
The command requires at least one member argument.
The work grows with the number of members checked.
SMISMEMBER was added in Redis Open Source 6.2.0.
gotchas: A missing key produces 0 for every checked member.

Sorted Set.summary: Redis sorted sets store unique string members with scores. Redis orders members by score, and uses lexicographical order when scores are equal.
Sorted Set.explanation: A sorted set stores unique string members with floating-point scores. Redis orders members by score; members with equal scores are ordered lexicographically. Commands can add, update, remove, count, rank, and read members by score or position.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The key that identifies the sorted set.

parameters.name: score
parameters.description: A floating-point value used to order a member.

parameters.name: member
parameters.description: A unique string stored in the sorted set.

parameters.name: range
parameters.description: For range commands, a score or rank boundary and optional range options.

Sorted Set.returns: Commands return results based on their operation: members, scores, ranks, counts, or status. ZADD and other write commands can create or update the sorted set.

example.title: Create and read a leaderboard
example.code:
ZADD leaderboard 1250 alice
ZADD leaderboard 980 bob
ZRANGE leaderboard 0 -1 REV WITHSCORES
example.explanation: This adds two members and then returns them from the highest score to the lowest.

useCases.title: Leaderboards
useCases.scenario: Keep players ordered by score and retrieve their positions.

useCases.title: Sliding-window rate limiting
useCases.scenario: Store request timestamps and query a moving time range.

useCases.title: Lexicographical indexing
useCases.scenario: Use equal scores and member ordering for string-range queries.

interview.question: What is a Redis sorted set?
interview.answer: A sorted set contains unique string members. Each member has a floating-point score, and Redis orders members by score, then lexicographically when scores match.
interview.followUp: How would you read members between two scores? Use ZRANGE with BYSCORE, or the score-range commands documented for sorted sets.

interview.question: How do you build a leaderboard?
interview.answer: Use ZADD to add members or change their scores. Use ZRANK for ascending position and ZREVRANK for descending position.
interview.followUp: What is the cost of ranking a member? ZRANK and ZREVRANK are O(log(N)).

interview.question: How can scores change over time?
interview.answer: Use ZINCRBY when a member's score should increase by a numeric amount. It updates the member's score and is listed as O(log(N)).
interview.followUp: How can you remove the lowest-scoring entries? Use ZPOPMIN or a score-based removal command, depending on whether you need the removed values.

keyPoints: Members are unique strings, and every member has a score that controls its order.
Sorted sets fit leaderboards because they keep members ordered by score.
A sorted set can represent request times for a sliding-window rate limiter.
ZADD inserts members and also changes scores for members that already exist.
ZCARD gives the total number of members.
ZSCORE reads one member's current score.
gotchas: Equal scores do not create an arbitrary order. Redis uses the member strings to break ties.
Pop commands remove members. If the operation removes the final member, Redis removes the key too.

SPOP.summary: SPOP removes and returns one or more random members from a Redis set. It can remove one member or up to a requested count.
SPOP.explanation: SPOP chooses random members from the set stored at key, returns them, and removes them in the same operation. Without count it removes one member; with count it removes up to that many, based on the set size. If the last member is removed, Redis deletes the set key.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key that holds the set.

parameters.name: count
parameters.description: The number of members to pop. If omitted, one member is popped.

SPOP.returns: Without count, the removed member as a bulk string reply. With count, an array of removed members. A missing key returns a nil reply.

example.title: Remove random set members
example.code:
SADD colors red green blue
SPOP colors 2
SMEMBERS colors
example.explanation: Adds three members, removes up to two random members, then shows the members left.

useCases.title: Consume a random item
useCases.scenario: Take one available item from a set and remove it so another worker does not take the same item later.

useCases.title: Draw a batch
useCases.scenario: Remove several members from a set in one command when the set is used as a temporary pool.

useCases.title: Process random tasks
useCases.scenario: Use a set as a pool of tasks and discard tasks as they are selected.

interview.question: What does SPOP do?
interview.answer: SPOP removes and returns random members from a set. Its syntax is SPOP key [count], and without count it returns one removed member.
interview.followUp: How does SPOP differ from SRANDMEMBER? SRANDMEMBER returns random members without removing them, while SPOP removes them.

interview.question: What does the count argument control?
interview.answer: With count, SPOP returns up to count members. The actual number can be smaller when the set contains fewer members.
interview.followUp: What happens when count is larger than the set size? Redis returns all available members and removes them; the set then becomes empty.

interview.question: What is the time complexity of SPOP?
interview.answer: A call without count has O(1) time complexity. With count, the complexity is O(N), where N is the supplied count.
interview.followUp: What should guide the choice of count? Use a count that fits the expected work because larger counts require more command work.

keyPoints: SPOP returns random set members and removes them.
Redis deletes the key when the operation removes the set's final member.
If count is omitted, exactly one member is requested.
With count, the result contains no more members than count or the set can provide.
The operation is O(1) without count and O(N) when count is supplied.
A missing key produces a nil reply.
gotchas: Do not use SPOP when your application needs a guaranteed uniform distribution of selected members.

SRANDMEMBER.summary: Returns one or more random members from a Redis set without removing them. A positive count gives distinct members; a negative count can give repeats.
SRANDMEMBER.explanation: SRANDMEMBER reads random members from the set stored at a key. Without a count, it returns one member; with a positive count, it returns different members, while a negative count allows repeated members.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The set key to read.

parameters.name: count
parameters.description: Optional integer controlling how many members to return. Positive values request distinct members; negative values allow repeats.
