SRANDMEMBER.returns: Without count, one random member or a null reply if the key does not exist. With count, an array of members, or an empty array if the key does not exist.

example.title: Read random set members
example.code:
SADD colors red green blue
SRANDMEMBER colors
SRANDMEMBER colors 2
SRANDMEMBER colors -4
example.explanation: The first command adds members. The next command gets one random member, then two different members, then four members where repeats are allowed.

useCases.title: Choose one random member
useCases.scenario: Pick one random item for a sample, recommendation, or test.

useCases.title: Select distinct members
useCases.scenario: Read a random group while ensuring each selected member is different.

useCases.title: Allow repeated choices
useCases.scenario: Generate a fixed number of random choices where the same member may appear more than once.

interview.question: What does SRANDMEMBER do?
interview.answer: SRANDMEMBER returns random members without changing the set. With no count it returns one member; with a positive count it returns distinct members.
interview.followUp: How does a negative count change the result? It allows repeated members, and the result length is the count's absolute value.

interview.question: How does the count argument affect the result?
interview.answer: A positive count requests distinct members. Redis returns at most the set's cardinality, so the result length is the smaller of count and the number of set members.
interview.followUp: What happens when the key is missing? A counted call returns an empty array, while an uncounted call returns null.

interview.question: What is the time complexity?
interview.answer: Without count, the operation takes O(1). With count, it takes O(N), where N is the absolute value of count.
interview.followUp: Does the command remove selected members? No. It only reads them; use SPOP when members should be removed.

keyPoints: Use it to read one or more random members from a Redis set.
A positive count returns an array without duplicate members.
The result cannot contain more distinct members than the set contains.
Without count, the reply is a single randomly selected member.
The optional count form was added in Redis 2.6.0.
The no-count form is constant time; counted calls scale with the absolute count.
gotchas: A negative count allows duplicates. The number of returned members is the absolute value of the count.
With a count, a missing key produces an empty array. Without a count, a missing key produces a null reply.

SREM.summary: SREM removes one or more members from a Redis set. It reports how many existing members it removed and deletes the key when the set becomes empty.
SREM.explanation: SREM removes the listed members from the set at the given key. Missing members do not cause an error, and removing the final member deletes the set.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The key that stores the set.

parameters.name: member [member ...]
parameters.description: One or more set members to remove.

SREM.returns: An integer containing the number of members removed. Members that were not present are excluded from the count.

example.title: Remove a set member
example.code:
SADD users alice bob
SREM users alice
SMEMBERS users
example.explanation: This adds two members, removes one, and then lists the remaining member.

useCases.title: Update membership
useCases.scenario: Remove a user from a group, role, or feature set without changing other members.

useCases.title: Remove several values
useCases.scenario: Process a cleanup list in one command when several known values should leave a set.

useCases.title: Idempotent cleanup
useCases.scenario: Attempt removal safely when a value may already be absent.

interview.question: What does SREM do, and what does it return?
interview.answer: SREM removes one or more members from a set. It returns the number of members that it actually removed, so absent members are not counted.
interview.followUp: What happens if the key does not exist? Redis treats it as an empty set and returns zero.

interview.question: What is the syntax of SREM?
interview.answer: The syntax is `SREM key member [member ...]`. The key identifies the set, and at least one member must be supplied.
interview.followUp: Can one command remove several members? Yes. Redis accepts multiple member arguments.

interview.question: What are SREM's time complexity and deletion behavior?
interview.answer: SREM has time complexity O(N), where N is the number of members supplied for removal. If the last member is removed, Redis deletes the set.
interview.followUp: What if the key stores a string instead? Redis returns an error because the value is not a set.

keyPoints: The command accepts one or more members in a single call.
The integer reply counts only members that were present and removed.
When the final member is removed, Redis removes the set key.
The work grows with the number of members requested for removal.
Support for multiple member arguments was added in Redis 2.4.0.
gotchas: The command fails if the key contains another Redis data type.
A missing key behaves like an empty set, so the command returns zero.
Members that are absent are skipped and do not reduce the returned count.

SSCAN.summary: SCAN iterates over key names in the selected Redis database. Call it repeatedly with the returned cursor until the cursor is 0.
SSCAN.explanation: SCAN uses a cursor to read the current database in small parts. Start with cursor 0, pass the returned cursor to the next call, and stop when the cursor is 0 again. MATCH filters names, COUNT gives a size hint, and TYPE filters by data type.

parameters.name: cursor
parameters.description: The cursor position. Use 0 to start, then use the cursor from the previous reply.

parameters.name: pattern
parameters.description: Optional glob-style pattern used to filter key names.

parameters.name: count
parameters.description: Optional hint for the number of keys returned in one call. The default is 10.

parameters.name: type
parameters.description: Optional Redis data type filter, such as string, list, or set.

SSCAN.returns: A two-element reply: the next cursor as an unsigned 64-bit number, followed by an array of keys.

example.title: Scan matching keys
example.explanation: This loop scans all database keys that match user:* and stops when Redis returns cursor 0.

useCases.title: Filter keys by name
useCases.scenario: Find keys with a known naming pattern without requesting the whole database at once.

useCases.title: Incremental key processing
useCases.scenario: Process a large database in smaller batches.

useCases.title: Type-based inspection
useCases.scenario: Find keys belonging to one Redis data type.

interview.question: How do you complete a full SCAN iteration?
interview.answer: SCAN is a cursor-based iterator for keys in the selected database. Begin with cursor 0 and keep calling it with the returned cursor until Redis returns 0.
interview.followUp: How do you handle duplicate keys? Make the operation safe to repeat, or track processed keys when the operation is not idempotent.

interview.question: What do MATCH and COUNT do?
interview.answer: MATCH applies a glob-style pattern to returned key names. COUNT is only a hint about how many keys Redis should return in one call; its default is 10.
interview.followUp: Does COUNT guarantee the exact number of results? No. The server may return fewer or more, and the client must continue until the cursor is 0.

interview.question: What is the time complexity of SCAN?
interview.answer: Each call has O(1) time complexity. A complete iteration is O(N), where N is the number of elements in the collection, including all calls needed to return the cursor to 0.
interview.followUp: Why is SCAN preferred over KEYS for large databases? It returns small batches incrementally, avoiding one long blocking operation.

keyPoints: SCAN reads key names from the currently selected Redis database.
Use the returned cursor as the input to the next call.
MATCH can restrict results to names that fit a glob-style pattern.
COUNT suggests a batch size but does not define an exact result count.
TYPE can limit results to a Redis type such as string, list, or set.
Keys that remain present throughout a full iteration are guaranteed to be returned.
gotchas: The same key can appear more than once. Code that processes results should tolerate duplicates.
Keys added or removed while scanning have no fixed result. A changing database can produce incomplete or extra results.
SCAN is non-blocking in small calls, but it does not provide a fixed snapshot of the database.

Stream.summary: Redis Streams provide an append-only event log. Producers use XADD, consumer groups use XREADGROUP, consumers use XACK, and XAUTOCLAIM recovers idle pending entries.
Stream.explanation: A Redis Stream is an append-only log. Producers add field-value entries with XADD. Consumer groups read entries with XREADGROUP. Each group has its own cursor, and each consumer has a pending-entry list. After processing, the consumer uses XACK. XAUTOCLAIM can move idle pending entries to a healthy consumer.
Stream.syntax:
XADD key [MAXLEN ~ count] * field value [field value ...]
XREADGROUP GROUP group consumer STREAMS key >
XACK key group id [id ...]
XAUTOCLAIM key group consumer min-idle-time start [COUNT count]
XRANGE key start end [COUNT count]

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The stream key that stores the entries.

parameters.name: field-value pairs
parameters.description: A field and value pair stored in the entry.

parameters.name: group
parameters.description: The consumer group that reads the stream.

parameters.name: consumer
parameters.description: The consumer name within the group.

parameters.name: ids
parameters.description: The entry IDs to acknowledge.

Stream.returns: XADD returns the new entry ID. XREADGROUP returns entries for a consumer. XACK returns the number of acknowledged entries. XAUTOCLAIM returns claimed entries, deleted IDs, and a continuation ID. XRANGE returns entries in an ID range.

example.title: Add an event
example.code: XADD orders * type order.placed customer alice
example.explanation: This adds one entry to the orders stream. Redis creates the entry ID.

useCases.title: Event distribution
useCases.scenario: Send order or notification events to several independent applications.

useCases.title: Worker scaling
useCases.scenario: Split work among several workers in one consumer group.

useCases.title: History replay
useCases.scenario: Read old entries for audit, repair, or replay.

useCases.title: Crash recovery
useCases.scenario: Recover entries left pending after a worker crash.

interview.question: Which commands form the basic producer and consumer flow?
interview.answer: XADD appends field-value data to the stream and can create an ID automatically. XREADGROUP reads entries for a consumer group. XACK removes processed entries from that consumer's pending list.
interview.followUp: How would you recover a crashed consumer? Read its pending entries with an explicit ID such as 0-0, or let another consumer use XAUTOCLAIM after the idle threshold.

interview.question: How do consumer groups distribute and isolate work?
interview.answer: A consumer group has one last-delivered ID. Each consumer also has a pending-entry list for messages delivered but not acknowledged. Consumers in one group split new work, while different groups each receive the stream independently.
interview.followUp: How can two applications process every event? Create two separate consumer groups; each group keeps its own cursor and pending entries.

interview.question: How does XAUTOCLAIM recover stuck messages?
interview.answer: XAUTOCLAIM scans a group's pending entries and transfers entries idle for at least the configured time to a named consumer. It returns a continuation ID, so a full sweep can use repeated calls until the cursor returns to 0-0.
interview.followUp: What should happen when the result contains DeletedIds? Log them and send them to a dead-letter store because retention already removed their payloads.

keyPoints: A stream stores ordered entries. Each entry has fields and values, and Redis can generate its ID.
Call XACK after successful processing so Redis removes the entry from the consumer's pending list.
Separate groups can read the same stream independently. Their progress does not share one cursor.
Adding consumers to one group lets Redis distribute new entries among them.
Use XRANGE to inspect or replay historical entries without changing a group's cursor.
A generated ID contains milliseconds and a sequence number. IDs increase within one stream.
gotchas: Approximate MAXLEN can leave more entries than the requested limit. Use it as a retention guardrail, not as an exact size limit.
A slow consumer can lose the payload if retention trims it before recovery. XAUTOCLAIM reports such IDs as deleted entries, which cannot be retried.

String.summary: Redis strings store byte sequences as values. They are useful for simple key-value data, caching, counters, and bit operations.
String.explanation: Redis strings store byte sequences. A value can contain text, serialized data, or binary data. Use strings for simple key-value storage, caching, counters, and bit operations. SET creates or replaces a value, while GET reads it.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The key whose string value is read or written.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The bytes to store as the value.

String.returns: SET returns a success result. GET returns the string value, or no value when the key is missing.

example.title: Store and read a string
example.code:
SET bike:1 Deimos
GET bike:1
example.explanation: This stores the string "Deimos" under "bike:1" and then reads it.

useCases.title: Caching
useCases.scenario: Store and retrieve a cached page or other small value.

useCases.title: Counters
useCases.scenario: Keep a numeric value that changes by increments or decrements.

useCases.title: Serialized or binary data
useCases.scenario: Store serialized objects or binary arrays under a key.

interview.question: What is a Redis string?
interview.answer: Redis strings store byte sequences as values. Common uses include caching, simple key-value data, counters, and bit operations.
interview.followUp: How can you update a numeric string atomically? Use INCR, INCRBY, or INCRBYFLOAT; a missing key starts at zero.

interview.question: How do SET and GET work?
interview.answer: SET writes one string value and GET reads it. Both operations have O(1) time complexity in the documented basic case.
interview.followUp: How do you handle several keys? Use MSET and MGET; their complexity is O(N), where N is the number of keys.

interview.question: How can a string write be conditional?
interview.answer: Use SET with NX to write only when a key does not exist, or XX to write only when it already exists. These conditions make the write conditional.
interview.followUp: How can a write also set a lifetime? Use an expiration option with SET, or use SETEX or PSETEX for a value with an expiration.

keyPoints: A Redis string is the basic value type and represents a sequence of bytes.
Strings are useful for caching and can also support counters.
SET creates a missing key and writes its string value.
GET reads the string value stored at a key.
MGET reads several string keys in one atomic operation.
INCR adds one to an integer string and treats a missing key as zero.
gotchas: A string is bytes, not only human-readable text. You can store serialized or binary data too.
Plain SET can replace an existing value. Use SETNX, or SET with NX, when replacement must not happen.

STRLEN.summary: Returns the length of the string value stored at a key. Missing keys return 0, while keys holding non-string values cause an error.
STRLEN.explanation: STRLEN reads the string stored at a key and returns its length as an integer. If the key is absent, it returns 0; if the key contains another Redis data type, the command returns an error.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key containing the string to measure.

STRLEN.returns: Integer reply: the length of the string stored at key, or 0 when the key does not exist.

example.title: Measure a Redis string
example.code:
redis-cli SET mykey "Hello world"
redis-cli STRLEN mykey
# (integer) 11
redis-cli STRLEN missing-key
# (integer) 0
example.explanation: Stores a string, measures its length, then demonstrates the zero result for an absent key.

useCases.title: Check string size
useCases.scenario: Validate or inspect stored text before processing it.

useCases.title: Inspect key contents
useCases.scenario: Distinguish an empty string from a missing key when combined with existence checks.

useCases.title: Operational diagnostics
useCases.scenario: Measure a Redis string in scripts, monitoring commands, or command-line workflows.

interview.question: What does STRLEN return for an existing string and for a missing key?
interview.answer: STRLEN takes one key and returns an integer reply containing the length of the string stored there. A missing key produces 0.
interview.followUp: What happens if the key stores a list? Redis returns an error because STRLEN only accepts string values.

interview.question: What is the time complexity of STRLEN?
interview.answer: Its documented complexity is O(1), so retrieving the length does not require scanning the string contents.
interview.followUp: How would you measure a JSON string instead? Use JSON.STRLEN with a key and optional path.

interview.question: What is the command signature and required argument?
interview.answer: The command syntax is `STRLEN key`. The required argument is the name of the key whose string value should be measured.
interview.followUp: What related command appends data while working with a string key? APPEND adds a value and creates the key if it does not exist.

keyPoints: STRLEN reports the character/byte length of the string value associated with the supplied key.
The result is an integer, and an absent key is represented by zero rather than an error.
Its only required argument is the key name.
For the documented `Hello world` example, STRLEN returns 11.
gotchas: The key must contain a Redis string; using STRLEN on another data type produces an error.

SUBSCRIBE.summary: Subscribes the client to one or more exact channel names. Redis then pushes matching published messages and subscription confirmations through that connection.
SUBSCRIBE.explanation: SUBSCRIBE registers the current client for one or more exact channel names. After the client enters subscribed mode, Redis pushes matching published messages over the connection and sends a subscription confirmation for each channel; with RESP2, only a limited set of commands remains available until the client leaves that mode.

parameters.name: channel [channel ...]
parameters.description: One or more exact channel names to which the client should subscribe.

SUBSCRIBE.returns: On success, Redis does not return a conventional value. Instead, it pushes one subscription confirmation message for each requested channel, with `subscribe` as the first element.

example.title: Subscribe to an exact channel
example.code: SUBSCRIBE cache:events
example.explanation: Run this command in redis-cli to enter Pub/Sub mode and listen for messages published to the exact channel `cache:events`. The client remains waiting for pushed messages until it unsubscribes or exits.

useCases.title: Exact-topic event delivery
useCases.scenario: A service needs real-time notifications for a known topic such as `orders:created`.

useCases.title: Multiple channel subscriptions
useCases.scenario: Several known application topics should share one subscriber connection.

useCases.title: Interactive Pub/Sub monitoring
useCases.scenario: A lightweight client needs to observe live channel traffic during development or operations.

interview.question: What does SUBSCRIBE do?
interview.answer: SUBSCRIBE takes one or more channel names and switches the connection into subscribed mode. Redis pushes a confirmation for each subscription, followed by messages published to those channels.
interview.followUp: How would you subscribe to a family of channels? Use PSUBSCRIBE with a pattern, because SUBSCRIBE matches only the explicitly named channels.

interview.question: What is the time complexity of SUBSCRIBE?
interview.answer: The command's complexity is O(N), where N is the number of channels being subscribed to. Each specified channel contributes to the subscription operation.
interview.followUp: What is the practical implication of subscribing to many channels? The command processes each channel, so the work grows linearly with the number supplied.

interview.question: Which commands are allowed after entering subscribed state?
interview.answer: A RESP2 client in subscribed state is restricted to subscription-management commands and a few connection commands such as PING and QUIT. A RESP3 client can issue any commands while remaining subscribed.
interview.followUp: How can a RESP2 client return to normal command use? It must unsubscribe from its channels and leave subscribed mode.

keyPoints: The command creates exact-match subscriptions for every channel named in the request.
At least one channel is required, and multiple channels can be supplied in the same command.
Redis sends one subscription-confirmation push message per channel after successful registration.
Published messages are delivered to every client subscribed to the corresponding channel.
The operation scales linearly with the number of channels in the request.
The command has been available since Redis Open Source 2.0.0.
gotchas: In RESP2 subscribed mode, do not send ordinary commands; use the permitted subscription, unsubscription, PING, RESET, or QUIT commands. RESP3 permits any commands while subscribed.
SUBSCRIBE provides exact channel matching, not pattern matching; use PSUBSCRIBE when a glob-style channel pattern is required.

SUNION.summary: SUNION returns all distinct members found across two or more Redis sets. It reads the input sets and does not store the result.
SUNION.explanation: SUNION reads two or more Redis sets and returns one result containing every distinct member from them. It does not save the result to a key; use SUNIONSTORE when you need a stored set.

parameters.name: key [key ...]
parameters.description: The first set key and any additional set keys to combine.

SUNION.returns: The members in the union of all supplied sets. RESP2 returns an array; RESP3 returns a set.

example.title: Combine two sets
example.code:
SADD key1 a b c
SADD key2 c d e
SUNION key1 key2
example.explanation: This creates two sets, then returns every distinct member found in either set.

useCases.title: Merge set memberships
useCases.scenario: Combine membership lists from several sets, such as users in different groups.

useCases.title: Build a combined view
useCases.scenario: Create a temporary combined result for an application to read.

useCases.title: Read unique values
useCases.scenario: Check all unique values across multiple collections without changing them.

interview.question: What does SUNION do?
interview.answer: SUNION returns the distinct members present in at least one of the supplied sets. It accepts one or more set keys and does not modify those sets.
interview.followUp: How would you keep the result? Use SUNIONSTORE, which writes the union into a destination key.

interview.question: What arguments does SUNION take?
interview.answer: The command syntax is SUNION key [key ...]. The first key is required, and additional set keys are optional but at least one key must be supplied.
interview.followUp: What should happen if one supplied key is missing? Redis treats that key as an empty set.

interview.question: What are its complexity and return formats?
interview.answer: Its time complexity is O(N), where N is the total number of elements in all input sets. RESP2 returns an array, while RESP3 returns a set.
interview.followUp: How does SUNION differ from a count-only operation? SUNIONCARD returns the cardinality of the union instead of the union members.

keyPoints: The result contains each member that appears in any input set.
Pass at least one key, followed by any additional set keys.
The work grows with the total number of members across all supplied sets.
SUNION has been available since Redis Open Source 1.0.0.
gotchas: A missing key acts like an empty set, so it does not cause an error or add a value.
When using Redis Cluster, check multi-key operation rules because the command can behave differently across clustered keys.

TOUCH.summary: TOUCH updates the last-access time of each supplied key that exists and returns how many supplied keys were found. It does not alter key values.
TOUCH.explanation: TOUCH updates the last-access time for each named key that exists, without changing its value. It returns how many supplied keys were found and touched; the operation costs O(N), where N is the number of keys listed.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: One or more key names whose access times should be updated when the keys exist.

TOUCH.returns: Integer reply: the number of supplied keys that exist after their last-access times are updated.

example.title: Touch an active session key
example.code:
SET session:42 active
TOUCH session:42 missing:key
example.explanation: Refreshes the access time for the existing session key; the command returns 1 because only one of the two keys exists.

useCases.title: Cache access tracking
useCases.scenario: Refresh recency for cached entries while leaving their values unchanged.

useCases.title: Batch existence measurement
useCases.scenario: Touch several potentially present keys and use the count to measure partial existence.

useCases.title: Eviction-aware workflows
useCases.scenario: Keep selected keys active for LRU/LFU-oriented access accounting.

interview.question: What does Redis TOUCH do, and what does it return?
interview.answer: TOUCH refreshes the last-access time of every supplied key that exists and returns the count of those existing keys. It does not modify the stored values.
interview.followUp: What is its complexity? O(N), where N is the number of keys supplied for touching.

interview.question: What is the syntax and result semantics of TOUCH?
interview.answer: The command accepts one or more key names using the syntax TOUCH key [key ...]. The integer result is the number of supplied keys that exist.
interview.followUp: How would a caller detect partial success? Compare the returned count with the number of keys sent.

interview.question: What is the complexity of TOUCH?
interview.answer: TOUCH has linear complexity in the number of keys it processes: O(N). This matters when a request contains many key names.
interview.followUp: What design response follows from that complexity? Keep batches appropriately sized when access-time refreshes are performed at scale.

keyPoints: For each existing key, Redis refreshes its last-access timestamp.
The command requires at least one key and supports a variable-length key list.
The integer reply reports how many supplied names currently exist.
Processing cost grows linearly with the number of keys in the request.
gotchas: The result counts existing keys only, so nonexistent names contribute zero.
Large key lists increase work linearly; avoid treating TOUCH as a constant-time operation.

TTL.summary: Returns a key's remaining expiration time in seconds. It distinguishes missing keys from existing keys that have no expiration.
TTL.explanation: TTL inspects a key's expiration and returns the number of seconds until Redis removes it. It returns special negative values when the key is missing or exists without an expiration, allowing clients to distinguish those states.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The key whose remaining expiration time should be inspected.

TTL.returns: An integer number of seconds remaining; -1 if the key exists without an expiration; -2 if the key does not exist.

example.title: Check a key's remaining lifetime
example.code:
SET session:123 active EX 60
TTL session:123
example.explanation: Stores a key with a 60-second expiration, then reports its remaining lifetime in seconds.

useCases.title: Cache lifetime monitoring
useCases.scenario: Inspect how long a cached value can remain before Redis removes it.

useCases.title: Session and token expiry checks
useCases.scenario: Check whether a session or token key is nearing expiration.

useCases.title: Key-state diagnostics
useCases.scenario: Identify whether a key is absent, persistent, or configured to expire.

interview.question: What does TTL do?
interview.answer: TTL returns the remaining time to live for a key in seconds. It is an introspection command, so it checks expiration without changing the key.
interview.followUp: How would you obtain finer resolution? Use PTTL, which reports the corresponding expiration information in milliseconds.

interview.question: What do TTL's negative return values mean?
interview.answer: TTL returns -2 when the key does not exist and -1 when the key exists but has no expiration. A nonnegative result is the remaining lifetime in seconds.
interview.followUp: How can a key acquire an expiration? Set one with EXPIRE, or write it using an expiration option such as SET with EX.

interview.question: When should TTL be preferred over PTTL?
interview.answer: Use TTL when second-level precision is sufficient for checking cache or session lifetime. For millisecond resolution, use PTTL instead.
interview.followUp: What should a client do when TTL returns -2? Treat the value as absent and avoid assuming that an expiration is merely near.

keyPoints: TTL reports the remaining lifetime only for a key with a configured timeout.
The command lets clients inspect the lifetime in seconds without retrieving the stored value.
The result estimates how long the key remains part of Redis's dataset.
Use PTTL when the application needs the same check at millisecond resolution.
gotchas: A missing key produces -2, not a normal zero-second lifetime.
A persistent key produces -1, so do not interpret it as imminent expiration.

TYPE.summary: TYPE reports the Redis data type stored at a key. It returns none when the key does not exist.
TYPE.explanation: TYPE examines the value associated with one key and returns its Redis data-type name. If the key is absent, it returns none; otherwise the documented result can identify strings, lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes, streams, or vector sets.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The name of the key whose value type should be returned.

TYPE.returns: Simple string reply: the type of key, or none when key does not exist.

example.title: Inspect Redis value types
example.code:
redis-cli <<'EOF'
SET profile:name Ada
HSET profile:stats visits 3
TYPE profile:name
TYPE profile:stats
TYPE profile:missing
EOF
example.explanation: Creates a string and a hash, then reports each stored value's Redis type or none for the absent key.

useCases.title: Validate a data structure
useCases.scenario: Inspect a key before issuing type-specific commands.

useCases.title: Debug key contents
useCases.scenario: Diagnose unexpected values in a shared keyspace.

useCases.title: Check cache state
useCases.scenario: Distinguish missing cache entries from populated entries.

interview.question: What does TYPE return for a missing key?
interview.answer: TYPE takes one key and returns a simple string naming the stored value's type. If the key does not exist, the result is none.
interview.followUp: How would you distinguish an absent key from a key holding a string? Check whether TYPE returns none; string indicates an existing string value.

interview.question: What is the syntax and required argument?
interview.answer: The command syntax is TYPE key. The required key argument is the name of the key whose value should be inspected.
interview.followUp: What should be done when the key name is dynamic? Pass the key as a properly encoded command argument and interpret the returned type string.

interview.question: Which Redis types can TYPE report?
interview.answer: TYPE can report string, list, set, zset, hash, stream, or vectorset. It is useful before selecting commands that operate on a particular Redis data structure.
interview.followUp: Why must command selection still be validated after inspection? The key's type can change between separate commands, so atomic or error-handling strategies may be needed.

keyPoints: TYPE converts the stored value's data structure into a type-name string.
Recognized results include string, list, set, and sorted set values.
The command also recognizes hashes, streams, and vector sets.
Its required input is the key name to inspect.
The response is a simple string containing the type, or none when the key is missing.
gotchas: An absent key produces none rather than an error, so callers should handle that result separately from a stored type.

UNLINK.summary: UNLINK asynchronously deletes one or more Redis keys. It removes keys from the keyspace promptly while reclaiming their memory in a background thread.
UNLINK.explanation: UNLINK removes the specified keys from Redis's keyspace immediately, while memory reclamation runs asynchronously in another thread. It accepts one or more keys, ignores keys that do not exist, and returns how many keys were unlinked.

parameters.name: key [key ...]
parameters.description: One or more keys to delete asynchronously.

UNLINK.returns: Integer reply: the number of keys that were unlinked.

example.title: Asynchronously remove keys
example.code:
SET key1 "Hello"
SET key2 "World"
UNLINK key1 key2 key3
example.explanation: Creates two keys, then asynchronously unlinks them; the missing third key is ignored.

useCases.title: Delete large cache entries
useCases.scenario: Removing large cached values without synchronously blocking Redis's main thread.

useCases.title: Best-effort multi-key cleanup
useCases.scenario: Deleting several known keys while tolerating keys that may already be absent.

useCases.title: Cluster-aware cleanup
useCases.scenario: Performing non-blocking key removal in a clustered deployment after checking multi-key constraints.

interview.question: Why use UNLINK instead of DEL for large values?
interview.answer: UNLINK removes one or more keys without making memory reclamation block the main Redis thread. It unlinks each key from the keyspace and performs the heavier reclamation work asynchronously.
interview.followUp: How does its complexity compare with DEL? UNLINK is O(1) per removed key regardless of value size in the command path, followed by O(N) reclamation work in another thread.

interview.question: What does UNLINK return?
interview.answer: The command accepts one or more keys using the form UNLINK key [key ...]. Missing keys are ignored, and the integer reply reports how many keys were actually unlinked.
interview.followUp: What does a reply of 2 mean for three supplied keys? Exactly two supplied keys existed and were unlinked; the third was absent or otherwise not counted.

interview.question: What cluster consideration applies to multi-key UNLINK?
interview.answer: UNLINK can remove multiple keys in one command, but clustered Redis environments impose multi-key behavior constraints. Keys may need to satisfy the cluster's requirements for multi-key operations.
interview.followUp: What should be checked before issuing a multi-key UNLINK in a cluster? Review Redis's multi-key operation rules and ensure the selected keys are valid for the target cluster topology.

keyPoints: The unlinking operation is O(1) per key, independent of the size of the value stored there.
Memory reclamation is proportional to the deleted object's allocations and is handled by another thread.
Supplying a nonexistent key does not produce an error or increase the returned count.
The keyspace no longer exposes the unlinked keys after the command processes them.
The required argument is a variadic list containing at least one key.
gotchas: In clustered Redis, multi-key behavior has cluster-specific constraints; consult the multi-key operations rules when the keys may be distributed across shards.
A successful reply means the keys were unlinked from the keyspace, not that all associated memory has already been reclaimed.

UNSUBSCRIBE.summary: UNSUBSCRIBE stops a Redis client from listening to channel messages. Give channel names to remove selected subscriptions, or give none to remove all of them.
UNSUBSCRIBE.explanation: A subscribed Redis client can send UNSUBSCRIBE with one or more channel names. If it sends no names, Redis removes every channel subscription. Redis sends one unsubscribe confirmation message for each channel removed.

parameters.name: channel
parameters.description: One or more channel names. Omit this argument to unsubscribe from all channels.

UNSUBSCRIBE.returns: No ordinary value is returned. Redis pushes one confirmation message for each unsubscribed channel; its first element is `unsubscribe`.

example.title: Remove channel subscriptions
example.code:
import redis

r = redis.Redis(decode_responses=True)
p = r.pubsub()
p.subscribe("news", "alerts")

# Stop listening to one channel.
p.unsubscribe("news")

# Stop listening to every remaining channel.
p.unsubscribe()
example.explanation: This Python example subscribes to two channels, removes one subscription, then removes all remaining channel subscriptions.

useCases.title: Leave one channel
useCases.scenario: A client no longer needs updates from one topic.

useCases.title: Leave all channels
useCases.scenario: A client is shutting down its subscription work.

useCases.title: Replace channel subscriptions
useCases.scenario: A client changes which topics it receives.

interview.question: What does UNSUBSCRIBE do?
interview.answer: UNSUBSCRIBE stops a client from receiving messages published to selected channels. It accepts one or more channel names.
interview.followUp: What happens with no channel names? Redis removes all channel subscriptions and sends one confirmation for each removed channel.

interview.question: What is the syntax and complexity?
interview.answer: The syntax is `UNSUBSCRIBE [channel [channel ...]]`. The channel argument is optional and can be repeated.
interview.followUp: What is the cost for several channels? The time complexity is O(N), where N is the number of channels being removed.

interview.question: How does Redis report success?
interview.answer: The command has no ordinary return value in either RESP2 or RESP3. Instead, Redis pushes one confirmation message per unsubscribed channel.
interview.followUp: How can a client verify completion? It should consume and inspect each pushed message, whose first element is `unsubscribe`.

keyPoints: Use UNSUBSCRIBE to stop receiving published messages from channels.
You can name one channel or several channels in one command.
Leaving out the channel list removes every channel subscription.
The command takes time proportional to the number of channels removed.
Redis pushes a separate confirmation for every channel that is removed.
The command has been available since Redis Open Source 2.0.0.
gotchas: Do not expect a normal command return value. Read the pushed confirmation message for each channel.
The confirmation message starts with the word "unsubscribe" and is sent separately for every channel.

UNWATCH.summary: UNWATCH clears all keys watched for a Redis transaction. It takes no arguments and returns OK.
UNWATCH.explanation: UNWATCH removes every key previously watched for the current transaction. Use it when the client should stop checking those keys before the transaction runs. After EXEC or DISCARD, Redis already clears the watched keys, so an extra UNWATCH is not needed.

example.title: Clear watched keys
example.code: UNWATCH
example.explanation: This clears the keys watched by the current transaction context. Redis returns OK.

useCases.title: Stop watching transaction keys
useCases.scenario: Cancel optimistic checks

useCases.title: Clear watched keys
useCases.scenario: Reset transaction watch state before continuing

interview.question: What does UNWATCH do?
interview.answer: UNWATCH clears all keys watched for a transaction. It takes no key arguments and has O(1) time complexity.
interview.followUp: When is an explicit UNWATCH unnecessary? It is unnecessary after EXEC or DISCARD because those commands clear the watched keys.

interview.question: What does UNWATCH return?
interview.answer: The command syntax is simply UNWATCH. Redis returns the simple string reply OK in both RESP2 and RESP3.
interview.followUp: Does UNWATCH return the watched keys? No. Its documented reply is only OK.

interview.question: How fast is UNWATCH, and when was it added?
interview.answer: UNWATCH belongs to Redis transactions and is in the @fast and @transaction ACL categories. It has been available since Redis Open Source 2.2.0.
interview.followUp: What is its complexity? It is O(1), as documented for the command.

keyPoints: It clears every key currently watched by the transaction.
The documentation does not provide a client-library method signature.
The command has constant time complexity.
Its ACL categories are @fast and @transaction.
Redis added this command in Redis Open Source 2.2.0.
A successful call returns OK.
gotchas: Do not call UNWATCH after EXEC or DISCARD just to clear the watched keys; Redis handles that automatically.

WATCH.summary: WATCH monitors keys for changes before a Redis transaction runs. If a watched key changes before EXEC, Redis aborts the transaction.
WATCH.explanation: WATCH marks one or more keys for a conditional transaction. Redis checks them when EXEC runs. If any watched key changed after WATCH and before EXEC, Redis aborts the whole transaction and returns a null reply. EXEC then clears the watched keys.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: A key to monitor. Add more keys by separating them with spaces.

example.title: Conditional update
example.code:
WATCH balance
current = GET balance
MULTI
SET balance updated_value
EXEC
example.explanation: Watch the key, read its value, then queue the update in a transaction. If another client changes the key before EXEC, retry the operation.

useCases.title: Check-and-set updates
useCases.scenario: Update a value based on its current value without overwriting a concurrent update.

useCases.title: Optimistic locking
useCases.scenario: Remove or change an item only if its related key stayed unchanged.

useCases.title: Custom atomic operations
useCases.scenario: Build an atomic operation from reads and writes when no single Redis command provides it.

interview.question: What does WATCH do?
interview.answer: WATCH provides optimistic locking for a Redis transaction. If a watched key changes before EXEC, Redis aborts the complete transaction and EXEC returns a null reply.
interview.followUp: How should an application handle this result? Retry the read, calculation, and transaction, usually with a retry limit or backoff.

interview.question: What is the syntax and return value?
interview.answer: The syntax is WATCH key [key ...]. It accepts one or more keys and returns a simple string OK reply in RESP2 and RESP3.
interview.followUp: Can a client add keys later? Yes. WATCH can be called multiple times, and each call adds keys watched from that call until EXEC.

interview.question: How is WATCH used for an atomic conditional update?
interview.answer: WATCH is used with GET, MULTI, commands queued in the transaction, and EXEC to implement a check-and-set update. The client reads after WATCH, queues the write, and checks whether EXEC succeeds.
interview.followUp: What can clear the watched state without executing? UNWATCH clears all watched keys, and closing the connection also clears them.

keyPoints: Use WATCH before a transaction when its writes depend on values read from keys.
A change to any watched key makes the entire transaction fail.
WATCH is optimistic locking: it detects conflicts instead of blocking other clients.
One WATCH command can monitor multiple keys.
Multiple WATCH calls add to the set of keys being monitored.
Use UNWATCH with no arguments to stop watching all currently watched keys.
gotchas: Behavior can differ in a Redis cluster. Check the rules for multi-key operations.
Commands queued inside the transaction do not themselves cause the watch to fail before EXEC.
EXEC removes all watched keys whether the transaction succeeds or is aborted.

XACK.summary: XACK removes processed messages from a stream consumer group's Pending Entries List. It returns how many message IDs were successfully acknowledged.
XACK.explanation: XACK removes message IDs from a stream consumer group's Pending Entries List. Use it after a consumer finishes processing messages delivered through the group. Removing the entry prevents it from being returned as pending and also frees the related pending-entry memory.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The stream key.

parameters.name: group
parameters.description: The consumer group name.

parameters.name: id [id ...]
parameters.description: One or more message IDs to acknowledge.

XACK.returns: An integer showing how many supplied message IDs were successfully acknowledged. IDs that are no longer in the Pending Entries List are not counted.

example.title: Acknowledge a stream message
example.code: XACK mystream mygroup 1526569495631-0
example.explanation: Acknowledge one message in the consumer group.

useCases.title: Confirm processed messages
useCases.scenario: A consumer finishes handling a message read through a consumer group and confirms completion.

useCases.title: Acknowledge a batch
useCases.scenario: A consumer handles several stream entries and sends their IDs together.

useCases.title: Confirm claimed messages
useCases.scenario: A consumer has taken ownership of a pending message and later finishes it.

interview.question: What does XACK do?
interview.answer: XACK confirms that a consumer group has processed one or more stream messages. It removes those messages from the group's Pending Entries List.
interview.followUp: What happens if an ID is already acknowledged? The command does not count it in the returned total.

interview.question: What arguments does XACK require?
interview.answer: The command takes the stream key, the consumer group name, and one or more message IDs. Its syntax is XACK key group id [id ...].
interview.followUp: How can you acknowledge several messages efficiently? Pass all their IDs in one XACK command.

interview.question: What does XACK return, and how does it scale?
interview.answer: XACK returns the number of message IDs that were successfully removed from the Pending Entries List. Its time complexity is O(1) for each message ID processed.
interview.followUp: Does the result equal the number of IDs supplied? Not always, because IDs missing from the Pending Entries List are excluded.

keyPoints: It can acknowledge one message or several messages in one command.
Messages normally enter the pending list when a consumer group reads them with XREADGROUP.
A message can also become pending after another consumer takes ownership with XCLAIM.
Call XACK after successful processing, not before the work is complete.
Acknowledging a message also removes its pending-list entry and releases its related server memory.
Processing cost is constant for each message ID supplied.
gotchas: Only IDs that are still in the group's Pending Entries List count as acknowledged. An ID already acknowledged is not counted again.

XADD.summary: XADD appends a field-value entry to a Redis stream. It can create the stream, generate an entry ID, and optionally trim old entries.
XADD.explanation: XADD appends one entry to a Redis stream. It creates the stream key when needed, unless NOMKSTREAM is used. The entry contains one or more field-value pairs and receives an automatic ID when you use *.
XADD.syntax: XADD key [NOMKSTREAM] [KEEPREF | DELREF | ACKED] [IDMPAUTO producer-id | IDMP producer-id idempotent-id] [<MAXLEN | MINID> [= | ~] threshold [LIMIT count]] <* | id> field value [field value ...]

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The stream key to update.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: * for an automatic ID, or a valid milliseconds-sequence ID.

parameters.name: field value
parameters.description: One or more field-value pairs for the entry.

parameters.name: NOMKSTREAM
parameters.description: Prevents creating a missing stream.

parameters.name: MAXLEN | MINID
parameters.description: Trims by maximum length or minimum ID; supports =, ~, and LIMIT.

parameters.name: IDMPAUTO | IDMP
parameters.description: Identifies the producer and idempotent message, available in Redis 8.6.

XADD.returns: The ID of the newly added stream entry. With idempotent options, a duplicate can return the original entry's ID.

example.title: Add and read a stream entry
example.code:
XADD mystream * name Sara surname OConnor
XLEN mystream
XRANGE mystream - +
example.explanation: Adds one entry with an automatic ID, then checks the stream length and reads all entries.

useCases.title: Append stream events
useCases.scenario: Store ordered events, logs, or messages in a Redis stream.

useCases.title: Bound stream retention
useCases.scenario: Keep a stream near a target size while adding entries.

useCases.title: Idempotent production
useCases.scenario: Avoid duplicate entries from repeated producer requests.

useCases.title: Assign entry IDs
useCases.scenario: Use explicit IDs when the application controls stream ordering.

interview.question: What does XADD do?
interview.answer: XADD appends a field-value entry to a stream and returns its entry ID. With *, Redis generates the ID; with a supplied ID, the ID must use the milliseconds-sequence form.
interview.followUp: How can you stop XADD from creating a missing stream? Use NOMKSTREAM.

interview.question: What is NOMKSTREAM for?
interview.answer: NOMKSTREAM prevents creation when the key does not exist. Without it, XADD creates the stream as a side effect.
interview.followUp: What happens when NOMKSTREAM targets a missing key? No new stream is created, so the append does not occur.

interview.question: How does XADD trimming work?
interview.answer: MAXLEN limits by stream length, while MINID removes entries below an ID threshold. The ~ form allows approximate trimming, and LIMIT restricts how many entries Redis examines during trimming.
interview.followUp: When is exact trimming useful? Use = when the stream must meet the exact trimming threshold; approximate trimming is cheaper when a soft limit is enough.

keyPoints: XADD is the command used to append data to a stream.
A missing stream key is created automatically unless NOMKSTREAM is present.
Use * when Redis should generate the entry ID.
You can also provide an ID in milliseconds-sequence form, such as 1526919030474-55.
Field and value order is preserved when the entry is stored and read.
Redis 8.6 adds IDMPAUTO and IDMP for preventing duplicate entries.
gotchas: The command needs at least one field and value.
Adding is constant time, but trimming can take time proportional to the number of removed entries.
IDMPAUTO and IDMP require an automatically generated entry ID.

XGROUP.summary: XGROUP contains Redis stream consumer-group management commands. Use its subcommands to create and manage groups and their consumers.
XGROUP.explanation: XGROUP is a container for commands that manage consumer groups for Redis streams. Use its subcommands to create, change, inspect, or remove groups and consumers.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The stream key.

parameters.name: group
parameters.description: The consumer group's name.

parameters.name: id | $
parameters.description: The last delivered entry ID from which the group starts, or $ for the stream's last entry.

parameters.name: MKSTREAM
parameters.description: Create the stream if it does not exist.

parameters.name: ENTRIESREAD entries-read
parameters.description: Initial entries-read counter used for lag calculation.

XGROUP.returns: XGROUP CREATE returns the simple string OK when successful. Other XGROUP subcommands have subcommand-specific results.

example.title: Create a group
example.code: XGROUP CREATE mystream mygroup 0 MKSTREAM
example.explanation: Creates the group and creates an empty stream if it does not exist.

useCases.title: Create a consumer group
useCases.scenario: Set up workers that share stream work.

useCases.title: Read from the beginning
useCases.scenario: Start processing all entries already in a stream.

useCases.title: Start at the stream end
useCases.scenario: Start a group only for new entries.

useCases.title: Create a missing stream
useCases.scenario: Create a group before any stream entries exist.

interview.question: What is XGROUP used for?
interview.answer: XGROUP is a container command for managing stream consumer groups. The available operations include creating, deleting, and changing groups, plus managing consumers.
interview.followUp: How can you see the available operations? Run XGROUP HELP.

interview.question: How does XGROUP CREATE choose the starting position?
interview.answer: XGROUP CREATE creates a group for a stream. Its ID sets the last entry delivered from the new group's point of view; 0 lets consumers read from the beginning, while $ starts at the current end.
interview.followUp: How can creation also create a missing stream? Add MKSTREAM after the ID.

interview.question: What are XGROUP's version and complexity details?
interview.answer: The command's complexity depends on the subcommand. XGROUP itself is available starting with Redis Open Source 5.0.0 and belongs to the @slow ACL category.
interview.followUp: Which subcommand has constant complexity? XGROUP CREATE is O(1).

keyPoints: Use XGROUP as the parent command for stream consumer-group management.
Run XGROUP HELP to list the supported XGROUP operations.
XGROUP CREATE makes a named group for a stream.
A stream cannot have two consumer groups with the same name.
Use ID 0 when the new group should begin with the stream's existing entries.
Add MKSTREAM to create an empty stream when the target stream does not exist.
gotchas: A group name must be unique within its stream. Creating the same group again returns a BUSYGROUP error.
XGROUP CREATE fails when the stream is missing unless you add MKSTREAM.
Using $ starts the group at the current end, so existing entries are not delivered to the group.

XLEN.summary: Returns the number of entries in a Redis stream. A missing key returns zero, so check the key separately if you must distinguish a missing stream from an empty one.
XLEN.explanation: `XLEN` reads the number of entries in the stream stored at `key`. It returns zero when the key is missing. The operation takes constant time, and it does not remove or change the stream.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The key of the stream to count.

XLEN.returns: An integer equal to the number of entries in the stream at the key.

example.title: Count stream entries
example.code:
XADD mystream * item 1
XADD mystream * item 2
XLEN mystream
example.explanation: Adds two entries to `mystream`, then returns `2`.

useCases.title: Monitor stream size
useCases.scenario: Check how many records a stream currently contains.

useCases.title: Inspect stream changes
useCases.scenario: Verify the result of adding or deleting stream entries.

useCases.title: Read-only stream check
useCases.scenario: Read stream size without modifying its contents.

interview.question: What does XLEN do, and what is its complexity?
interview.answer: `XLEN key` returns the number of entries in the stream at `key`. It returns an integer reply and has O(1) time complexity.
interview.followUp: How can you distinguish a missing key from an empty stream? Check the key with `EXISTS` or `TYPE`, because both cases can make `XLEN` return zero.

interview.question: What argument does XLEN require?
interview.answer: The command accepts one required argument: the stream key. For example, `XLEN mystream` counts entries in `mystream`.
interview.followUp: What should happen if the key does not exist? Redis returns zero, treating the missing stream as empty for this command.

interview.question: Can a stream have zero entries and still exist?
interview.answer: `XLEN` counts entries currently in the stream. A stream can remain after its entries are removed, for example after `XDEL`, because it may have consumer groups.
interview.followUp: Why might an empty stream still be useful? Its associated consumer groups may still exist and need the stream key.

keyPoints: Use `XLEN` to count the entries in a Redis stream.
A missing stream key produces the integer result `0`.
The command takes one required argument: the stream key.
The command runs in constant time, O(1), regardless of stream length.
Redis Open Source added `XLEN` in version 5.0.0.
The command belongs to the `@read`, `@stream`, and `@fast` ACL categories.
gotchas: A result of zero does not prove that the key is missing. An existing stream can have no entries, so use `TYPE` or `EXISTS` when that distinction matters.
Deleting all entries does not necessarily delete the stream key. Consumer groups can keep an empty stream present.

XRANGE.summary: XRANGE returns stream entries whose IDs are within a specified range. You can limit the result count and use inclusive or exclusive boundaries.
XRANGE.explanation: XRANGE reads stream entries whose IDs fall between start and end. The range includes both limits unless an ID starts with (. Use - and + for the smallest and largest possible IDs. COUNT limits how many entries Redis returns.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The stream key to read.

parameters.name: start
parameters.description: The inclusive lower ID boundary. Use - for the smallest ID. Prefix with ( for an exclusive boundary.

parameters.name: end
parameters.description: The inclusive upper ID boundary. Use + for the greatest ID. Prefix with ( for an exclusive boundary.

parameters.name: count
parameters.description: Optional maximum number of entries to return.

XRANGE.returns: An array of stream entries whose IDs match the requested range. Each entry contains its ID and field-value data.

example.title: Read two stream entries
example.code: XRANGE writers - + COUNT 2
example.explanation: Returns the first two entries in the writers stream.

useCases.title: Query a time range
useCases.scenario: Read a time window from a stream by using complete or millisecond-only IDs.

useCases.title: Page through a stream
useCases.scenario: Fetch a fixed number of entries, then continue from the last ID with an exclusive start.

useCases.title: Fetch one entry
useCases.scenario: Pass the same entry ID as both boundaries.

interview.question: What does XRANGE do?
interview.answer: XRANGE returns stream entries between two IDs, in increasing ID order. The interval includes both endpoints unless an endpoint is exclusive.
interview.followUp: How would you read the next page without repeating the last entry? Use the last returned ID as the next start ID and prefix it with (.

interview.question: What is COUNT used for?
interview.answer: COUNT sets the maximum number of entries in the reply. With a fixed count, the documented complexity can be treated as O(1); otherwise it is O(N), where N is the number returned.
interview.followUp: How can COUNT help find the first matching entry? Set COUNT to 1 and choose a suitable start ID.

interview.question: How do you fetch one stream entry?
interview.answer: To fetch one known entry, pass its ID as both start and end. Redis then returns that entry if it exists.
interview.followUp: How can you fetch all entries from one millisecond? Use that millisecond as both endpoints, so Redis covers sequence numbers from 0 through the maximum.

keyPoints: XRANGE reads messages from one stream over an ID interval.
Use - as the start to begin at the stream's first possible ID, and + as the end to read through the last possible ID.
COUNT limits the number of entries in the result.
Exclusive starts let you page through a stream without returning the previous page's final entry again.
Read one entry by using its ID for both the start and end values.
The work grows with the number of entries returned. A fixed COUNT can make the operation effectively constant time.
gotchas: Both start and end are included by default. Prefix an ID with ( to exclude that boundary.
A partial ID uses its millisecond timestamp. Redis fills the start sequence with 0 and the end sequence with the maximum value.

XREAD.summary: XREAD reads newer entries from one or more Redis streams. It can return available entries immediately or wait for new entries with BLOCK.
XREAD.explanation: XREAD reads entries from one or more streams when their IDs are greater than the IDs you provide. Without BLOCK, it returns available entries at once. With BLOCK, it waits for new entries or returns a null result after the timeout.
XREAD.syntax: XREAD [COUNT count] [MAXCOUNT maxcount] [MAXSIZE maxsize] [BLOCK milliseconds] STREAMS key [key ...] id [id ...]

parameters.name: COUNT count
parameters.description: Maximum entries returned for each stream.

parameters.name: BLOCK milliseconds
parameters.description: Maximum time to wait for entries, in milliseconds. Zero waits indefinitely.

parameters.name: STREAMS key [key ...] id [id ...]
parameters.description: One or more stream keys, followed by one ID for each key. Entries newer than each ID are returned.

XREAD.returns: A list of streams and their matching entries. If BLOCK times out without new data, or no stream can be served, the result is null.

example.title: Read stream entries
example.code: XREAD COUNT 2 STREAMS orders 0-0
example.explanation: Reads up to two entries from the orders stream, starting after ID 0-0.

useCases.title: Batch stream consumption
useCases.scenario: Read a stream in batches by saving the last returned ID and using it on the next call.

useCases.title: Blocking event reads
useCases.scenario: Wait for new entries from one or more streams without frequent polling.

useCases.title: Read only new entries
useCases.scenario: Start with $ to receive entries added after the consumer begins waiting.

interview.question: How does XREAD select stream entries?
interview.answer: XREAD returns entries whose IDs are greater than the ID supplied for each stream. It can read several streams in one command, and COUNT limits entries separately for each stream.
interview.followUp: How can a client avoid polling? Use BLOCK with a millisecond timeout. Redis wakes the command when a requested stream receives new data.

interview.question: How does blocking work?
interview.answer: Use BLOCK followed by milliseconds. A value of 0 waits without a time limit; a timeout with no new data produces a null reply.
interview.followUp: What happens if data already exists when BLOCK is used? Redis returns the available data immediately instead of waiting.

interview.question: How are multiple streams and IDs paired?
interview.answer: The IDs after STREAMS are matched by position with the stream keys before them. The command returns entries newer than each matching ID.
interview.followUp: Why can a multi-stream read return many entries? COUNT applies per stream, so several streams can return up to the per-stream limit each.

keyPoints: XREAD can read from several streams and returns only entries newer than each supplied ID.
COUNT limits the number of returned entries independently for every stream.
BLOCK uses milliseconds for its timeout. BLOCK 0 waits indefinitely when no matching entries exist.
The special + ID selects the latest available entry for a stream.
The time cost is O(M) for each stream, where M is the number of entries returned from that stream.
gotchas: STREAMS must be the last option. Put all stream keys first, then provide one matching ID for each key.
Use $ only on the first call when you want new entries. Later calls must use the last returned ID, or entries can be missed.
The + ID returns only the last entry for that stream, so COUNT does not change that stream's result.

XREADGROUP.summary: XREADGROUP reads stream messages for a consumer in a consumer group. It can wait for new messages, track pending work, and optionally claim idle messages.
XREADGROUP.explanation: XREADGROUP reads messages for a named consumer in a Redis stream consumer group. With the `>` ID, it reads messages not delivered to another consumer; another ID reads this consumer's pending messages. Read messages stay pending until XACK removes them, unless NOACK is used.
XREADGROUP.syntax: XREADGROUP GROUP group consumer [COUNT count] [MAXCOUNT maxcount] [MAXSIZE maxsize] [BLOCK milliseconds] [CLAIM min-idle-time] [NOACK] STREAMS key [key ...] id [id ...]

parameters.name: group consumer
parameters.description: The consumer group and consumer name used for the read.

parameters.name: COUNT count
parameters.description: Maximum entries returned for each stream.

parameters.name: MAXCOUNT maxcount
parameters.description: Maximum total entries across all listed streams.

parameters.name: BLOCK milliseconds
parameters.description: Maximum wait time in milliseconds. Zero waits indefinitely.

parameters.name: CLAIM min-idle-time
parameters.description: Minimum idle time, in milliseconds, for messages to claim.

parameters.name: NOACK
parameters.description: Do not add read messages to the pending entries list.

parameters.name: STREAMS key [key ...] id [id ...]
parameters.description: Stream keys followed by one ID for each key. Use `>` for new messages.

XREADGROUP.returns: An array in RESP2 or a map in RESP3 containing each stream name and its entries. A nil or null reply means a BLOCK timeout or that no stream can be served.

example.title: Read new stream messages
example.code: XREADGROUP GROUP orders worker-1 COUNT 10 BLOCK 2000 STREAMS orders >
example.explanation: Reads up to 10 new messages for worker-1. It waits up to 2 seconds when no message is ready.

useCases.title: Distribute stream work across workers
useCases.scenario: Several workers should split work from one Redis stream.

useCases.title: Recover pending messages
useCases.scenario: A worker must retry messages left unfinished after a crash.

useCases.title: Claim idle messages
useCases.scenario: A failed consumer leaves messages idle in the group.

interview.question: Why use XREADGROUP instead of XREAD?
interview.answer: XREADGROUP reads stream entries as one consumer in a consumer group. The group distributes messages among its consumers instead of sending every message to every client.
interview.followUp: How does a consumer recover after a crash? Read pending entries with ID `0`, process them, and use XACK. After the pending list is empty, switch back to `>` for new entries.

interview.question: What do `>` and `0` mean in STREAMS?
interview.answer: With `>` and no CLAIM, Redis returns messages that have not been delivered to another consumer. Redis records them in the group's pending entries list, and XACK removes them after successful processing.
interview.followUp: What does an ID such as `0` do? It returns pending entries for the consumer with IDs greater than the supplied ID; it does not read new entries.

interview.question: How do COUNT and BLOCK affect XREADGROUP?
interview.answer: COUNT limits the number of entries returned per stream. BLOCK waits for new entries for the given number of milliseconds; `0` waits forever.
interview.followUp: What is the cost? For each stream it is O(M), where M is the number of returned entries; blocked readers also make XADD serve all blocked clients.

keyPoints: The command reads either new messages or this consumer's earlier pending messages.
Create the consumer group with XGROUP before using XREADGROUP.
A consumer name is created automatically when Redis first sees it.
Acknowledge successfully processed messages with XACK so Redis removes them from the pending list.
Use `>` to request only messages that were never delivered to another consumer.
COUNT sets a separate maximum for each stream in the command.
CLAIM can take idle pending messages from another consumer when their idle time reaches the given threshold.
gotchas: Use an ID other than `>` to read this consumer's pending messages. In that mode, BLOCK, NOACK, and CLAIM are ignored.
NOACK skips the pending entries list. Use it only when losing an unread or unacknowledged message is acceptable.
Give each client a unique consumer name inside the group.

XTRIM.summary: XTRIM removes older entries from a Redis stream. It can limit the stream by length with MAXLEN or by entry ID with MINID.
XTRIM.explanation: XTRIM removes older entries from the start of a stream. MAXLEN keeps the stream at or below a length threshold, while MINID removes entries with IDs below a threshold. Exact trimming is the default; ~ can make trimming faster but may leave extra entries.
XTRIM.syntax: XTRIM key <MAXLEN | MINID> [= | ~] threshold [LIMIT count] [KEEPREF | DELREF | ACKED]

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The stream key to trim.

parameters.name: strategy
parameters.description: MAXLEN limits stream length. MINID removes entries below an ID.

parameters.name: threshold
parameters.description: A non-negative entry count for MAXLEN, or a stream ID for MINID.

parameters.name: operator
parameters.description: Optional exact (=) or approximate (~) trimming operator.

parameters.name: count
parameters.description: Optional maximum number of entries to examine during trimming.

parameters.name: reference policy
parameters.description: Optional reference policy: KEEPREF, DELREF, or ACKED.

XTRIM.returns: An integer containing the number of entries deleted from the stream.

example.title: Trim a stream approximately
example.code:
XADD mystream * field value
XTRIM mystream MAXLEN ~ 1000 LIMIT 100
example.explanation: Adds an entry, then removes older entries while keeping the stream near 1,000 entries. The LIMIT option caps the number of entries removed in this operation.

useCases.title: Limit stream length
useCases.scenario: Keep a stream near a fixed size for bounded storage.

useCases.title: Remove old history by ID
useCases.scenario: Remove entries older than a chosen stream ID.

useCases.title: Use efficient approximate trimming
useCases.scenario: Reduce trimming work when a small size difference is acceptable.

interview.question: What does XTRIM do, and what are its two trimming strategies?
interview.answer: XTRIM removes old stream entries. MAXLEN uses the stream length as its threshold, and MINID removes entries with IDs below a stream ID. MAXLEN is available from Redis 5.0, while MINID was added in Redis 6.2.
interview.followUp: How does approximate trimming differ from exact trimming? The ~ option can stop early when Redis can save work, so the result may contain slightly more entries.

interview.question: What is the difference between exact and approximate trimming?
interview.answer: Exact trimming is the default and uses = when written explicitly. With MAXLEN, the final length is limited to the threshold; with MINID, entries below the threshold ID are removed.
interview.followUp: When would you choose ~ instead? Use it when small size variation is acceptable and lower trimming overhead matters.

interview.question: What does the LIMIT option control?
interview.answer: LIMIT restricts how many entries Redis examines or evicts during trimming. It was added in Redis 6.2. If omitted, Redis uses a default based on the number of entries in a macro node.
interview.followUp: What does LIMIT 0 do? It disables the limiting mechanism, allowing the command to process without that cap.

keyPoints: XTRIM removes entries from the oldest side of a stream.
MAXLEN keeps no more than the requested number of entries after exact trimming.
MINID uses a stream ID boundary and removes entries below it.
Use = or omit the operator when the result must follow the threshold exactly.
Use ~ when faster trimming matters more than an exact boundary.
The command returns the number of stream entries it removed.
gotchas: The ~ option does not guarantee the exact threshold. The stream can keep some extra entries.
LIMIT 0 removes the cap on the trimming work.
ACKED can leave entries that at least one consumer group has not acknowledged.

ZADD.summary: Adds members with scores to a sorted set, updating existing members and creating the key when needed. Options can restrict updates, count changed entries, or increment one member's score.
ZADD.explanation: ZADD adds score-member pairs to the sorted set at key. A missing key is created; an existing member is repositioned when its score changes. Options can restrict updates, count changed entries, or return the new score while incrementing one member.
ZADD.syntax: ZADD key [NX | XX] [GT | LT] [CH] [INCR] score member [score member ...]

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Name of the key that holds the sorted set.

parameters.name: score member [score member ...]
parameters.description: One or more score-member pairs; each score is a double-precision floating-point number.

parameters.name: NX
parameters.description: Add only new members.

parameters.name: XX
parameters.description: Update only existing members.

parameters.name: CH
parameters.description: Count changed members, including score updates.

parameters.name: INCR
parameters.description: Increment one member's score instead of setting it.

parameters.name: GT
parameters.description: Update only when the new score is greater.

parameters.name: LT
parameters.description: Update only when the new score is less.

ZADD.returns: Integer reply: newly added members by default, or newly added and updated members with CH. With INCR, returns the updated score as a double. A null reply is returned when a conditional NX, XX, GT, or LT operation is aborted.

example.title: Add and conditionally update leaderboard scores
example.code:
redis-cli ZADD leaderboard 100 alice 125 bob
redis-cli ZADD leaderboard GT 130 alice
redis-cli ZRANGE leaderboard 0 -1 REV WITHSCORES
example.explanation: Adds two members, raises Alice's score only when the new score is greater, then lists the leaderboard from highest to lowest score.

useCases.title: Leaderboards
useCases.scenario: Maintain a ranking that changes as players or entities receive scores.

useCases.title: Priority ordering
useCases.scenario: Store items ordered by numeric priority for range and rank queries.

useCases.title: Score increments
useCases.scenario: Atomically update a single member's score while retrieving its new value.

interview.question: What does ZADD do?
interview.answer: ZADD inserts members into a sorted set and associates each with a double-precision score. If a member already exists, its score is updated and the member is placed according to the resulting order; a nonexistent key is created.
interview.followUp: How does ZADD behave when the key has another type? It returns an error because the key must hold a sorted set.

interview.question: How do CH and INCR affect the reply?
interview.answer: Without CH, the integer reply counts only newly added members. With CH, it counts both newly added and updated members.
interview.followUp: What does INCR return? It returns the member's updated score as a double, or a null reply when the conditional operation is not performed.

interview.question: What are the conditional ZADD options?
interview.answer: NX permits only new members, while XX permits updates only for existing members. GT and LT constrain updates to cases where the new score is respectively greater or less than the current score.
interview.followUp: Can GT and LT be used together? No; the mutually exclusive option pairs must not be combined, and INCR permits only one score-member pair.

keyPoints: ZADD supports one or many score-member pairs in a single command.
A missing key becomes a new sorted set containing the supplied members.
Changing an existing member's score also restores its sorted-set position.
Scores use double-precision floating-point representations, including the documented infinity values.
The default integer result reports how many members were newly inserted.
CH changes counting to include score updates as well as insertions.
gotchas: The target key must contain a sorted set; ZADD fails with a wrong-type error for other Redis data types.
INCR mode accepts exactly one score-member pair, unlike ordinary ZADD calls that can update multiple pairs.
When a conditional option prevents the operation, the reply is null rather than an integer count.

ZCARD.summary: ZCARD returns the number of members in a sorted set. It returns 0 when the key does not exist.
ZCARD.explanation: ZCARD reads the sorted set stored at the given key and returns how many members it contains. It does not change the set, and it returns 0 when the key is missing.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The key that stores the sorted set.

ZCARD.returns: An integer containing the number of members in the sorted set, or 0 when the key does not exist.

example.title: Count sorted-set members
example.code:
ZADD leaderboard 100 alice
ZADD leaderboard 250 bob
ZCARD leaderboard
example.explanation: Adds two members to a sorted set, then returns 2, the number of members.

useCases.title: Count leaderboard entries
useCases.scenario: Check how many entries a leaderboard or ranking set contains.

useCases.title: Check for an empty set
useCases.scenario: Verify whether a sorted set has any members before processing it.

useCases.title: Read set size
useCases.scenario: Measure the current size of a sorted-set index in constant time.

interview.question: What does ZCARD return, and how fast is it?
interview.answer: ZCARD returns the number of members in a sorted set. Its time complexity is O(1), so the count is available in constant time.
interview.followUp: How would you count only members within a score range? Use ZCOUNT, which is listed as a related sorted-set command and supports score-range counting.

interview.question: What argument does ZCARD require?
interview.answer: The command takes one argument: the key containing the sorted set. Its syntax is ZCARD key.
interview.followUp: What should the application do if the key contains another Redis data type? Handle the command error rather than treating it as a count; this page documents ZCARD for sorted sets.

interview.question: Can ZCARD modify the sorted set?
interview.answer: ZCARD is a read-only sorted-set command. It belongs to the @read, @sortedset, and @fast ACL categories.
interview.followUp: Which command can add members before counting them? ZADD adds members with scores, after which ZCARD can return the set size.

keyPoints: ZCARD reports the sorted set's cardinality, meaning its member count.
Pass the key that stores the sorted set as the command's only argument.
The command runs in constant time.
Redis has provided this command since Open Source version 1.2.0
The command is classified as read-only, sorted-set, and fast for ACL purposes.
The result is an integer representing the number of members.
gotchas: A missing key is not an error. The result is 0.

ZCOUNT.summary: ZCOUNT counts members in a sorted set whose scores are within a given range. The range can include or exclude either endpoint.
